0.title: Romans
0.overview:
Martin Luther called the letter to the Romans "the chief part of the New Testament and the very purest gospel." John Calvin wrote that "when anyone understands this Epistle, he has a passage opened to him to the understanding of the whole Scripture." Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached 366 sermons on it over fourteen years and still felt he had not exhausted it. Romans is not one letter among many; it is the theological heart of the New Testament, the fullest and most systematic exposition of the gospel that God ever moved a human pen to write.

Paul wrote to a church he had never visited, in the capital of the empire, at the height of his apostolic ministry — probably from Corinth around AD 57. His purpose was not merely to introduce himself before a planned visit to Spain. It was to set before these believers, Jew and Gentile alike, the full panorama of the gospel: the universal guilt of humanity, the righteousness of God revealed in Christ, justification by faith alone, the transforming work of the Spirit, the sovereign purposes of God in election and in the mystery of Israel, and the shape of the redeemed life in the world. No letter covers more ground. No letter has changed more lives.

The structure follows the gospel's own logic. Chapters 1–3 establish the diagnosis: all humanity — pagan, moralist, and Jew — stands guilty before the righteous God, with no resources of its own to secure acquittal. Chapters 3–5 announce the remedy: the righteousness of God given freely through faith in Jesus Christ, who bore the wrath we deserved. Chapters 6–8 trace the fruit: union with Christ, death to sin, life in the Spirit, adoption as children, and the unshakeable security of those whom God has called. Chapters 9–11 address the mystery: if Israel is the covenant people, why has Israel largely rejected its Messiah? And chapters 12–16 show what the gospel-transformed life looks like in home, church, city, and empire.

We will draw on the great Reformed interpreters of this letter: Calvin's magisterial commentary, Luther whose reading of 1:17 unlocked the Reformation, Lloyd-Jones whose fourteen volumes remain the richest English-language treatment, John Stott whose Message of Romans is a model of accessible depth, Timothy Keller's Romans for You, and scholars Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner. Come expecting to be undone and remade. Romans has that effect on everyone who takes it seriously.

1.title: The Gospel and the Wrath of God
1.overview:
Romans 1 opens with one of the most carefully crafted sentences in ancient literature — a single Greek sentence spanning seven verses, in which Paul introduces himself, his gospel, and his Lord with the precision of a theologian and the ardour of a man in love with what he believes. By the time the chapter ends, the same pen that wrote of the gospel as "the power of God for salvation" has traced the terrifying arc of divine wrath against human idolatry. These two things belong together: the good news is only truly good when the bad news is truly bad.

The movement of the chapter is deliberate. Paul establishes the gospel (vv. 1–17), then demonstrates the need for it (vv. 18–32). The power of God for salvation is proportionate to the depth of human lostness — and that depth, as Paul will show, is vertiginous. The world Paul describes in vv. 18–32 is not ancient history; it is every human culture that has suppressed the knowledge of the God it cannot stop knowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Paul, the Gospel, and the Grace of Apostleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's opening sentence is a controlled explosion of theology. In seven verses he identifies himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God — a gospel promised in the Old Testament Scriptures, concerning God's Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power by the resurrection from the dead. Every phrase is a chapter of theology waiting to be unfolded. This is not a man warming up; this is a man who knows exactly what he believes and why it matters.

The word that unlocks everything is euangelion — gospel. It meant, in the first-century Roman world, the proclamation of good news, typically the accession of a new emperor or a great military victory. Paul seizes the word and repurposes it entirely. The great news is not that Caesar has triumphed; it is that Jesus Christ, Son of God, Lord, has been raised from the dead and now reigns over all things. This is a message with empire-shaking implications — which is precisely why Paul is eager to preach it in Rome itself.

The address of grace and peace — "to all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints" — is not a formality. It is a theological declaration. These people, in the capital of pagan power, are loved by God. They are called. They are saints — not by virtue of their moral achievement but by virtue of their union with Jesus Christ who is holy, and who has made them holy in Him. Before Paul preaches a word of gospel to them, he speaks a word of gospel over them. This is the Pauline method: ground identity before applying imperatives.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Pauline Gospel

One of the most important features of Romans 1:1–4 is Paul's insistence that the gospel he preaches was "promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures." The gospel is not a Pauline invention or a Gentile innovation — it is the fulfilment of Israel's own scriptures. Jesus is the descendant of David (2 Samuel 7), declared Son of God by resurrection (Psalm 2). Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. Any reading of the Old Testament that does not find Christ there has missed its point.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's designation of himself as a doulos — slave — of Christ Jesus was shocking in a world where slavery was degradation. He inverts the social order: the highest dignity available to a human being is not freedom but bondage to Jesus Christ. Now: In an age that prizes autonomy above all things, the Christian claim that the best possible life is one of radical submission to Christ still provokes the same offence — and still offers the same liberation to those who discover that the lordship of Christ is the only yoke that is easy and the only burden that is light.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three self-designations in one breath: slave (doulos), called apostle, set apart. The first establishes ownership — Paul belongs entirely to Christ. The second establishes commission — he did not volunteer; he was apprehended on the Damascus road. The third establishes singular purpose — as Jeremiah was set apart from the womb, Paul has been reserved for one thing: the gospel. Everything else in his life is subordinate to this central calling.

Take the first word slowly, because we have domesticated it. Most English Bibles render doulos as “servant”, and a servant is a man with a job. That is not what the word meant. A slave in the Roman world was not an employee but a possession — in law a thing, not a person. He owned nothing, because anything that came into his hands belonged to his master. He had no right to his own time, his own body, or his own plans. He could not refuse. He was often given his name by the man who bought him.

And remember where this letter is going. Rome, where something like a third of the population was enslaved, and where the church met in houses. When this letter was read aloud, there were people in the room who were slaves, and there were almost certainly people in the room who owned slaves. Into that room the greatest missionary in Christian history introduces himself — before his name is fully out of his mouth — by the legal status of the lowest people present. He is not reaching for a humble-sounding word. He is reaching for the one word in the Roman vocabulary that meant a man belongs entirely to somebody else, and using it as a title.

Yet a Jewish reader would have heard something else in it at the same instant, and Paul intends both. Servant of the LORD is one of the great titles of the Old Testament. It belongs to Moses, to Joshua, to David, to the prophets, and supremely to the mysterious Servant of Isaiah on whom everything turns. So in one word Paul takes the lowest rung on the Roman ladder and the highest title in Israel’s Scriptures, and says they are the same rung. That is not a rhetorical trick. It is the shape of the whole gospel he is about to spend sixteen chapters explaining.

Which makes an ordinary demand on the reader, and it is not about working harder. A slave’s defining condition is that he does not own his own time, and the quickest way to find out what you believe about ownership is to listen to yourself when a day is interrupted. Notice the word that arrives: my morning, my weekend, my evening — and notice the quality of the resentment when someone spends it for you. That reaction is not a small sin to be scolded over; it is simply information about who you think holds the deed. One guard, because this image has been used to injure people: Paul is describing ownership, not exhaustion. The Master in question is the one who ordered a sabbath, who told his workers to come away and rest, and who slept through a storm. A church that quotes this verse at a tired person to extract more work from them has understood neither the slave nor the Master.

Then watch the word that follows, because it does something you may not expect. Paul is called to be an apostle — and the Greek adjective he uses, klētos, turns up twice more before the sentence is over. You also are called to belong to Jesus Christ (v. 6). You are called to be saints (v. 7). Three times in seven verses, and the same word each time. Paul does not have a special vocabulary for his own vocation and an ordinary one for everybody else’s. Whatever happened to him on the Damascus road and whatever happened to you are named with the same adjective: neither of you volunteered, and neither of you was consulted.

And there is a quiet irony in the third phrase that Paul, of all men, could not have missed. He says he has been set apart for the gospel. He had spent his whole adult life set apart already — the name Pharisee most likely means precisely that, the separated ones, a movement whose entire discipline was separation from everything and everyone that might defile. Paul had been an expert in it. And God takes the separated man, keeps the verb, and reverses the preposition. He is no longer set apart from people; he is set apart for a message, and the message sends him straight to the Gentiles he had spent decades avoiding. It is the same word God used of him before he was born (Galatians 1:15) and the same word the Spirit used when the church at Antioch was told to release him (Acts 13:2). Nothing about him was wasted. It was requisitioned.

Which is worth hearing if you have ever suspected that you are not the kind of person God commissions — that other people have callings and you have a routine. The letter opens by putting the apostle and the reader under the same word. Paul’s assignment is not yours, and you should not manufacture a dramatic one. But if you belong to Christ you were called, in exactly the sense he was, and the parts of your history you consider unusable are the parts God is most practised at requisitioning.

And then the turn that Paul himself makes elsewhere, which puts the whole self-description in its place. When he wants to describe what the Son of God did in coming to us, he reaches for this same word: Christ “made himself nothing, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7) — the form of a slave. So Paul is not claiming a humility that Jesus did not stoop to. He is a slave of the one who became one. The title is not beneath him, because it was not beneath his Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel Paul preaches is not a novelty — it is the fulfillment of God’s long-standing promise, embedded in the Scriptures of Israel. Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in arrival. The Son is descended from David — the Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7) is not abandoned but fulfilled in this One.

Feel the weight of “promised beforehand”, because it answers an objection the Roman church was certainly hearing. Christianity in the first century looked like a novelty, and novelty was not a compliment in the ancient world — Rome respected age and distrusted new religions as superstition. So the charge would have been easy to make: this is a sect, barely twenty-five years old, gathered round an executed provincial. Paul’s reply is that it is nothing of the kind. The gospel is the oldest thing in the world, older than the Scriptures that promised it, and what happened outside Jerusalem was not the start of something but the keeping of something.

And notice how much is packed into the word promised, because it settles the character of God before a single doctrine is argued. A promise is only as good as the one who makes it, and the interval is the test. God said he would crush the serpent’s head in a garden, and then let four thousand years pass. He swore to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed in his offspring, and then the family went down to Egypt and was enslaved for four centuries. He told David that a son of his would have a throne for ever, and then the dynasty collapsed, the city burned, and the line dwindled to a carpenter in a village nobody respected. At every point it would have been reasonable to conclude that the promise had lapsed. And then it did not.

Which is the pastoral force of a verse that looks purely historical, and it is worth taking personally. If you are waiting on God for something he has said and it has been a long time — a prayer for a child who has walked away, a marriage you cannot see mending, a wrong you have watched go unaddressed for years — the argument of this verse is not that your wait is short. It is that God’s delays run to centuries and he has never yet failed to arrive. The promises of Genesis were kept in Bethlehem, and the people who had been waiting had long since died waiting. That is not a comfortable thought and it is not meant to be a soothing one. It is a solid one: the interval proves nothing except that we are not the ones who set the timetable.

Then the phrase that has been quietly doing work in the church ever since. The promise came “through his prophets in the holy Scriptures” — which means that when Paul preached the gospel he preached it out of a book his hearers already owned. He had no New Testament. Every sermon in Acts is an exposition of the Old. So the entry above is right that any reading of the Old Testament which does not find Christ there has missed its point — and the practical consequence for a modern reader is that the two-thirds of your Bible you find hardest is not the run-up to the gospel. It is the gospel, in promise, and Jesus said as much on a road to Emmaus when he began with Moses and all the Prophets and interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27).

Now the strange little phrase in verse 3 that most of us read straight past: the Son was descended from David according to the flesh. Paul is not being decorative. He is saying that God’s Son entered a genealogy. He had a human ancestry that could be traced, a family with a documented history — and if you have read that family’s history you know what is in it. David, who arranged a man’s death to conceal an adultery. Solomon, who ended in idolatry. Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood. The line runs through a foreign widow, a prostitute in Jericho, and a succession of kings the Bible itself calls evil. That is the family the Son of God consented to join, and he did not join it at a safe distance. He took their flesh.

And this is where the two halves of Paul’s sentence become one gospel rather than two facts. The promise required a real descendant — an actual body, in an actual bloodline, in an actual town, at a datable moment. Christianity is not a set of timeless spiritual principles that could have been discovered in any century by a sufficiently thoughtful person. It is a report about something that happened, to a particular man, in a family whose paperwork survives. Which is why it can be false — and why, if it is true, it is not merely inspiring but binding.

So the Son of God has a great-grandfather. The promise God made in a garden, renewed to a wandering herdsman and sworn to a shepherd king, came to rest at last not in a principle or a programme but in a person with an address — and the long silence between the promise and the keeping of it was never God losing interest. It was God taking the time to become one of us.

verseByVerse.quote: and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The resurrection is the divine verdict on Jesus: he who was Son of God in weakness and humiliation has been publicly declared Son of God in power by his rising. The resurrection is not merely a miracle — it is the Father’s own seal of approval on the Son’s person and work. Murray notes that ‘declared’ does not mean ‘made’ — Jesus was always the Son; the resurrection manifests and vindicates what was eternally true.

That distinction is worth defending rather than merely asserting, because this verse has been used for a very long time to argue that Jesus became the Son of God at some point — that he was a man whom God promoted, adopted at the resurrection, awarded a status he had not previously held. The answer is in the sentence itself, and it does not require Greek. Look at what Paul wrote one verse earlier. The gospel is “concerning his Son, who was descended from David” — the Son is the one who did the descending. He was already the Son before there was a genealogy to enter. A man cannot be promoted into a position he occupied before he arrived.

So what changed at the resurrection was not the Son but the public record. The word carries the sense of appointing, marking out, installing in the open — and the pattern is familiar from ordinary life, where a verdict does not create the fact it announces. A man wrongly convicted and later exonerated is not made innocent by the second trial; he was innocent throughout, and the court has finally said so. That is the resurrection. The world had reached its verdict on Jesus and published it in three languages over his head, and the grave was the establishment’s final word on the matter. Then God overturned it, and the overturning was not private.

Which is why the resurrection is never presented in the New Testament merely as a happy ending. Peter puts it as a straight contradiction: “this Jesus, whom you crucified, God has made both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). You said one thing. God has said another. And the reason this matters for the doctrine of the whole letter is that Paul will say the same thing about you a few chapters later — Christ was “raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25), and if the Father’s verdict on the Son was reversed in public then the verdict on everyone joined to him has been reversed with it. The empty tomb is God’s receipt. The debt was accepted as paid, and he said so by opening the grave.

Notice, too, the phrase in the middle that most readers step over: “according to the Spirit of holiness”. Paul has just said according to the flesh, and now he balances it. There are two spheres in view — the realm of ordinary human descent, in which Jesus is David’s descendant, and the realm of the Spirit, in which he is declared God’s Son in power. Both are true of the same person at the same time, and neither cancels the other. And the Spirit is not incidental here: the same Spirit who raised him is the one Paul will say lives in you, so that “he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:11). The power that opened that tomb has a residential address, and it is not a metaphor.

Then the two words at the end of the verse, which are the reason any of this can be sung rather than merely believed: our Lord. Paul has spent four verses on titles of enormous altitude — Son of God, descendant of David, declared in power, Spirit of holiness — and lands on a possessive pronoun. Not the Lord. Our Lord. The word kyrios was what the Greek Old Testament used to render the divine name, and it was also what the empire required people to say of Caesar; Paul is claiming both fields at once. But he does not leave it at altitude. The one who holds the name above every name is spoken of, by a slave writing to a house church in the capital, as though he belongs to them.

And here is a test worth running, because this verse quietly diagnoses what a person is actually resting on. Ask what you would say if someone told you tomorrow that they had found the body. Not whether you could refute it — whether it would matter. If your faith is mainly a set of values, a moral framework, a way of being decent and hopeful, the news would be sad but survivable; the principles would still be good ones. Paul’s faith would not survive it for an hour, and he says so plainly: if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, your faith is worthless, you are still in your sins, and we are of all people most to be pitied (1 Corinthians 15:14–19). He staked everything on an event that could in principle be disproved by a corpse.

So the resurrection is not the happy ending appended to the story of a good man. It is the Father standing up in the courtroom of the world, after the sentence has been carried out and the body sealed in a rock, and announcing that the accused was his Son the whole time.

verseByVerse.quote: ...through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations, including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ... — Romans 1:5-6
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The obedience of faith” — a phrase that brackets the entire letter (appearing again in 16:26) — is one of the most debated expressions in Romans. It means, most naturally, the obedience that consists in faith: the act of believing the gospel is itself the primary act of obedience to God. Faith is not passive; it is the most demanding act of the will, because it requires the surrender of self-reliance and the casting of oneself entirely on another.

The scope of the mission is universal: “all the nations” — all the Gentiles. Rome sits at the heart of the Gentile world. Paul is not visiting a church out of curiosity; he is a missionary with a mandate, writing to enlist the Roman church as a base for his westward advance. The letter is simultaneously theological masterwork and missionary strategy document.

Before the debated phrase, notice the pairing that carries it: “grace and apostleship”. Paul is almost certainly not listing two separate gifts. He means the grace that consisted in being made an apostle — and to feel why he puts it that way you have to remember who is writing. The man given the commission to preach is the man who had been arresting preachers. He held the coats at a stoning. He went to Damascus with letters of authority to drag Christians back in chains, and was intercepted on the road doing exactly that. He never got over it: “I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). So the commission is not a reward that followed the pardon. The commission was the pardon. God did not merely forgive the persecutor; he handed him the message and sent him to the people he had been hunting.

Now the phrase itself, and it is worth being honest that the grammar allows more than one reading. Some take it as the entry does — the obedience that consists in faith, so that believing is itself the first commanded act. Some read it as the obedience that springs from faith, the life that follows believing. Some read it as obedience to “the faith”, the body of Christian teaching. The honest answer is that Paul would probably have been puzzled by our need to choose, and the decisive evidence is where he puts the phrase: at the very beginning of the letter and again at the very end (16:26). It is a pair of bookends, and everything between them is the explanation.

Which is the point worth holding on to if you have ever been anxious about faith and works. This is the letter — the one letter above all others — which insists that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law, that the wages of work are debt and not grace, that Abraham was reckoned righteous while he was still uncircumcised. And it opens and closes by calling for obedience. Paul saw no tension whatever, and neither should you. Faith is not obedience’s substitute, and obedience is not faith’s wage. Faith is the first thing God commands and the root from which everything else he commands actually grows. Which is also why the entry above is right that faith is not passive. It is easy to admire Jesus. It costs nothing to agree that the gospel is probably true. What this phrase asks is that you stop underwriting your own life — and that is not a mild request, which is why the New Testament can speak of unbelief as disobedience without changing the subject.

Then the motive clause, which is the part we habitually skip: all of this is “for the sake of his name”. Not for the sake of the nations, though he loves them; not for the sake of the church growing, though he wants it. For the sake of the name. And that is worth turning into a test, because it exposes what we are actually after when we pray for people. Think of someone you long to see come to Christ, and ask honestly why. Most of our reasons are decent and partial: so that they would be happier; so that they would stop making choices that frighten us; so that the family would be at peace; so that we would not have to worry about where they will be when they die. Now run the harder version. If that person came to faith and never thanked you, never joined your church, never became easy to be with, and their life stayed every bit as hard as it is now — would you still count it as everything you had prayed for? If yes, you are praying for the sake of his name. If it hesitates, that is not a reason for shame; it is simply the place where Paul’s motive and ours are not yet the same, and it will bear praying about.

And “all the nations” is not a general enthusiasm for scale. It is a quotation waiting to be recognised. God had told Abraham that in his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 22:18) — the promise this passage has just said was made beforehand in the holy Scriptures (v. 2). So Paul’s travel plans are not an apostolic hobby. They are the mechanism by which a promise sworn to a childless herdsman two thousand years earlier is being kept, in real time, on actual roads, by a man with a tentmaker’s hands.

Which sets up verse 6, and it lands with a quiet thud that is easy to miss. Paul has been describing something enormous and far away — a mission to all the nations, for the sake of the name, in fulfilment of an ancient oath. Then: including you. The Christians in Rome are not the audience of this mission, watching it happen elsewhere and praying for the people who do it. They are the thing itself. They are what “all the nations” looks like when the sentence stops being a plan and starts being a room with people in it. And the description he gives them is the third of the three callings in this opening sentence — Paul called an apostle (v. 1), the Romans called to belong to Jesus Christ, and in the next breath called to be saints (see on v. 1). Note what they are called to: not called to achieve, or to understand, or to be useful. Called to belong. It is the word of ownership again, and it is the same word Paul used of himself before he used it of them.

So the greatest missionary who ever lived introduces his life’s work, names the ends of the earth as his parish, roots it in a promise older than the nation of Israel — and then turns to a few dozen believers meeting in borrowed rooms in a hostile city and tells them that they are not the spectators of that story. They are the evidence that it is true.

verseByVerse.quote: To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. — Romans 1:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Loved by God” — passive voice. These people did not love their way into God’s favour; they were loved before they did anything. The Reformation understanding of grace is here in seed: the initiative is entirely divine. They are also “called to be saints” — not aspiring to be saints, not trying to become saints, but already saints by virtue of the call of God that placed them in Christ. Their sainthood is not a moral category; it is a relational one.

Grace and peace — the signature Pauline greeting. Grace (charis) is the undeserved favour of God; peace (shalom) is the comprehensive well-being that results when the war between humanity and God has been ended by the blood of the cross. Paul pronounces both over his readers before he has written a single sentence of argument. The gospel is gift before it is demand.

It is worth knowing who was actually in that room, because this greeting is warmer than the situation was. Some years before Paul wrote, the emperor Claudius had expelled the Jews from Rome — Luke mentions it in passing, which is how Priscilla and Aquila came to be in Corinth (Acts 18:2). Whatever the precise cause, the effect on the young church is not hard to reconstruct. The Jewish believers, including many of the founders, were gone. For several years the Roman congregations were Gentile congregations. Then Claudius died, the edict lapsed, and the exiles came home — to churches that had learned to function entirely without them, with other leaders, other customs, and no particular memory of the synagogue.

Hold that in mind and much of this letter stops being abstract. The long argument that Jew and Gentile are equally guilty and equally justified; the ache of chapters 9 to 11 over Israel; the warning to Gentile believers not to be arrogant toward the branches that were broken off; the whole of chapter 14 on the strong and the weak, food and holy days and not despising one another — this is not Paul theorising. He is writing into a congregation with a seam running through it. And the first thing he does, before a word of argument, is to address them all with one description: loved by God, called, saints. Not the founding members and the newcomers. Not the returned and the established. One greeting over one church.

Then take the word saints, because centuries of church usage have made it mean the opposite of what Paul intends. We hear it as a category of exceptional Christians, mostly dead, formally recognised, with stained glass. In the Old Testament the root belongs first to things rather than people — the holy place, the holy garments, the holy vessels — and what made them holy was not their quality but their designation. A bowl in the tabernacle was not a better bowl. It was a bowl that had been set aside for God and could no longer be used for anything else. So when Paul calls a mixed room of tradesmen, slaves and immigrants in Rome the holy ones, he is not describing their record. He is describing what has happened to them: they have been set aside, and they are no longer available for ordinary use.

Which gives an unexpectedly practical consequence. If holiness began as your achievement you would have to keep proving it, and every failure would put your status back in question. If holiness is a designation, then failure is a contradiction of what you are rather than a disproof of it — and this is exactly how Paul writes to the most disorderly church he knew, opening a letter about lawsuits, drunkenness at the Lord’s table and a man sleeping with his stepmother by calling them saints (1 Corinthians 1:2). He does not withdraw the word in order to rebuke them. He rebukes them on the strength of the word: be what you are.

And the entry above is right that “loved by God” is passive, but do not let the grammar pass as a technicality, because it decides how the whole letter will be read. There is a way of being a Christian in which you are, in effect, auditioning — you believe God loves you, and you also believe the love is roughly proportional to how the week went. Here is a test for it, and it takes ten seconds. Think of a specific person and ask: does God love me more today than he did this time last year? If the honest answer is yes, and the reason is that you have been doing better, then the love has quietly become a wage. Paul’s participle rules it out. They were loved before they did anything, they will be loved after they have failed at a good deal, and the letter will eventually say the thing plainly: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (5:8). The love was at full strength at the worst possible moment. It has nowhere to grow to.

Then the greeting itself, which is not a formula either. Grace was roughly the standard Greek hello and peace the standard Jewish one — shalom, spoken across the Mediterranean every day — and Paul, writing to a church with Greeks and Jews eyeing each other across a room, opens with both. Even his hello is integrated. And he does not leave them as pleasantries: grace is the favour that was not owed to anyone, and peace is what that favour produces once the war is over. The order never reverses in Scripture. Nobody has ever found peace and then gone looking for grace.

One last thing, easily walked past, and it is the first time this letter says it: “God our Father”. It will not be the last — by chapter 8 Paul will have a room full of former slaves and shopkeepers crying Abba, and will make their adoption the ground of their security. But he says it here, at the door, before the argument begins. And that is the shape of the gospel in a single greeting: the God who is about to spend a chapter and a half describing his own wrath is introduced to these people, by name, as their Father.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Paul's Longing and His Debt to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established his gospel and his greeting, Paul opens his heart. He has prayed for the Roman Christians unceasingly. He has longed to visit them. He has been prevented — more than once. This passage is often passed over quickly on the way to the theological fireworks of vv. 16–17, but it deserves careful attention: it shows us what a gospel-shaped pastor looks like. Paul's longing is not merely strategic (Rome as a missionary base) but personal. He wants to see them, to be mutually encouraged, to share with them some spiritual gift.

The phrase "I am under obligation" (v. 14) — literally "I am a debtor" — is startling. Paul does not feel that preaching the gospel to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, is above and beyond the call of duty. He feels indebted to them. They have a claim on him. The grace that was lavished on him on the Damascus road was not for his private enrichment; it was for their benefit. He owes them what he received for free. This is the logic of all gospel ministry: grace received creates obligation discharged.

"I am not ashamed of the gospel" (v. 16) — the Greek construction implies the opposite: he is eagerly proud of it, itching to proclaim it in Rome's very centre. Rome was the most intimidating platform imaginable: the seat of empire, the crossroads of civilization, the city that had crucified the Lord of the gospel. And Paul cannot wait to get there.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pastoral and Missionary Logic of Paul

Romans 1:8–15 reveals that Paul's missionary strategy is inseparable from his pastoral affection. He does not view the Roman church as an audience for his theology or a resource for his mission; he views them as beloved brothers and sisters in whom he longs to rejoice. Reformed missiology has always insisted that mission and church are inseparable — the mission proceeds from the church, through the church, and for the establishment of the church. Paul's eagerness to visit Rome exemplifies this: he is not a lone-ranger evangelist but an apostle embedded in the body of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's sense of debt to all people — Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish — erased every cultural and social hierarchy. The gospel belonged to no class or culture. Now: The contemporary church is perpetually tempted to preach a gospel shaped for those who are already culturally similar to us. Paul's "debtor" language is a rebuke: the gospel is owed to every person in our reach, regardless of whether they seem like likely converts or comfortable neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I mention you
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s thanksgiving is striking: he thanks God for their faith, not their achievements. Faith is itself the gift — and the Giver deserves the thanks. The appeal to God as witness (“God is my witness”) is not rhetorical flourish but a solemn oath. Paul’s prayer life and his apostolic service were not two compartments; they were one seamless act of worship. He had been ministering to Rome on his knees for years before setting foot there.

Notice that he begins here at all. First, I thank my God — and this is Paul’s settled habit, the way he opens letter after letter, including letters to churches that were about to be told some very hard things. The Corinthians were tearing themselves apart over leaders, tolerating incest and getting drunk at the Lord’s table, and he still opens by thanking God for them. Which makes the one exception worth noticing: Galatians has no thanksgiving at all. He goes straight from the greeting to “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you.” When Paul omits the thanksgiving, you know something is seriously wrong. Here it is present, warm, and first.

And it is offered “through Jesus Christ”, which is easy to read as a formula and is not one. Paul cannot even say thank you to God on his own account. Gratitude, like everything else, goes up through the Mediator — because the problem the whole letter is about to describe is not merely that we sin but that we have no standing, and a man with no standing cannot simply address the throne. So the smallest prayer in the Christian life travels the same road as the greatest. Every “thank you, Lord” before a meal is carried by the same blood that carried the thief into paradise.

Then observe what he thanks God for, because it is oddly specific. Not their numbers, their generosity, their organisation, or their strategic position in the capital of the world. Their faith — and it is their faith that “is proclaimed in all the world”. Rome was the hub of the empire; every road led there and every road led out again, and travellers, traders, soldiers and slaves carried news along them constantly. So something about these believers had got into the traffic. Which is worth turning on ourselves for a moment. If people two countries away were talking about your congregation, what would they have heard? That it is large, or well run, or has good music, or holds the right line on a contested question? All of that can be true of a church whose faith is not the thing being reported. What travelled out of Rome was that these people believed God.

The oath in verse 9 is stranger than it looks, and the situation explains it. God is my witness. Why would a man need to swear to something as unremarkable as praying for people? Because they had no way of checking, and because they had reason to wonder. Paul had never been to Rome. He is writing to a church he did not found, whose founders he never met, in a city he is openly hoping to use as a base for a mission further west (15:24). It would have been very easy for someone in that room to conclude that the famous apostle’s sudden interest was strategic — that they were a stopping point on somebody else’s itinerary. So he calls God to witness what nobody else can verify: that for years, unseen, they have been on his list.

And the word he uses for his service is a surprise from a former Pharisee. Latreuō is temple language — the word for the priestly service of God, the sacrifices, the incense, the work done in the holy place by men in linen. Paul takes the vocabulary of the most sacred building in the world and applies it to what he does: talking about Jesus, mostly to small groups of unimportant people, in rented rooms and workshops and prisons, up and down the roads of the empire. He is not saying his work is like worship. He is saying it is the real thing, and that the smoke of the altar has moved outdoors.

Which leaves the phrase that intimidates every honest reader: without ceasing. Before it flattens you, be clear about what it does not mean. Paul was not praying every waking second; he made tents, argued in synagogues, sailed, wrote, ate and slept. The phrase was ordinary Greek for something unremitting and regular — used, for instance, of a fever that does not break. It means these people never dropped off his list. He did not forget them for six months and then feel guilty. And the guard matters, because a reader who takes it as a demand for continuous verbal prayer will conclude within a week that he cannot pray at all, which is exactly the result the verse was not written to produce.

But there is a test in it. Look at what actually fills your praying. For most of us the honest answer is situations — the diagnosis, the interview, the money, the decision, the thing that is worrying us this fortnight — and when the situation resolves, the subject disappears. Paul’s prayer life was populated by people, most of them not present, some of them not yet met. Read the last chapter of this letter and you will find him greeting twenty-six of them by name, in a city he had never visited. He knew who they were. He had been holding them up one at a time.

So here is the thing to sit with. The Christians in Rome had no idea any of this was happening. They had never seen his face. They could not have known that a man in another province had been carrying them by name for years, and they would only find out when this letter was read aloud. Which is almost certainly true of you as well: somewhere there is an old woman, or a friend from a church you left, or a parent, who mentions your name to God with a regularity you know nothing about. You will not learn who they were until it is all read out — and some of what has held you up was never yours to see.

verseByVerse.quote: always in my prayers, asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The qualification “if by God’s will” is not pious filler — it reflects the Pauline conviction that all missionary movement is ordered by divine providence. He had wanted to come before; he had been prevented. He does not interpret the delay as failure but as the shaping hand of God. This posture of submitted eagerness — burning desire held within the bounds of God’s sovereignty — is the mark of genuine gospel ministry.

It is worth saying how long this had been going on, because “now at last” is the sound of a man who has been waiting a considerable time. He says a few verses later that he has often intended to come and been prevented (v. 13), and by chapter 15 he puts a number on it: “I have longed for many years to come to you” (15:23). This is not a fortnight’s postponement. A plan he believed was right, formed for the best of reasons, had been blocked repeatedly over years — and he was still asking.

And notice what he does not do with the delay, because we would have done at least one of them. He does not decide the door is shut for good and stop asking. He does not conclude that the desire itself was wrong — that wanting Rome had been ambition dressed up as mission, and the mature thing would be to want nothing. Nor does he force it, treating the obstacles as opposition to be overridden by determination. He keeps wanting it, keeps asking for it, and leaves the timing where it belongs. That combination is rarer than it sounds. Most of us can manage desire without submission, which is impatience, or submission without desire, which is resignation wearing a pious face.

Which is why the small phrase matters so much: somehow, by God’s will. This is not the verbal tic that “if it be your will” often becomes at the end of our prayers — a disclaimer attached in advance so that nothing has really been asked and nothing can be seen to fail. Paul asks for the specific thing, plainly and repeatedly, and then submits the outcome. James says the same to men making business plans: you ought to say, “if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that” (James 4:15). The point is not that we should stop planning. It is that we are creatures who do not know whether we will be alive on Thursday, and any plan that forgets this is not confident but simply unrealistic.

Now the part that should be said out loud, because the entry above is right that Paul read his delays as the shaping hand of God, and a reader can easily hear that as a rebuke of his own experience. Most delays do not feel like providence at the time. They feel like a door closing for no reason: the job that went to somebody else, the treatment that did not work, the years of waiting for a child, the ministry you were sure God had given you that quietly failed. Paul himself did not always know what the prevention was for. When the Spirit blocked him from Bithynia (Acts 16:7) he was not given an explanation; he was simply stopped, and only later did a man from Macedonia appear in a dream. He did not have the interpretation while he was standing at the closed border. He had it afterwards, and often the church has had it afterwards, and sometimes nobody gets it at all this side of the end.

So the honest form of this doctrine is not “every delay has a visible reason you will eventually be shown”. It is that the delays are not random and are not neglect. And the proof of that, in this case, is sitting in your hands. If Paul had got to Rome when he first wanted to, he would have preached there — and we would almost certainly not have this letter. The greatest exposition of the gospel ever written exists because a man could not get to the city he wanted to visit and had to write instead. Nobody in that room knew they were reading the fruit of a frustration. He did not know it either.

And when the prayer was finally answered, it was answered in a form he had not asked for. He reached Rome — as a prisoner, after arrest, a shipwreck, and two years in custody at Caesarea, at the empire’s expense, chained to a soldier (Acts 27–28). He got the city. He did not get the itinerary. And the last verse of Acts leaves him there, receiving all who came to him and proclaiming the kingdom of God “with all boldness and without hindrance” — which is a remarkable thing for Luke to say about a man under guard, and is exactly what this prayer had asked for.

So take the encouragement in the shape God actually gives it. You may be asking, as Paul was, for something good, for the right reasons, and getting nothing but closed doors. This verse does not promise that the door will open on your terms. It promises that the one who is not opening it has not stopped listening — and that the thing he does instead may be the thing people are still reading two thousand years later.

verseByVerse.quote: For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith, both yours and mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul catches himself. He begins with apostolic confidence (“that I may impart to you some spiritual gift”), then immediately corrects the impression of condescension: “that we may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith.” The correction is theologically significant: even the apostle expected to receive from those to whom he ministered. The body of Christ has no passengers, and the apostle himself is not exempt from need. Lloyd-Jones saw here the model of all genuine Christian fellowship.

Watch the sentence actually break, because Paul’s self-correction is visible in the grammar and it is one of the most attractive moments in the letter. He starts confidently: I long to see you, to impart to you some spiritual gift, to strengthen you. Three phrases, all travelling one way — from the apostle to the church. And then he hears himself. The words that is are the sound of a man stopping mid-flow and reaching for a better sentence: that is, that we may be mutually encouraged, by each other’s faith, both yours and mine. He does not delete the first version; he lets us watch him revise it. The greatest theologian in the church’s history heard a note of condescension in his own draft and corrected it before he reached the full stop.

And the correction cost him something, which is why it is not merely charming. Paul had every credential a man could have. He had seen the risen Christ. He had been caught up to the third heaven. He wrote Scripture. The believers in Rome were tradesmen and slaves and immigrants, some of them a year or two old in the faith, and there was nothing they could teach him about justification. But that is not what he says he needs from them. He says he expects to be encouraged by their faith — and faith is not expertise. A frightened woman still trusting God after a bad year has something the most learned man in the room cannot generate for himself by knowing more. He can only watch it and be strengthened.

Which quietly demolishes the way most of us picture Christian growth, in both directions. If you are the one who normally teaches, leads, hosts, organises or fixes, notice what Paul thinks a strong Christian is: not a man with no needs, but a man who knows he has them and says so out loud to people less impressive than himself. And if you are on the other side — newer, quieter, convinced you are in the room to receive and have nothing to bring — this verse says the apostle to the Gentiles was looking forward to being helped by people exactly like you. The body of Christ has no passengers, as the entry above rightly says. It also has no spectators in the other seat: nobody attends only in order to give.

So here is a test with a sting in it, and it is short. When did you last tell another Christian, in plain words and without decorating it, that you needed their help — not a general “please pray for me”, but the actual thing? If you can name the occasion, good. If you cannot remember one, then whatever else is true of your Christian life, you are living it in a posture Paul refused to adopt, and probably at a cost you have stopped noticing: the loneliness of the person everyone assumes is fine. It is worth asking why. Usually it is not humility. Usually it is that being the one who needs help means giving up being the one who is depended upon.

One clarification, since “some spiritual gift” has been made to carry more than it can bear. Paul is not describing a technique for transferring a supernatural endowment from an apostle to a congregation, and he immediately blurs the direction of travel anyway by saying it will run both ways. He is being deliberately vague — some gift — because he does not yet know what these particular people will need when he arrives, and he trusts the Giver to supply it then. That is a healthier model for ministry than most of our planning: go, be present, and expect God to provide the specific good you cannot specify in advance.

And this is where the fine point about strength is, because Paul never says he is going to strengthen them by his personality or his authority. The strengthening happens through faith — theirs and his — which means the currency of Christian encouragement is not cheerfulness or advice or competence. It is somebody in front of you still trusting God. That is why sitting with a believer who is suffering well can leave you steadier than a conference will, and why the person who thinks they have nothing to offer the church because their life is hard has misunderstood what the church runs on.

So the apostle books his visit to the capital of the world, and the reason he gives is not that Rome needs him. It is that he needs Rome — and he says so to people who have never met him, in writing, before he arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has not forgotten Rome. His repeated prevention has not been indifference but divine restraint — the same Spirit who forbade him Bithynia (Acts 16:7) had other work for him first. The harvest language (“reap some harvest”) is striking: Paul views his visit not as a theological lecture but as evangelistic labor. Even a church that is already flourishing is a field in which the gospel can produce more fruit.

Start with how he opens it, because the phrase is a signal and Paul uses it deliberately. I do not want you to be unaware, brothers — a formula he reaches for when he is about to say something his readers genuinely do not know and might otherwise get wrong (he uses it of the hardening of Israel in 11:25, and of those who have died in 1 Thessalonians 4:13). So this is not small talk before the theology starts. He is correcting an impression. Someone in Rome had almost certainly noticed the obvious: the apostle to the Gentiles has been working the Mediterranean for twenty years and has never once come to the largest Gentile city on earth. Draw the natural conclusion and it is unflattering — he does not think we matter, or he is avoiding a church he did not found, or the great man goes where the reputation is.

And notice the shape of his answer, because it is the harder of the two available ones. He does not say he was too busy, which would have been true. He says he was prevented — and the word puts an agent behind the obstacle. Something stood in the way. This is a man who will not describe his own life in terms of scheduling, and the discipline is worth copying, because the two accounts of an identical year are entirely different to live inside. I never got round to it leaves you the manager of a life that is not going well. I was prevented leaves you a servant whose Master has other arrangements. The facts on the calendar are the same. The person who has to sleep at the end of the day is not.

Then the word he chooses for what he wants, which is stranger than it first appears: he hopes to reap some harvest among them. Not to teach them, address them, or hold meetings. Harvest is agricultural language and it carries three things a lecture does not. It is slow — nobody harvests in the week he sows. It is not manufactured — a farmer can plough, sow, water and weed, and cannot make a single seed germinate, which is precisely Paul’s point elsewhere: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6). And it is seasonal, which is why he can be prevented for years without the work being lost. A field left unvisited is not a field abandoned. It is a field not yet ripe.

Which is worth holding on to if you are the one doing the sowing and have seen nothing. The parent who has prayed for a son for eleven years and watched him move further away. The teacher of a class of teenagers who appear to absorb nothing. The Christian at work who has been kind and honest for a decade and has never once been asked why. The harvest image does not promise that you will see the crop, and Scripture is honest that often one sows and another reaps (John 4:37–38). It promises that the growing is not your department, and that the absence of visible fruit in June says nothing whatever about what is happening underground.

And do not miss what he assumes about the Roman church, because it is a quiet rebuke to the way we grade congregations. These are the believers whose faith is being talked about all over the empire (v. 8). By any measure they are a success. Paul still expects a harvest among them — more conversions, more growth, more fruit that is not yet there. He does not think of a healthy church as a finished one. Which is the difference between a building, which is completed and then maintained, and a field, which is never finished at all and is either being worked or going back to weeds.

So a test, and it is about expectation rather than effort. Think of the situation you have privately written off — the relative who will never believe, the colleague who is too far gone, the part of your own character you have decided is simply how you are. Ask when you stopped expecting anything there. Not when you stopped trying; when you stopped expecting. Because the difference between Paul’s twenty-year frustration and simple resignation is not that he kept working. It is that he was still, after all those years, planning the harvest of a city he had never seen.

verseByVerse.quote: I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. — Romans 1:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Greeks and barbarians” was the first-century way of saying everyone. Greeks were the cultured, literate, philosophically sophisticated world; barbarians were everyone else — those who spoke languages that sounded to Greek ears like “bar-bar” (hence the name). Paul’s gospel has no cultural prerequisites. The sophisticated Athenian philosopher and the rough Scythian tribesman stand equally in need of the same grace, and are equally capable of receiving it.

The eagerness Paul expresses for Rome is not the excitement of tourism. It is the urgency of a man who knows that people in Rome are perishing without the gospel and that he has been entrusted with the one message that can save them. Spurgeon used to say that if he believed what he claimed to believe about heaven and hell, he would crawl on his knees across broken glass to preach the gospel. Paul’s eagerness for Rome has that quality.

But the word Paul actually uses has been left standing untranslated in that account, and it is the strangest thing in the sentence. He does not say he is willing to preach to Greeks and barbarians, or burdened for them, or available to them. He says he is a debtor to them. That is the language of the ledger: it describes a man who owes something and has not yet paid it. And it raises an obvious question, because Paul had never met these people, borrowed nothing from them, and done them no wrong. How do you come to be in debt to strangers?

There are two ways to owe a man money, and only one of them fits. You can borrow from him — and Paul had not. Or somebody can hand you a sum with instructions to deliver it to him, in which case you are in debt to a person you have never met, for money that was never yours, and you will remain in debt until he has it in his hand. That is precisely Paul’s position. On the Damascus road he was given something that was not for him: a message, with a name on it, addressed to the nations. From that moment the Greeks and the barbarians had a claim on him — not because they had earned one, but because the gospel he had been handed was theirs.

Which turns the whole business of evangelism the right way up, and the difference is felt immediately in how it makes you look at people. If the gospel is my possession, then telling someone about it is generosity, and generosity is optional, and it can be postponed until I feel equipped, or brave, or until they seem receptive. If the gospel is a delivery, none of that applies. A courier does not congratulate himself for handing over a parcel, and he does not decide the recipient looks unlikely to appreciate it. He is simply carrying something that belongs to somebody else, and the only real question is whether it arrives. Grace received, as the section box puts it, creates obligation discharged.

And notice how carefully Paul draws the circle of people he owes: Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish. Two pairs, each covering the whole field from opposite ends — the cultured and the crude, the clever and the slow. He is deliberately naming the two groups a preacher instinctively avoids for opposite reasons. The sophisticated frighten us, because they can argue and we suspect we would lose. The unsophisticated bore us, or embarrass us, or seem unpromising. Paul says he is in debt to both, which is a way of saying that the church does not get to choose its creditors.

That is worth pressing, because the modern form of the failure is not usually contempt; it is sorting. We build congregations for people who are already culturally like us — same education, same politics, same accent, same anxieties — and then find, without ever having decided it, that the gospel we preach has quietly been shaped to fit them. So run the test on your own life rather than on the church in the abstract. Name the last five people you have spoken to about Christ, or would consider speaking to. How many of them are recognisably a version of you? If the list is uniform, the problem is not that you lack courage. It is that you have unconsciously decided who the message is for — and Paul’s pairs exist precisely to stop that decision being made.

One guard, because a debt can be preached in a way that crushes. If you owe everybody, and the payment is their eternal life, then every conversation you did not have becomes a debt in arrears, and a sensitive Christian can be flattened by that arithmetic. So note what Paul actually says he feels: not guilt but eagerness. He is not dragging himself towards Rome under the lash of an unpayable bill; he can hardly wait to get there. The debt has become a desire. And note also that he is one man with one life who cannot reach Spain and Rome in the same year, and does not pretend otherwise. Your debt is to the people God has actually put in your reach — the ones whose names you know, whose kitchens you sit in, who work at the next desk. Not to the world. He never asked you to be the apostle to the Gentiles; that post is filled.

So this is what a man looks like who has understood what he was given. He does not describe the people of the world as his mission field, his audience, or his responsibility. He describes them as his creditors — and he is on his way to Rome to pay what he owes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Theme: The Righteousness of God by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two verses. The entire letter in miniature. Everything Paul will argue across sixteen chapters is compressed here with the density of a diamond. "I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written: 'The righteous shall live by faith.'" This is the thesis statement of Romans, and it is the sentence that changed the world.

Martin Luther, tormented by the phrase "the righteousness of God" — understanding it as the terrifying standard by which God condemns sinners — wrestled with it until the light broke. "At last," he wrote, "meditating day and night...I began to understand that the righteousness of God is that by which the righteous lives by a gift of God, namely by faith. And this is the meaning: the righteousness of God is revealed by the gospel, namely, the passive righteousness with which the merciful God justifies us by faith. Here I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates." The Reformation began in these two verses.

The gospel is power — not advice, not inspiration, not a moral framework, but the very power of God actively at work to save. It is power for salvation — not merely forgiveness of past sins, but the complete rescue of a human being from the dominion of sin and death and the wrath of God, and the restoration of that person to the full flourishing of life in God. And it is for everyone who believes — the one condition, the one instrument, the one hand that receives what God freely gives: faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Righteousness of God: Attribute or Gift?

Reformed exegesis has understood "the righteousness of God" in Romans 1:17 as a righteousness that originates with God and is given by God to the believing sinner — what the Reformers called iustitia aliena, an alien righteousness, a righteousness that is not our own. Luther's breakthrough was recognising that this righteousness is not the demanding standard that condemns but the gracious gift that saves. This is the doctrine of imputation: Christ's perfect righteousness is credited to the account of the believing sinner, so that God can be simultaneously just (the sin has been punished in Christ) and the justifier (the sinner is declared righteous). Calvin called this the "wonderful exchange" — Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luther's discovery of Romans 1:17 broke the back of a system of salvation by merit and religious performance that had enslaved Western Christendom for centuries. The Reformation was, at its heart, a rediscovery of these two verses. Now: Every generation re-erects the system of merit that the gospel demolishes. Every human heart, left to itself, believes it must earn its standing with God. Romans 1:16–17 is the permanent, repeatable antidote: the gospel is not something you do; it is something done for you, received by faith, given by the merciful God who justifies the ungodly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. — Romans 1:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Not ashamed” — the negation suggests the real possibility of shame. In Rome, where power was measured in legions and the crucified Messiah was foolishness to the Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews, the gospel was not a prestigious thing to be associated with. Paul’s confidence is not bravado; it is grounded in what the gospel actually is: the power of God. He is not ashamed of a philosophy or a programme; he is not ashamed of the active, saving, transforming power of the living God working through ordinary preaching.

The order “Jew first and also Greek” is not merely historical courtesy. It reflects the covenant structure of redemption: God’s saving purposes moved through Israel to reach all nations. The Messiah came as Israel’s king. The gospel was first preached in Jerusalem. But the first is not the only, and the covenant with Abraham always had the nations in view. The gospel has no ethnic restrictions; it has one condition only — faith.

It is worth being concrete about what there was to be ashamed of, because we have had two thousand years to get used to the cross and Paul’s readers had not. Crucifixion was not merely a cruel execution; it was a deliberately degrading one, reserved in practice for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals, and Roman citizens were normally exempt from it by law. Cicero, arguing a case a century earlier, said the very word ought to be kept away not only from the body of a Roman citizen but from his thoughts, his eyes and his ears. Polite people did not discuss it. And the message Paul is carrying into the capital of that world has, at its centre, a Jewish provincial who was put to death that way.

We even have a picture of how it looked from outside. Scratched into plaster on the Palatine in Rome, a century or two after this letter arrived, someone drew a crude cartoon: a figure on a cross with the head of a donkey, and a man standing beside it with his hand raised in worship. Underneath, in scrawled Greek: Alexamenos worships his god. That is a schoolboy’s joke, and it is precisely the social reality Paul is writing into. To confess this gospel in Rome was not to hold a minority opinion. It was to be the person everyone else found faintly ridiculous.

And Paul had private reasons for the sentence as well as public ones. Read the map of the years just behind this letter and it is not a record of triumph: run out of Philippi after a beating, hurried out of Thessalonica by night, moved on from Berea, politely dismissed by the philosophers in Athens, and then Corinth, where he arrived by his own admission “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3) and where people said his personal presence was unimpressive and his speech worth nothing. This is not a man who has never felt the pull. It is a man who has felt it repeatedly and has decided where he stands.

Then the reason he gives, which is not what we would give. He does not say the gospel is true, though it is; or reasonable, though he will argue it for eleven chapters; or beautiful, though it is. He says it is power — and note the grammar, because he does not say the gospel has power or brings power. It is the power of God for salvation. The message is not a description of something powerful that happens elsewhere; the message is the instrument God uses to do the thing. Which is why ordinary preaching, and ordinary Christians saying ordinary sentences about Christ, keep producing results out of all proportion to the people involved. One small correction while we are here: preachers sometimes tell you this word gives us “dynamite”, and the arrow points the other way — Nobel named his explosive after the Greek word, and the picture of a detonation is not Paul’s. His word means effective might, the capacity to accomplish. Not a blast. A working power.

And the range of it is stated twice over, in a way the divided congregation in Rome could hardly miss. To everyone who believes — no other qualification is offered anywhere in the sentence. Then, in case anyone wants to know how that applies to the seam running through their own church, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. First is a matter of sequence, not of rank — the promises came to Israel, the Messiah came as Israel’s king, the preaching began in Jerusalem — and Paul will give three whole chapters to what that priority means now (see on 1:7 for the situation in Rome that makes this urgent). But he has already settled the thing that mattered most in that room: one power, one condition, two peoples, and the same door.

So here is the test, and it is not about whether you would deny Christ under interrogation. Almost nobody reading this will be asked to. Shame is quieter than that. It is the sentence you began and did not finish. It is the small disclaimer — “I’m not really religious, but” — that you attach in advance so that nobody misfiles you. It is how you describe your Sunday to a colleague on Monday: vague, generic, edited so that it will not require a follow-up question. Watch for the edit this week. Not the denial; the edit. That is where the shame actually lives.

And when you find it, the answer is not to work up more nerve, because the verse does not end with a demand for courage. It ends with an argument: I am not ashamed for it is the power of God. Confidence in this message is not a personality trait you either have or lack. It grows in the man who has actually seen it work — who has watched someone he had written off become a Christian, or has watched it hold a friend together through something that should have destroyed him.

Then the last thing, which is the deepest reason Paul can write this sentence at all. The cross was shameful; he is not pretending otherwise, and the world was right about what it looked like. But Hebrews says that Jesus endured the cross, despising the shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God (Hebrews 12:2). He took the humiliation and did not think it too high a price. So when Paul says he is not ashamed of the gospel, he is not being brave about an embarrassing story. He is refusing to be ashamed of something his Lord was willing to be shamed by — and there is no ground on which a servant may be more fastidious than his Master.

verseByVerse.quote: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.' — Romans 1:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
“From faith for faith” — a phrase that has generated enormous debate. Most likely it means that the righteousness of God is received by faith from beginning to end: not faith at the entry point followed by works for maintenance, but faith all the way down, from first to last. The Christian life does not begin in grace and continue in effort; it is grace from first to last, received by faith from first to last.

The citation from Habakkuk 2:4 is loaded with Old Testament context. Habakkuk had cried out to God about injustice and chaos, and God had answered with a promise that seemed impossibly deferred. “But the righteous shall live by his faith” — the one who trusts God in the darkness, who holds on to the promise when the evidence seems to point the other way, this person will live. Paul takes this text and places it at the heart of his doctrine of justification: the life that God gives comes to those who trust his promise, not those who earn his approval.

All of which assumes we know what “the righteousness of God” means, and that is the phrase the whole verse turns on. It can be read three ways, and the difference between them is the difference between despair and joy. It might mean an attribute — God’s own perfect rightness, the standard he is and by which he measures. It might mean an activity — God acting to put things right, doing justice in the world. Or it might mean a gift — a righteous status that God gives to people who do not have one of their own. Now notice what happens to a guilty man under each reading. If the gospel reveals God’s standard, that is not good news; that is the problem restated with greater clarity. And this is precisely where the verse becomes a biography rather than a definition.

Martin Luther was a monk who took sin seriously enough to be destroyed by it. He fasted, kept vigils, confessed for hours at a stretch until his confessor lost patience with him, and could not find peace, because he knew the standard and he knew himself. And when he came to this verse, it was the worst sentence in the Bible. The gospel reveals the righteousness of God? The one thing a man in his condition could not survive was more of God’s righteousness. He later wrote that he had hated the phrase, and hated the God he thought stood behind it — not the admission of a sceptic but of a man who had given his life to the church and found no relief in it.

Then the meaning broke open. He saw that the righteousness revealed in the gospel is not the standard God demands but the standing God gives; not the righteousness by which he condemns, but the righteousness with which he clothes. In his own account of it: meditating day and night, he began to understand that this is the passive righteousness with which the merciful God justifies us by faith, and “I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” The Reformation came out of that sentence. Every Protestant church in the world is, in one sense, a footnote to a monk finally understanding a preposition.

The Reformers had a name for the thing he had seen: iustitia aliena, an alien righteousness — alien not in the sense of strange but of belonging to someone else. It is not produced in you; it is credited to you, the way a sum can be entered into an account that did not earn it. Christ’s obedience is reckoned as yours; your sin was reckoned as his and dealt with at the cross. Calvin called it the wonderful exchange. And it is the only arrangement that lets God be, as Paul will say later in this letter, both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (3:26) — the debt genuinely paid rather than waived, and the guilty genuinely acquitted rather than excused.

Which is why the tense of the verb matters. The righteousness of God is revealed — present, continuous, still happening. Paul does not say it was revealed once in Palestine and is now a matter of record. Every time this gospel is preached the curtain goes back again, and the thing Luther saw is shown to somebody else. It is being revealed in the reading of this sentence.

Now put that against the way most of us actually live, because the merit system is not a medieval problem that the sixteenth century solved. It is the default setting of the human heart, and it reassembles itself in every generation, including in churches that would sign every Reformation confession without hesitation. So here is a test, and it takes one honest answer. Suppose you were asked tonight why God should accept you. Not what you would say in a Bible study — what actually rises first. If the answer includes the words I try, or I have been, or at least I never, then whatever your doctrine is, your account is being kept in your own name. The gospel’s answer to that question contains no information about you at all.

And there is a second test, quieter and more revealing: watch what happens to your sense of acceptance after you sin badly. If it drops, and then slowly recovers over a few days of doing better, you have discovered experimentally what you are living on. An alien righteousness does not fluctuate, because it was never generated by you and cannot be damaged by you. The bad days do not lower the balance any more than the good days raised it.

Which is what makes the Habakkuk citation land where it does. The prophet was not a man enjoying a settled faith; he was watching injustice go unanswered and being told the answer would come in a form he would not like, on a timetable he would not choose. Into that God says: the righteous shall live by faith. So the sentence has always meant a life held up by trusting God rather than by seeing results — and Paul, quoting it into a letter about justification, is saying that the same faith which receives a righteousness you did not earn is the faith you go on living by afterwards, in the dark, when nothing is visible. It gets you in, and it is also the whole of how you walk once you are in.

Luther spent years trying to give God a righteousness God would accept. He was looking at the wrong side of the transaction the entire time. The gospel does not tell you how to produce a righteousness for God. It announces a righteousness from God — and the only hand that can take it is the one that has stopped trying to manufacture its own.
