The praise that matters in this verse is awarded by the only person who has seen the whole of it — the years of quiet obedience nobody thanked you for, the sins fought in private, the prayers said into an empty room. Paul has spent an entire chapter taking away every commendation that human beings are able to give. He does it in order to hand you one that they cannot give, and therefore cannot take back.

3.title: No One Righteous — But Now, Righteousness
3.overview:
Romans 3 is one of the most concentrated pieces of theological argument in the entire Bible. It moves through three distinct but connected moments: the faithfulness of God despite human faithlessness (vv. 1–8), the universal verdict of guilt on the entire human race from the Old Testament's own testimony (vv. 9–20), and then — with the two most beautiful words in the letter — "But now" (v. 21): the announcement of a righteousness from God that is apart from the law, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe.

The emotional architecture of the chapter is deliberate. Paul has spent two chapters building the case for universal human guilt — the Gentile guilty through creation and conscience, the Jew guilty despite law and covenant. Now he delivers the verdict that springs from the evidence: no one righteous, not even one. And then, from within the deepest valley of human hopelessness, he sounds the trumpet of the gospel: the righteousness of God has been manifested. The darkness is real. The light is realer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — God's Faithfulness and Human Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If Jewish identity and covenant privilege provide no buffer against divine judgment (chapter 2), an obvious question arises: what advantage has the Jew? Was the entire covenant history of Israel pointless? Paul will not allow this conclusion. The advantage is real and great: "they were entrusted with the oracles of God." The Torah, the prophets, the promises — these are not nothing. They are the priceless repository of God's self-revelation and covenant purposes. The problem is not the oracles; the problem is the people who received them.

But what about God's faithfulness? If Israel has been faithless to the covenant, does that mean God's covenant promises have failed? Never, Paul declares — and the energy of his negation (mē genoito — "by no means!", "God forbid!", the strongest possible denial in Greek) is palpable. God's faithfulness is not contingent on human faithfulness. He remains true even when every human being is a liar. The covenant will not fail because the Covenant God cannot fail.

This brief passage anticipates the great argument of chapters 9–11: the apparent failure of Israel to embrace her Messiah does not represent a failure of God's word. His purposes stand. His faithfulness endures. The mystery of Israel's unbelief is not the defeat of God's plan but a part of it — and Paul will unfold that mystery with breathtaking scope later in the letter.

The second half of the section (vv. 5–8) turns to a pair of objections that Paul was evidently hearing in real life, and both are attempts to turn grace into a licence. If our unrighteousness only serves to display God’s righteousness more brightly, is God not unjust to punish it? And if my lie makes his truth more evident, why am I still condemned — why not simply “do evil that good may come”? Paul reports that last slander as something people were actually saying he taught, which tells us how radical his gospel of free grace sounded to its first hearers; no one ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging sin. He does not argue the point here — he refuses it, notes that God could judge nothing at all if the objection held, and reserves the full answer for chapter 6. But the objection itself is a compliment in disguise. A gospel that cannot be misheard as permission is probably not the gospel Paul preached.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divine Faithfulness and Human Failure

The question of whether human sin can thwart God's covenant purposes is one of the deepest in all theology. Romans 3:3–4 gives the Reformed answer: it cannot. God's faithfulness is not a function of human response; it is grounded in His own immutable character. Calvin wrote that God's truth stands firm even against the unfaithfulness of the whole world. This has practical implications for Christian assurance: our standing in the covenant does not rest on our faithfulness but on God's. He who called us is faithful; He will do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish readers would have been relieved by Paul's affirmation of Israel's covenant privileges, but troubled by his insistence that these privileges provide no exemption from judgment. The tension — covenant advantage, yet equal accountability — was genuinely new, though rooted in the Old Testament prophets. Now: Christians face the same tension. The advantages of covenant community — Scripture, sacrament, preaching, prayer — are real and great. They are also not saving substitutes for personal faith and repentance. Privilege and accountability always travel together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has just argued that circumcision without obedience is worthless — but he immediately forestalls the conclusion that Jewish privilege is therefore nothing. It is “much in every way”. The primary advantage is the entrusting of God’s oracles — the Scriptures of Israel, the living word of the living God. To possess the Scriptures is to possess the covenant promises, the moral framework of the universe, the prophecies of the coming Messiah. This is an advantage of incalculable weight. The problem Paul has been exposing is not the gift but the receiver’s response to it.

Notice first that Paul asks the question at all, and that he asks it against himself. He has just spent a chapter dismantling every advantage his own people possessed, and he knows exactly what the man in front of him is now thinking: then none of it meant anything, and two thousand years of covenant history were a waste of everyone’s time. A lesser writer would have let that stand rather than complicate a good argument. Paul stops the flow of his own case to answer it, which tells you something about the difference between winning a debate and telling the truth.

And the answer is not a grudging concession. Much in every way — he does not retreat an inch from chapter 2 and he does not allow the privileges to be belittled. Both things are true at once, and holding them together is the whole art of this passage: a gift can be genuinely magnificent and genuinely insufficient to save the man holding it.

Then the word he chooses for what they were given: they were entrusted. That is not the language of a possession but of a deposit — something handed to you which belongs to somebody else and which you will be asked about. A trustee does not own the fund. He administers it, and he is accountable for what happens to it. Which quietly answers the question the whole passage raises: the advantage is real precisely because it is a trust, and a trust is the one kind of advantage that increases your liability rather than reducing it.

And what were they entrusted with? The oracles of God — the utterances, the things God actually said. It is worth pausing on how strange this is as an answer, because Paul could have listed a dozen things and later, in chapter 9, he does: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the temple service, the promises, the patriarchs, and the Messiah himself according to the flesh. Here he names one, and it is not the temple or the land or the throne. It is that God had spoken, and that they had it in writing.

Consider what that meant in the ancient world, because familiarity has flattened it for us. Every nation had gods, and every nation had priests who could tell you what the gods were thought to want — read from entrails, from stars, from the flight of birds, from the ambiguous mutterings of a woman at Delphi, and always subject to interpretation and revision. Israel alone had sentences. Not impressions of the divine will but actual words, in a known language, that could be copied, memorised, checked, argued about, and read aloud to a child. In a world of religious guesswork, one people had a text.

Which is exactly the advantage a Christian holds today, and it is worth noticing that we hold it more fully than they did. You own, in a language you can read, more of God’s speech than Isaiah ever saw. Most of us keep several copies. And the whole thrust of chapter 2 falls on this point: the deposit does not benefit a man who never opens it. There is no category in Scripture called owning the word of God. There is only hearing it and doing it, or hearing it and not.

So a small test, and it is factual rather than introspective. Over the past month, how many hours did you spend with the oracles of God — reading, hearing, thinking about them — compared with the hours spent on the things you would describe as recreation? Do not moralise the answer; just get the number. It is the truest available measure of what you actually believe you have been entrusted with, and it is not the number you would have guessed.

And then the sentence that should govern how you read the rest of this chapter. The problem was never the gift. Everything Paul is about to say about human ruin is said by a man who has just insisted, in the strongest terms available to him, that what God gave was magnificent. The indictment of chapters 1 to 3 is not the story of a deficient revelation. It is the story of what happened to a priceless deposit in the hands of people exactly like us.

verseByVerse.quote: What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, "That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The faithfulness of God does not depend on the faithfulness of his people — this is one of the most important assertions in all of Paul. Israel’s widespread unbelief does not falsify God’s covenant promises; it throws them into even sharper relief. “Let God be true though every one were a liar” is one of the most bracing sentences in Scripture: the trustworthiness of God is the one fixed point in a universe of human unreliability. The citation from Psalm 51 shows that even David’s confession of sin was, at its deepest, a vindication of God’s justice and truth.

The sentence turns on a play that English cannot keep. Their faithlessness and God’s faithfulness are the same root in Greek, negated on one side — as if to say, does their un-faith un-faith the faith of God? Paul is deliberately setting the two words against each other so that the answer is visible before it is argued: one is a quality of God, and the other is merely its absence in somebody else. An absence cannot cancel a substance. The dark in a room has never once put out a lamp.

Then comes the explosion. Mē genoito — the strongest negative available to him, and a phrase he will use ten times in this letter, always when a conclusion is not merely wrong but intolerable. The older translations reached for “God forbid”, which is not a literal rendering and catches the tone exactly. This is not the language of a man weighing a proposition. It is the language of a man recoiling from one.

And what he puts in its place is one of the great rules of the Christian mind: let God be true though every one were a liar. It is worth turning that into the working principle it is, because every believer meets the situation it is built for. Sooner or later what God has said and what you can see will fail to agree. He says he works all things for good, and you are standing in a hospital corridor. He says he is near to the brokenhearted, and you have felt nothing for eight months. He says his discipline is love, and it does not feel like love. In that moment one of two things has to give, and Paul tells you which: God is true. The consensus of the entire human race, your own eyes, and your own heart at four in the morning are all admitted as evidence, and they lose. Not because your experience is unreal, but because a witness who has been wrong before is not permitted to overrule one who never has.

Which is not a call to pretend, and the guard matters. Paul does not say let God be true and every man be silent. The Bible is full of people telling God exactly what they see, at length and without editing — half the Psalter does little else. You are allowed to say that it looks as though he has forgotten you. What you are not allowed to do is conclude it. Say the whole of what you see; then let his word have the last sentence rather than the first.

Now go and look at the psalm Paul quotes, because a citation left unopened is a claim left unproved — and this one is startling. The words come from Psalm 51, and Psalm 51 is David after Bathsheba: after the adultery, after the pregnancy, after arranging for a loyal soldier to be abandoned in the front line so that the husband would not come home. That is the man saying “against you, you only, have I sinned… so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment” (Psalm 51:4). He is not defending himself. He is agreeing with the verdict, in advance, without conditions — declaring that when God judges him, God will be in the right.

Which is exactly why Paul reaches for it here. He needs to show that God’s truthfulness is not damaged by human failure but displayed by it, and the proof is a man at the bottom of his own life saying so. The worst thing David ever did did not make God’s word less reliable. It demonstrated it: God had said what such a man is, and such a man turned out to be exactly that.

So here is the test, and it is the most searching use of this verse. Take the last time you were rebuked — by Scripture, by a sermon, or by a person who loved you enough to say it. Did you come out of it agreeing with God, or explaining yourself? Almost all of us explain. We supply the context, the provocation, the tiredness, the other party’s share. And every syllable of explanation is a small attempt to keep the verdict from being wholly just. David does something that costs a great deal more and pays a great deal better: he stops arguing and lets God be right about him.

And there is deep comfort in the same doctrine turned round, which is where this passage is finally aiming. If God’s faithfulness were contingent on ours, then the assurance of every Christian would rise and fall with the quality of his last fortnight. It is not, and it does not. He remains faithful even when we are faithless, for he cannot deny himself (2 Timothy 2:13) — which means the fixed point in your life is not your grip on him. It is his character, which was never in your keeping and therefore was never at risk.

verseByVerse.quote: But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) By no means! For then how could God judge the world?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul engages a sophistic objection: if human sin provides the dark background against which divine righteousness shines more brightly, is God’s condemnation of sinners not unjust? The objection sounds clever; Paul dismisses it as human reasoning (kata anthrōpon) that cannot survive contact with the nature of God. God’s role as Judge of the world — acknowledged by all who believe in God at all — requires that his judgment be just. A God who rewarded sin because it served his glory would not be the righteous Judge; he would be the patron of wickedness.

It is worth stating the objection in modern dress, because put in Paul’s terms it can sound like an academic curiosity, and it is nothing of the kind. It runs like this. God gets glory from forgiving sinners. No sinners, no forgiveness; no forgiveness, no glory. Therefore my sin is, in a roundabout way, a service — and it is a bit hard for God to be furious about the raw material of his own reputation. Nobody says this out loud. A great many people run some version of it quietly, and it is the oldest trick in the human repertoire: to find a way in which the thing you were going to do anyway turns out to be useful.

Watch what Paul does with it, because his method is as instructive as his answer. First he flags his own sentence: I speak in a human way. He has just voiced an argument he considers blasphemous and he does not want it left in the air with his name attached. Then he refuses it with the same explosive negative as two verses earlier. And then — this is the part worth noticing — he does not construct a philosophical rebuttal. He asks a question: for then how could God judge the world?

That is not evasion; it is the argument. Every party to this conversation, Jew or Greek, agreed on one thing: that God will judge the world. It is the fixed point. And the objection, followed to its end, abolishes it — because if evil that serves God’s glory cannot be punished, and all evil somehow serves God’s glory, then nothing whatever can be punished, and there is no judgment of anything by anybody. The objector has not found a loophole. He has sawn off the branch he is sitting on, and Paul simply points at the saw.

And the flaw underneath is worth naming, because it recurs in a hundred forms. God can and does bring good out of evil; he is not thereby implicated in the evil. Joseph told his brothers exactly this and did not soften either half: “as for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Both clauses stand. The brothers’ intention was wicked and God’s intention was good, and the fact that the second used the first does not convert it into the second. The supreme instance is the cross, where the worst act in human history accomplished the salvation of the world — and Peter, preaching it, manages both truths in one sentence: delivered up according to the definite plan of God, and you crucified and killed him (Acts 2:23). Nobody at Pentecost heard that as an acquittal.

Which brings the verse where it needs to land, because this is not really a debating point. It is a mechanism people use, and the modern versions are easy to recognise once named. God can bring good out of this. He knows my heart. I will be a better help to people afterwards for having been through it. My testimony will be all the more powerful. Every one of those sentences is true in its place, and every one of them can be deployed in advance, as a permission slip, which is the precise moment it stops being theology and becomes a lie.

So here is the test, and it turns on tense rather than content. Notice when you reach for the sovereignty of God. Afterwards, looking back on something you regret, saying that God has been better to you than you deserved and has brought something out of the wreckage — that is faith, and it is what Genesis 50:20 is for. Beforehand, while a decision is still open, saying that God can work anything out — that is not faith. It is the objection of verse 5, in your own voice, doing exactly the work Paul says it does. The same sentence is worship in the past tense and self-permission in the future one.

And note where the confidence of the whole passage rests. Paul does not defend God’s justice by explaining it. He assumes that a God who did not punish evil would be a worse God, not a kinder one — that a Judge who could be argued out of a verdict by a clever man is no protection to anybody. Which is finally the comfort in this hard little exchange: the God who cannot be talked round when the argument is in your favour also cannot be talked round when it is not.

verseByVerse.quote: But if through my lie God's truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? And why not do evil that good may come? — as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The objection escalates to its logical extreme: if God’s glory is served by human sin, why not maximise the glory by maximising the sin? Paul does not pause to refute this at length — he simply notes that some have slanderously attributed this antinomian conclusion to him (probably in reaction to his doctrine of grace), and pronounces their condemnation just. The logic of “do evil that good may come” is the reductio ad absurdum of every attempt to conscript God’s purposes into an excuse for sin. Grace is never a licence; it is always a power.

Do not hurry past the most remarkable detail in these two verses, which is not the objection but the parenthesis: as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Paul is reporting that there were people going around claiming this was his actual teaching. He had preached free grace so unreservedly — righteousness apart from works, God justifying the ungodly, nothing to bring and nothing to pay — that respectable religious people concluded he must be telling converts that sin no longer mattered.

That is worth sitting with, because it functions as a test of preaching that has never failed. Nobody ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging immorality. Nobody has ever misheard a sermon about trying harder as permission to sin. The charge of antinomianism is only ever levelled at a message of grace so free that it sounds dangerous — which means that if your gospel has never once been misunderstood in this particular direction, it is worth asking whether you have actually preached the thing Paul was preaching. A gospel nobody could possibly abuse is usually a gospel with a condition quietly attached.

And notice how Paul handles a false accusation about his own ministry, because it is not what we would do. He gives it one clause. He does not devote a paragraph to clearing his name, does not enumerate the ways he has been misrepresented, and does not appeal for fairness. He corrects the record in seven words and moves on to the argument, which was always more important than his reputation. Anyone who has ever been misquoted knows how much restraint that takes.

Then the sentence that stops the reader: their condemnation is just. It is startling in its brevity — Paul has just been asked a question and answers with a verdict rather than an argument, and some readers find that unsatisfying. But it is deliberate, and it is right. Some propositions are not to be debated but refused, because to argue them on their merits is already to concede that they might have some. A man who asks whether it might be good to do evil has not made an intellectual error you can correct with information. He has revealed what he wants, and dressed it in a syllogism.

Which is why the answer Paul does not give here is as important as the one he does. He will come back to this precise question in chapter 6 — “are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?” — and the answer there is not a rule but a fact: you died to sin, how can you still live in it? The reason he defers it is that the full answer requires a doctrine he has not laid out yet, namely union with Christ. He cannot explain why a Christian will not want to sin more until he has explained what a Christian is. So here he simply blocks the road, and three chapters later he shows you the country on the other side of it.

Meanwhile the everyday form of this is not the bald proposition but something subtler, and it is worth naming so it can be recognised. Almost nobody thinks I shall sin in order that grace may abound. What people think, at eleven at night, is: this is forgivable. And it is. That is the whole trouble. The doctrine is being used, in the moment before the act, to reduce the cost of it — which is not the abuse of a bad doctrine but the abuse of the best one there is, and it is only possible because grace really is that free.

So here is the test, and it is short. When you consider doing something you know is wrong, does the thought of God’s forgiveness make it easier or harder? For a man who has understood the gospel, the answer moves in a direction that surprises him: knowing what the forgiveness cost makes the sin more expensive, not less. He is not restrained by fear of punishment — that was settled — but by something considerably stronger, which is the difficulty of casually doing the thing that killed his friend. If the forgiveness is functioning as a discount, then whatever is being believed, it is not this gospel.

Because grace was never a permission. It is a power, as the entry above says, and the difference shows in what it produces. The grace of God that brings salvation does not merely pardon; it trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions (Titus 2:11–12). The men in verse 8 had understood the pardon and never met the trainer — which is why Paul does not argue with them. You cannot reason someone into a household he has not entered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — No One Is Righteous: The Verdict of Scripture
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has argued the guilt of the Gentile from creation and conscience. He has argued the guilt of the moralist and the Jew from their own failure to live by the law they possess. Now he seals the case with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures. The catena of Old Testament citations in vv. 10–18 — drawn from Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10, 36, and Isaiah 59 — forms a comprehensive indictment: no one is righteous, no one understands, no one seeks God; their throats are open graves, their mouths full of cursing and bitterness, their feet swift to shed blood, and there is no fear of God before their eyes.

The theological move is masterful. Paul is not importing foreign charges against Israel; he is using Israel's own sacred texts to establish Israel's own guilt. The Torah was given to the Jew; and the Torah says that no one is righteous. Therefore the Jew who trusts in the Torah as a source of righteousness has not read the Torah carefully enough. The law's purpose is not to provide righteousness but to reveal the absence of it: "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (v. 20).

"No one" — the universality is relentless. Not most people. Not unreformed people. Not people without religion. No one. The scope of the verdict prepares for the scope of the remedy: the gospel is for everyone because everyone needs it equally. There are no moral high achievers who need it slightly less. There are no spiritual derelicts for whom it is too late. The ground is completely level: all have sinned, all fall short (v. 23), all are justified freely by grace (v. 24).

And the section closes with a courtroom image worth naming, because it is the most vivid thing in it. The purpose of the whole indictment, Paul says, is “so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God” (v. 19). A stopped mouth is what happens at the end of a trial that has gone badly: the defendant who arrived with explanations has run out of them, and the silence in the dock is the verdict arriving before the judge speaks it. That silence is not the aim of the passage but its precondition — because a man still talking is a man still defending himself, and nobody has ever been justified by grace while he was still presenting a case.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity

Romans 3:9–20 is the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of total depravity. The doctrine does not mean that every human being is as bad as possible, but that sin has corrupted every dimension of human nature — the mind ("no one understands"), the will ("no one seeks for God"), the affections, the speech, the conduct, the very orientation of the soul. No part of the human person is untouched by the fall. This means that the human contribution to salvation is precisely zero: we do not contribute our goodwill, our moral achievement, our religious sensitivity. Salvation is entirely of God from beginning to end. This is why Paul can say in v. 24 that justification is "freely" given — there is nothing in us to which it could be a response.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The catena of psalms and prophets Paul deploys was drawn from Israel's own worship book. These were texts sung in the temple, prayed in the synagogue, memorised by devout Jews. Their application to Israel's own guilt was deeply confrontational — like a church being indicted by its own hymns. Now: The contemporary church sometimes prefers a more optimistic anthropology — emphasising human potential and the image of God while minimising the ravages of the fall. Romans 3:9–20 is the permanent corrective. The doctrine of human depravity is not pessimism; it is realism. And realism about the disease is the precondition for gratitude for the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: "None is righteous, no, not one;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verdict is total. Having given both Gentile (ch. 1) and Jew (ch. 2) their separate indictments, Paul now pronounces the comprehensive judgment: all, both Jews and Greeks, are “under sin” — not merely “guilty of sins” but enslaved beneath sin as a dominating power. The plural sins are symptoms; the singular Sin is the disease. “None is righteous, no, not one” — the absolute negation admits no exceptions. The citation from Psalm 14 was Israel’s own Scripture turning on Israel: not just the heathen, but all.

Notice the legal vocabulary, because Paul has been building a case and this is the moment he sums up. We have already charged — the word belongs to a prosecutor bringing a formal accusation. Chapters 1 and 2 were not a survey of human behaviour; they were the presentation of evidence, and the reader has been in a courtroom since 1:18 without necessarily realising it.

And the charge, when it comes, is not the one we expect. Paul does not say that all have committed sins. He says that all are under sin — a preposition of authority, the same construction you would use for a soldier under orders or a debtor under obligation. The entry above puts it exactly: the plural is the symptom and the singular is the disease. And this is the difference between two entirely distinct diagnoses of the human condition. If the problem is sins, then the problem is a record, and what a man needs is a pardon. If the problem is Sin, then the problem is a power he is under, and he needs to be rescued. This letter will say that God did both, and it will spend chapter 3 on the first and chapters 6 to 8 on the second.

Which is why the objection people raise here misses its mark. Someone always says: but I know perfectly decent people who are not enslaved to anything. Of course. Paul is not saying that everyone is a criminal or that no unbeliever is kind; he has just conceded that Gentiles do by nature what the law requires (2:14). He is saying something less visible and more serious. A man may be honest, generous, faithful to his wife, admired by everyone who knows him, and still be living his entire life without reference to the God who made him — and that is what being under sin looks like in a respectable postcode. The chains are not always the kind that chafe.

Then the citation, and the way Paul uses it. Psalm 14 opens with the fool who says in his heart there is no God, and the original readers knew exactly who that was about: the nations, the enemies of Israel, the people outside. It was a comfortable psalm if you were inside. Paul takes it and turns it round on the very people who sang it. The effect is something like a congregation being indicted by its own hymnbook — the words are familiar, everyone knows the tune, and this morning they are about you.

And feel how the sentence lands: none is righteous, no, not one. Paul is not content with the general statement. He adds the clause that closes the last available exit, because the human mind, presented with a universal negative, immediately begins hunting for the exception — and it always has a candidate in view, usually itself. Not one is there to prevent the search.

So a test, and it is simply a matter of noticing your own reflex. As you read the catena that follows — throats, tongues, feet, eyes — watch what your mind does with it. Most of us begin quietly assigning the verses: this one fits my brother-in-law, that one describes the state of the country, and here is a good description of somebody at work. That reflex is the very thing chapter 2 exposed, and it is remarkably persistent. Try reading the next eight verses with one discipline: every time you find yourself thinking of another person, stop and ask where the sentence touches you. It takes about four minutes and it is one of the more uncomfortable things you can do with a Bible.

And keep hold of why Paul is doing this, because a man can read these verses and conclude that Christianity thinks poorly of people. It does not. The physician who tells you the growth is malignant is not a pessimist about your body; he is the only person in the room who is going to be any use to you. Paul is levelling the ground, and the reason he is levelling it is that he is about to build something on it that will not fit on an uneven site. Fourteen verses from now the same word appears again — all have sinned, and all are justified freely by his grace. The verdict is total because the remedy is.

verseByVerse.quote: no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three negations — no understanding, no seeking, no good — and they are universal. The Reformed tradition has drawn from these verses the doctrine of total depravity: not that every person is as sinful as they could possibly be, but that every faculty — mind, will, affections — has been affected by the fall, so that unaided human nature neither understands God’s ways nor moves toward him. “No one seeks for God” does not mean that no one is religious; it means that natural religion is always a flight from the true God, not a search for him.

Take the second of those negations on its own, because it is the one people stumble over and the entry above states the answer so compactly that it deserves unfolding. No one seeks for God. Every generation objects: the world is full of seekers. There are pilgrimages, retreats, bookshops with whole walls of spirituality, people who describe themselves as on a journey. How can Paul say nobody is looking?

Because of what is actually being sought. Human beings look tirelessly for what God gives — for meaning, for peace, for forgiveness, for a sense that their life amounts to something, for the assurance that they are loved. Nobody has to be persuaded to want any of that. What nobody seeks, left to himself, is God on his own terms: a God with authority over him, who has the right to name his sin, who will not be edited, and whose company he cannot leave when it becomes inconvenient. We are looking for the benefits. We are not looking for the Person, and religion is very often the most sophisticated method available for having the first without the second.

Which is exactly what happened the first time. In the garden, after the fall, God comes walking in the cool of the day and the man is not looking for him; he is behind a tree (Genesis 3:8). And the whole Bible follows that pattern: it is not the record of humanity’s search for God but of God’s search for humanity. He calls to Adam, he comes down to Moses, he pursues Jonah across a sea, he sends prophet after prophet to a people who kill them. And in the end our Lord defines his own mission in the same terms — the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). To seek. If nobody is searching, then somebody has to come.

So here is a test that will settle the question in your own case, and it is uncomfortably simple. Think of what you most want God to do for you at the moment. Now suppose he offered you that thing on the condition that you would have nothing further to do with him — the healing, the restored relationship, the job, the peace of mind, delivered in full, and God himself off the table. Would you take it? Everyone knows their own answer within about two seconds. This is the difference between seeking God’s hand and seeking his face, and Psalm 73 has been the test case for three thousand years: whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (Psalm 73:25).

And note what the passage says about the mind before it says anything about the will: no one understands. This is not a comment on intelligence. It is the claim that something is wrong with the faculty itself where God is concerned, which is why the most brilliant people alive can examine the evidence and come away unmoved while a person of no education whatever grasps the gospel and is transformed by it. Paul says elsewhere exactly this: the natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them (1 Corinthians 2:14). Not unwilling merely. Not able.

Then all have turned aside — a shepherd’s word, and it is the picture Isaiah chose for the same condition: all we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way (Isaiah 53:6). Note the last phrase, because it saves the doctrine from a caricature. Nobody has to be taught to sin and nobody follows a common script; each turns to his own way. Depravity does not produce uniformity. It produces a world of highly individual people going, with great originality, in the same general direction.

All of which would be intolerable reading if the sentence stopped here — and this is the point at which a Christian should notice something about himself. If you are reading this and find that you do want God, that his existence is a comfort rather than a threat, that you would not take the gift without the Giver — then you have just produced evidence that something has happened to you which this verse says does not happen naturally. You did not seek him. The wanting is itself the sign of a work already done, which is why our Lord could say that no one comes to him unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). The seeking you are conscious of is the far end of a search that began somewhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: "Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive." "The venom of asps is under their lips." "Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul strings together citations from Psalms 5, 140, and 10 to describe the corruption of human speech. The throat as “open grave” — something that corrupts everything it touches, that emits death rather than life. The tongue as vehicle of deception; the lips as the delivery system for venom. Human communication, which was designed to be the medium of truth and love, has become the primary instrument of destruction. Augustine observed that the sins of the tongue — slander, flattery, deception, cursing — are among the most socially corrosive sins precisely because they are so easy to commit and so hard to detect.

Before the images, notice the proportions, because they are startling once you count. Paul is walking down a body — throat, tongue, lips, mouth, then feet (v. 15), then eyes (v. 18). Seven items. And four of the seven are the organs of speech. Out of the whole of human wickedness, with murder and violence available to him and duly mentioned, he gives more than half his anatomy to the mouth.

That is not an accident of the texts he happened to string together; it is a judgment about where the trouble surfaces. Our Lord said the same and gave the reason: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:34). Speech is where the inside becomes audible. You can conceal your character in almost every other department for years — nobody sees your thoughts, and conduct can be managed — but you cannot talk for long without giving yourself away, which is why he could add, in the same breath, that on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word (Matthew 12:36). Not the considered ones. The careless ones, because those are the ones that were not edited.

Then the first image, and it is worse than it sounds in English. Their throat is an open grave. For a Jewish reader that phrase carried two things at once. There is the obvious one: a tomb standing open gives off the smell of what is inside, and the throat is simply the passage from a man’s interior to the outside world — so if what comes up out of him smells of death, the report is about what is down there. But there is also the ritual weight, which we miss entirely. Under the law, a man who so much as touched a grave was unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:16). An open grave did not merely offend; it contaminated, and it contaminated people who had done nothing but come near. That is Paul’s claim about human speech. It does not stay with the speaker.

And the four organs are not four ways of saying one thing; they are a sequence. The throat is the source, what comes up from inside. The tongue is the method — they keep on deceiving, and the tense is habitual rather than occasional. The lips are the concealment, and this is the sharpest of the four: the venom of a snake is not on the fangs where you could see it but under them, and by the time you know it is there, it is in you. And the mouth is the overflow — cursing and bitterness, the point at which a man stops bothering to hide it.

Stay with the venom, because it names something we have no other word for. It describes speech that is lethal precisely because it is smooth. Not the shouted insult, which at least announces itself and can be answered. The compliment with a hook in it. The concerned question that plants a doubt about somebody and leaves no fingerprints. The sentence beginning I only say this because I care about you, which is very occasionally true. The observation made in front of others that is perfectly accurate and perfectly timed to humiliate. None of it would stand out on a recording. All of it is under the lip.

James wrote a whole paragraph on the subject and reached for the same picture — the tongue is a restless evil, full of deadly poison, a small fire that sets a great forest ablaze, and no human being can tame it (James 3:5–8). He also makes the observation that puts verse 14 in a church rather than in a gutter: with the same mouth we bless our Lord and Father and curse people who are made in the likeness of God. The mouth that had been singing in the service is the mouth that dismantles somebody in the car afterwards, and it does not even change gear.

And our generation has industrialised this in a way Paul could not have imagined. Most people in history spoke to a few dozen others and their words died in the air. We now speak constantly, in writing, to strangers, at speed, with no tone of voice to soften anything, and the words do not decay — a sentence composed in ninety seconds of irritation can reach thousands of people and still be sitting there in five years. The open grave has been given a distribution network.

So the test, and it is precise to the image rather than general. Do not ask whether you swear. Think of one sentence you said this week that was entirely polite, that nobody in the room would have identified as unkind, and that you knew, as you were forming it, would land somewhere tender. Perhaps you told yourself it was honesty. That sentence is not on your lips. It is under them, and it is the one this verse is about.

And there is a way out, which Scripture gives in the form of a man who made exactly this diagnosis about himself. Isaiah, shown the throne, does not cry out that the nation has unclean lips, though he says that too. He says I am a man of unclean lips — and a coal is taken from the altar and touched to his mouth, and the guilt is taken away (Isaiah 6:5–7). Note where the fire came from: not from his effort at better speech, but off an altar where something had died. And note what happened to that mouth afterwards. It was sent to speak. Which is exactly the reversal this letter is heading for, because the same organ that is called an open grave in chapter 3 turns out, in chapter 10, to be the one you confess with, and are saved (10:9–10).

verseByVerse.quote: "Their feet are swift to shed blood;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the organs of speech (throat, tongue, lips, mouth — vv. 13–14), Paul moves to the feet — the whole body pressed into service of destruction. “Swift to shed blood” echoes Proverbs 1:16 and Isaiah 59:7: the eagerness with which violence is pursued. The catalogue is moving from internal disposition (throat, lips) to external action (feet, paths). Sin is not merely felt; it moves, it travels, it arrives at the place of destruction with terrible efficiency.

Two words carry this line, and the second is the disturbing one. Not that their feet shed blood — that would be an indictment of what people do. Swift. It is an indictment of how quickly they get there, and speed is a measure of desire. Nobody hurries toward something he is reluctant about. The verse is not describing a race that occasionally ends in violence; it is describing an eagerness, and it is the eagerness rather than the violence that tells you what is in the runner.

Which is why the source text is worth opening, because the proverb Paul is echoing describes not a mob but a recruitment. It is the father in Proverbs 1, warning his son about the men who will invite him along: come with us, let us lie in wait for blood, we shall find all precious goods, throw in your lot with us — and then the father’s comment, “their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed blood” (Proverbs 1:11–16). The point of the passage is that the invitation is attractive. It offers company, adventure, and a share of the proceeds. Evil rarely presents itself as evil; it presents itself as belonging.

And feel the change of gear in the catena. Everything up to here has been the inside of a man and the noise he makes. Now the body is in motion, and something has crossed a line that cannot be uncrossed: thought is private, speech is recoverable, but a man who has gone somewhere and done something has produced a fact in the world. Feet are how intention becomes history.

A modern reader will want to file this verse under people unlike himself, and Paul’s whole argument forbids it — so it is worth asking what the sentence covers. Our Lord answered that when he took the sixth commandment and traced it back to its root: everyone who is angry with his brother is liable to judgment, and whoever says you fool is liable to hell (Matthew 5:21–22). John said it flatly: everyone who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). This is not a claim that a harsh word equals a homicide in its consequences. It is a claim about the substance being measured: the desire to see someone diminished, silenced, humiliated, ended — and that desire is available to respectable people at their own kitchen tables. Most of us never reach the deed because we lack the opportunity, the nerve, or the anonymity, which is a mercy but is not innocence.

And bloodshed has always had its clean forms, in which nobody’s feet appear to move at all. David never touched Uriah; he sent a letter and let the Ammonites do it. Ahab did not stone Naboth; a court was convened and witnesses were found. Pilate washed his hands in public and signed the order in private. The distance between the decision and the death is the oldest device in the world for keeping one’s feet unmarked, and it works on the conscience without deceiving the Judge for a moment.

So here is the test, and it is about speed rather than deeds. Notice what you move toward quickly. When somebody you resent is in difficulty, how fast does the news reach you, and how fast do you pass it on? When there is an argument at church, how quickly are you across the room and in it? When a story arrives that confirms what you already thought about someone, how long does it take you to believe it? Nobody has to be dragged toward those things. That is the whole point of the word swift: our feet are perfectly capable of hurrying, and what they hurry toward is the evidence in this trial.

Which is why it is worth remembering what Scripture does with beautiful feet, because it uses the identical image in the opposite direction. Isaiah watched a runner come over the mountains and wrote that his feet were lovely, because of what he was carrying: good news, peace, salvation — and Paul quotes it later in this very letter about the people who bring the gospel (Isaiah 52:7; Romans 10:15). The same organ, the same haste. Feet that ran to shed blood are not, in the end, amputated. They are sent somewhere else, in a hurry, carrying something worth the speed.

verseByVerse.quote: "in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they do not know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The way of peace they do not know” — drawn from Isaiah 59, where the prophet confesses the corporate sin of Israel in exile. Shalom — the comprehensive flourishing of a life rightly ordered to God and neighbour — is simply absent wherever God is absent. The path of the ungodly does not merely bypass peace; it actively produces ruin and misery as its wake. Human civilisation’s track record of violence and wreckage is the exegesis of these two verses across every century.

Notice where the ruin is. It is not in front of them as a destination they are heading for; it is in their paths — behind them, along the route, in the places they have already been. This is the only line in the catena that looks at the damage from the outside, and it changes the camera angle entirely. Every other verse has been an examination of the sinner: his throat, his tongue, his feet, his eyes. This one steps back and photographs the road he has walked down.

And that is the part of sin we are least equipped to see, because we experience our own lives from the inside, as a sequence of understandable decisions, each with its reasons. The wreckage is not in our field of vision. It is in other people: the child who grew up learning to read a father’s mood before coming into a room; the friend who stopped calling and was never asked why; the colleague who was made to look foolish in a meeting eleven years ago and still thinks about it; the marriage that did not end but went quiet. None of that appears on the sinner’s own account of his life. All of it is in the path.

The two words are worth separating, too. Ruin is breakage — something that was whole is now not. Misery is what the breakage costs the people living in it. So the verse gives both the fact and the feeling: a thing destroyed, and somebody carrying it. Sin is never only an offence against God registered in heaven; it always has a second address, and there is usually a person at it.

Then the sentence that names what is missing: the way of peace they do not know. Peace here is not the absence of trouble but shalom — everything in its proper place, working, whole. So the charge is not merely that these people fight. It is that they have never learned the road to the thing every one of them wants. And the wording is exact: not that they refuse the way of peace, but that they do not know it. There is real pathos in that. The whole human race is trying to arrive somewhere it cannot find, which is why every generation produces its own confident method — better education, better systems, better technology, better politics — and why each one produces a fresh crop of ruin along the way. Isaiah, from whom this comes, watched his own nation do it and said they were like men groping along a wall at midday (Isaiah 59:10).

So here is the test, and it is harder than the usual sort because you cannot run it alone. Pick the three people closest to you and ask, honestly, what it costs to be in a relationship with you. Not what you provide — what it costs. Where do they walk carefully? What subject do they avoid raising? What have they stopped expecting? Most of us can answer for other people immediately and go blank about ourselves, which is the point. And there is a braver version, which is to ask one of them. The answer will not be a catalogue of atrocities. It will be small, specific, and about ten years old, and it will be in your path.

Which is why repentance in Scripture so often involves other people and not only God. Zacchaeus did not merely confess; he calculated fourfold and started writing cheques (Luke 19:8). Our Lord told a man to leave his gift at the altar and go and be reconciled to his brother first (Matthew 5:23–24) — an extraordinary instruction, since it interrupts an act of worship for the sake of a repair. Guard one thing there: not every path can be walked back down. Some people are dead, some are unreachable, some would be harmed by your returning, and in those cases the road back is closed and forgiveness is not thereby withheld. But where it is open it should be walked, and the walking is usually the last thing we want to do.

And there is one more thing to say, which is the whole reason this verse can be read without despair. The way of peace is not known — so somebody had to come and be it. “He himself is our peace”, Paul writes to another church, of the one who made peace by the blood of his cross and came and preached peace to those who were far off (Ephesians 2:14–17). The road that nobody could find turned out not to be a road at all. It is a Person, and he came looking for the people leaving ruin in their paths — and this letter will shortly say that he did it while they were still doing it (5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: "There is no fear of God before their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The capstone of the catena. Psalm 36:1 identifies the root of all the wickedness described in vv. 13–17: no fear of God. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10) — and where it is absent, wisdom collapses and every vice catalogued above follows. “Before their eyes” — the phrase suggests habitual orientation: the eyes are pointed away from God, and all that follows is a consequence of that turning. Sin is, at bottom, a failure of worship before it is a failure of morality.

Notice that the body is now complete. Throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet — and finally eyes. And the order is worth seeing, because Paul has built the catena backwards: he begins with what a man is, moves to what he says, then to where he goes, and arrives last at what he is looking at. Six charges of symptom, and then the cause. Everything above this line is a consequence of this line.

So it is worth being clear about what the fear of God is, because the phrase has been damaged by association. It does not mean terror, and it does not mean a nervous religion of cringing before a temperamental deity. We use the expression ourselves in exactly the right sense and never notice: he has no fear of his employer, we say, or that boy has no fear of his father — and nobody hearing it thinks we mean the man should be frightened. We mean that the other person’s reality does not weigh with him. He is not restrained by it, does not consult it, and behaves in that person’s presence exactly as he would in his absence. That is the charge here. Not that these people are insufficiently scared. That God’s existence makes no practical difference to them at all.

And the phrase before their eyes is precise: it describes what a man keeps in view while he is deciding. Everyone knows a speed limit exists; the appearance of a patrol car in the mirror alters behaviour instantly, and nothing about the belief has changed — only what is in the frame. That is how it works with God, which is why almost nobody sins while consciously aware of him. The Christian’s problem is rarely that he stops believing (chapter 1 has already described the quieter version of this, at 1:28). It is that at the moment of choosing, God is simply not in the picture, and the picture is what governs conduct.

Which is exactly why this verse belongs at the end of the list rather than anywhere else. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7) — so its absence explains the first charge in the catena as well as the last. Verse 11 said no one understands; verse 18 says why. It is not that these people are unintelligent, but that they have removed from view the one fact that makes sense of every other, and a man reasoning about his life with God left out of the frame will reason with great sophistication to conclusions that are reliably wrong.

Now, since a Christian reading this may be uneasy about the whole idea: is a believer supposed to fear God? John says that perfect love casts out fear, and he is right — but he is careful about which fear, adding that fear has to do with punishment (1 John 4:18). The dread of being condemned is gone, and this letter will say so in the plainest terms at 8:1. What is not gone, and grows, is the other thing. A child of a good father is not afraid of him and would not dream of being flippant about him; the boy is entirely at ease on his knee and would go white if he heard someone speak of his father with contempt. Both at once, and neither weakening the other. That is the fear this verse says is missing.

And where does anybody get it? Not by working himself into a state of reverence, which does not last past Tuesday. It is a covenant gift, promised in so many words: “I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me” (Jeremiah 32:40). Note the purpose clause — the fear is given as the thing that keeps a man. It is not the opposite of assurance; it is part of the machinery by which God holds on to people.

So here is the test, and it is exact to the phrase. Ask what you would do differently in the next hour if Christ were standing in the room, visible. Not the next year, and not a heroic change — the next hour. What would you not open, not say, not watch, not put off? Whatever appears on that list is the measure of how much of your day is currently lived with God out of frame, and the gap is not a matter of belief, because you already believe he is there. It is a matter of sight.

And Paul’s last quotation carries its own cure, if you follow it home. This line comes from Psalm 36, which opens with the wicked man who has no fear of God before his eyes — and then turns, eight verses later, to say: your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens; with you is the fountain of life; and in your light do we see light (Psalm 36:5–9). The psalm that diagnoses the eye is the psalm that supplies the light. The catena ends in darkness, and Paul knew perfectly well where the rest of it goes.

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin. — Romans 3:19-20
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Every mouth stopped” — the image is of a courtroom where the defendant, having heard the indictment, has nothing to say. The law’s function in this context is prosecutorial: it silences every human excuse, every plea of mitigating circumstances, every claim of comparative righteousness. Before God, no one can say “but I was better than most” or “consider what I did achieve”. Every mouth is stopped.

“Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (v. 20b) — this is the law’s diagnostic function, which Luther and Calvin called the first use of the law. The law is a mirror, not a ladder. It shows us what we are, not how to become what we should be. The person who understands this has been prepared by the law to receive the gospel — because she has been stripped of every alternative source of righteousness and left with only the grace of God.

Take the first clause on its own, because it closes the last door and most readers walk straight past it. Whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law. Paul has just quoted six passages, and every one of them is from Israel’s own Scriptures — which invites an obvious escape. A Jewish reader could grant every word and conclude that the psalmist was describing the nations, the wicked, the enemies of God: bad people, elsewhere. Paul blocks it with a single procedural observation. Those texts were addressed to the people who possess them. Scripture speaks to the congregation that owns it. You do not get to receive the Bible as a description of somebody else.

Which is worth transferring, because the instinct is identical in a church. We are all competent at hearing a sermon on behalf of others — this would help my son, my wife should be here for this, I do hope he is listening. The rule of verse 19 is that the word lands first on the people in the room, and there is no arrangement whereby you may pass it along without receiving it yourself.

And notice the sequence Paul builds: the law speaks, mouths are stopped, and only then is the world accountable. That order is deliberate. A man does not become guilty when he stops arguing; he was guilty already. What the silence does is end the process of defence, and until the defence ends, nothing can be given — because a man who is still presenting a case is asking for a verdict, and the gospel does not offer verdicts to people who want to be judged fairly. Grace has nothing whatever to say to a man who still believes he might win.

Then verse 20, which is the sentence the whole letter has been walking toward since chapter 2, and it should be read as the answer to a question already asked. Back at 2:7 Paul stated the standard: patient continuance in well-doing, and God will give eternal life. It was a genuine offer on honest terms. At 2:13 he stated the rule: not the hearers of the law but the doers will be justified. Both left one question open — and who has done it? Here is the answer, and it is delivered as a verdict rather than an argument: by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight. The standard was real. The finding is that nobody meets it. Chapter 2 was the statute; chapter 3 is the judgment.

Note also the precise wording, because it does not say what people often hear. It does not say the law is bad, or that obedience does not matter, or that God has lowered the standard. It says that by this route no one arrives. The road is not condemned; it is simply reported to be impassable, and the report is made by the surveyor who laid it out.

And the final clause explains what the road is for, which the entry above rightly calls the first use of the law (developed at 2:21–22 and not repeated here). Through the law comes knowledge of sin — and the word is the stronger one, full recognition rather than vague awareness. Everyone knows in some general way that they are not what they should be. The law converts that fog into an itemised statement. Which is why an honest reading of the Ten Commandments is more use to an unconverted man than any amount of encouragement: you cannot want a Saviour while your problem remains a mood.

So the test here is not another examination of conscience but a question about what you do with the results. When Scripture shows you something true about yourself, where do you go next? Some go to despair, which is the law doing half its work and stopping. Some go to resolve, which is the law doing none of it — the man has heard that he cannot climb and has responded by training harder. The law has done its full work only when a man stops climbing and starts looking for a rescue. Anything else means the mouth is not yet stopped.

And it is worth saying what this passage is not. This is the darkest sentence in the letter, and it is not the end of the paragraph. Every mouth stopped, the whole world accountable, no human being justified — and the next words Paul writes are but now. He has spent two and a half chapters demolishing every possible refuge, not because he enjoys demolition, but because what he is about to offer will only be received by people who have nowhere else to stand. The silence in that courtroom is not the end of the trial. It is the pause before the Judge announces that he has provided a righteousness of his own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — But Now: The Righteousness of God Through Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"But now" — nuni de. Two words in Greek that change everything. After three chapters of unrelenting diagnosis — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the Jew convicted by his own scriptures, the entire world accountable to God — these two words open a door out of a sealed room. The righteousness of God has been manifested. Apart from the law. Through faith in Jesus Christ. For all who believe. Freely. By grace. Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

This is the centre of Romans. This is the centre of Paul's gospel. This is the theological core of the Reformation. Every word of vv. 21–26 has been weighed and debated and celebrated for two millennia — and still it burns with the same fire. God put Christ forward as a propitiation — a mercy seat, a place of atonement — by His blood, to be received by faith. In this act, God demonstrated His own righteousness: He passed over former sins (under the patient forbearance of the old covenant) and He condemned the sin that deserved condemnation — in His own Son, at Calvary. The God who justifies the ungodly (4:5) is not a God who winks at sin. He is a God who bore its full weight in the person of His Son.

Boasting is excluded (v. 27). The person who is justified by faith through Christ has nothing to boast of but Christ. The Jew cannot boast in the Torah; the Greek cannot boast in philosophy; the moralist cannot boast in her record; the religious cannot boast in his devotion. The ground is level. There is one God, and He justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. The gospel is the great leveller — and the great glorifier, because it redirects all glory from the creature to the Creator.

Two things at the edges of the section should not be lost. The first is the sentence on which the whole offer rests, and it is the shortest in the passage: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (v. 23). It is not an insult dropped into a paragraph about grace; it is the reason there is a paragraph about grace, and everything from 1:18 onward has been written to make those seven words land as a plain description rather than an accusation. The second is the question Paul asks last, which is the one his critics had been asking loudly: do we then overthrow the law by this faith (v. 31)? He has just said righteousness comes apart from the law, and the obvious inference is that the law has been discarded — the very charge of 3:8. His answer is the strongest denial in his vocabulary, and then four words that will take him the whole of chapter 4 to prove: we uphold the law. Justification by faith does not abolish the Old Testament. It is what the Old Testament was about.
verseByVerse.theology:
Propitiation: The Heart of the Atonement

Romans 3:25 introduces one of the most important words in the New Testament: hilastērion — propitiation. This word carries the specific meaning of an offering that averts divine wrath by satisfying it. Leon Morris demonstrated exhaustively that this is the correct reading against C.H. Dodd's attempted substitution of "expiation" (which only removes sin, without reference to wrath). Christ's death on the cross was not merely a moral demonstration or a removal of guilt; it was the bearing of the holy wrath of God against sin, so that God could be both just (the sin was punished) and the justifier (the sinner is acquitted). The Reformed tradition has always insisted on this: without propitiation, justification has no foundation. If the wrath was not truly satisfied, the forgiveness is not truly free.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of vv. 24–25 deliberately echoes the Day of Atonement ritual of Leviticus 16: the mercy seat (hilastērion) where blood was sprinkled to cover the sins of the people. Paul is saying: what the Day of Atonement pointed to, Christ has accomplished — once for all, for all who believe. The entire sacrificial system of the old covenant found its fulfilment and its terminus in the cross. Now: Every human religion has some mechanism for dealing with the problem of guilt — sacrifice, ritual, moral achievement, reincarnation, denial. Romans 3:21–31 announces that the only mechanism that actually works is the one God provided: the substitutionary death of His own Son, received by faith. There is no other name, no other blood, no other righteousness that avails.

verseByVerse.quote: But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it — the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But now” — two of the most momentous words in Paul. After the unrelenting darkness of 1:18–3:20, the light breaks. The righteousness of God has been manifested — not constructed or invented, but revealed, disclosed, brought into the open. It is “apart from the law” (not earned by law-keeping) yet “witnessed by the Law and Prophets” (not discontinuous with Israel’s Scriptures). It comes “through faith in Jesus Christ” — or, in the reading preferred by many: through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ. In either case, the righteousness is anchored in Christ, not in human achievement.

Stand still at the hinge for a moment, because the whole letter turns on it and it is easy to read past two small words. Everything from 1:18 has been a closing down. Creation leaves nobody an excuse; conscience convicts the man without the law; the law convicts the man who has it; the moralist is condemned by the standard he applies to others; and the Scriptures themselves supply the verdict, until every mouth is stopped and there is nothing left to say. It is the most sustained demolition in the Bible. And into that silence: but now.

Note that Paul does not say therefore. There is nothing in chapters 1 to 3 from which grace follows. He does not present the gospel as the conclusion of an argument but as an interruption of one — an announcement from outside the courtroom, which is exactly what the word gospel always meant: news, not advice. And the tense is worth having: the righteousness of God has been manifested, a completed act with standing results. It is not on offer pending conditions. It has happened, in public, at a datable moment, and the announcement is simply catching up with it.

Then the phrase that must be held in both hands: apart from the law, and yet the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it. Those look like opposite claims and are not. The law is not the source of this righteousness — it never produced any, as the last verse established — but it has been pointing at it from the beginning. Every sacrifice, every high priest going in on the Day of Atonement, every prophet who spoke of a servant wounded for our transgressions, was a signpost. And a signpost is apart from the destination in the sense that you cannot live in it, and utterly connected to it in the sense that it exists for nothing else.

Which is why Paul is at such pains to say this. He is not founding a new religion; he is announcing that the old one has arrived at what it was for. The charge that his gospel was a novelty has already been answered in the first sentence of the letter — promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures (1:2) — and here he answers it again at the moment of maximum pressure. The God of the gospel and the God of Israel are not two Gods with two schemes.

The entry above rightly flags the disputed phrase, and it is worth a plain word for a reader who has met the debate. Does Paul mean faith in Jesus Christ — our believing — or the faithfulness of Jesus Christ — his obedience unto death? The Greek permits both, serious scholars divide, and the reason it does not much matter here is that Paul immediately says the other one: for all who believe. Whichever way the first phrase is taken, the second supplies the missing half in the same breath. The righteousness rests on what Christ has done, and it reaches a person by faith. Nobody who holds both has lost anything.

And then the phrase that decides who this is for: for all who believe. Not for all who believe and. There is no second clause anywhere in the sentence — no qualifying period of probation, no minimum standard of improvement, no requirement that you first become the sort of person to whom such an offer could decently be made. Paul has spent three chapters establishing that no such person exists, precisely so that the offer could be phrased this way.

So the test is not an examination of your life but of what you are actually resting on, and it is best run at the point where it is hardest. Think of your worst week this year — the one with the failure in it that you have not told anybody about. Now ask what changed about your standing with God during that week. If the honest answer is that it dropped and has since partially recovered, then you are still living under chapter 2, whatever you believe about chapter 3. A righteousness that is manifested apart from the law is not affected by your performance under the law, because it never rested on it at any point.

Two words, then, standing between the worst news ever delivered to the human race and the best. Everything behind them is true and nothing behind them has been withdrawn — the diagnosis stands, and it stands over you. And then God says but now, which is not a softening of the verdict but the announcement that he has done something about it himself.

verseByVerse.quote: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” — the universal diagnosis that makes the universal offer necessary. The glory of God — the full, shining reality of what human beings were made to reflect — is what sin has stolen. But where sin has universally destroyed, grace universally offers: “justified by his grace as a gift” (dōrean — freely, without payment). Redemption (apolytrōsis) is a marketplace and ransom word: liberation of a slave or prisoner at a price. The price was paid in Christ Jesus. This is the centre of the Bible.

Notice first that these are not two sentences but one. We are used to hearing verse 23 on its own — it is the verse people memorise, and it gets quoted as a standalone verdict on the human race. In Paul it has no full stop. All have sinned… and are justified by his grace as a gift. The diagnosis and the remedy arrive in a single breath, and the same word governs both halves. It is the most important comma in the Bible.

And the word is all, which is doing something the English can miss. Paul has spent three chapters building a list long enough to catch everybody — the idolater, the moralist, the gossip, the man with four Bibles — precisely so that when this sentence arrives it lands as a description rather than an insult. Nobody in the room gets to feel singled out, because nobody has been.

Then the phrase we translate blandly: they fall short of the glory of God. It is not a moral score. The picture is of something you were made to display and do not. Human beings were made in the image of God — made, that is, to be the one creature in the world that shows what he is like — and the charge is that we do not. Which explains the peculiar ache that accompanies being human and is very difficult to account for on any other view: the sense, available to everyone, of falling short of yourself. You know you were meant for more than you are. Not more successful; more real. That intuition is not vanity and it is not neurosis. It is accurate reporting, and this verse is its explanation.

Note also the tense, because Paul does not leave it in the past. All have sinned — completed, a matter of record — and all fall short, present and continuous. The second verb is not describing the day you were converted. It is describing this morning. Which is worth saying to any Christian who assumes that this half of the sentence has stopped applying to him: you are still falling short as you read, and the next clause is written in exactly the same tense.

Because verse 24 does not say were justified as a distant event. It says they are being justified — freely, by his grace, as a gift. And that word for gift deserves its own moment. Dōrean means gratis, at no cost to the recipient — and the same word turns up in a sentence our Lord quoted about himself: they hated me without a cause (John 15:25). Same word. It is used for hatred that had no reason in its object and for grace that has no reason in its object. There was nothing in him to justify the hatred, and there is nothing in you to justify the gift.

And then the word that stops the sentence being sentimental: redemption. The entry above is right that it belongs to the marketplace — the price paid to release a slave or a prisoner of war. Which tells you two things at once. It tells you what your position was: not that of a man with a poor record, but of a man owned by somebody. And it tells you that grace was free to you and to nobody else. A gift the giver did not pay for is merely a formality; a gift that cost him everything, given to someone who could not contribute a penny, is what this verse means by grace. Free is not the same as cheap. It never was.

So here is a test, and it works because most of us pass verse 23 too quickly. Say the sentence in the first person and see whether it survives: I have sinned and I fall short of the glory of God. Most people can affirm the doctrine and flinch at the pronoun. Then try the second half the same way — and I am justified freely by his grace — and notice which of the two is harder to say without qualifying it. For most Christians it is the second, and the reason is instructive: we can accept a diagnosis that puts us with everybody else far more readily than a gift that puts us in debt to somebody.

The great danger with this verse is that it becomes a slogan, and a slogan is the one thing it cannot afford to be. Read as a standalone, it makes Christianity a low view of people. Read as Paul wrote it, in one sentence with what follows, it says something no religion has ever said: the same all that condemns is the all that is offered the gift, and the only qualification for receiving it is the one every human being already possesses.

verseByVerse.quote: ...whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. — Romans 3:25-26
verseByVerse.commentary:
God put Christ forward — the initiative is entirely divine. This is not a Son appeasing a reluctant Father; the Father himself provides the propitiation. The love of God and the justice of God meet at the cross, not in opposition but in unity.
