God demonstrates his love by giving his Son (5:8); God demonstrates his justice by not passing over sin but bearing it in his Son. The cross is simultaneously the greatest act of love and the most rigorous expression of justice in the history of the universe.

“To be received by faith” — the atonement, objectively accomplished at Calvary, is subjectively received through faith. The bridge between what Christ did and what the sinner receives is faith — not as a meritorious act, but as the God-given instrument of reception. Faith does not earn the righteousness; it lays hold of it. It is the hand that takes the gift, not the labour that earns the wage.

Now the sentence the entry has not yet reached, and it is the one the whole letter has been built to say. Why did the cross have to happen at all? Paul’s answer is not, in the first place, that we needed rescuing — true as that is. It is that God had a problem with his own record. For centuries he had been forgiving people: Abraham lied twice about his wife and remained the friend of God; David committed adultery and murder and was told the LORD had put away his sin; the whole sacrificial system ran on the blood of animals, which, as Hebrews says flatly, can never take away sins (Hebrews 10:4). So an accusation was accumulating against heaven itself. On what grounds had all this been let through?

That is the force of he had passed over former sins. The word is not the word for forgiveness; it means to let go by, to leave unpunished for the present, and it puts God in the position of a judge who has been suspending sentences for two thousand years without ever explaining himself. Which is why Paul says the cross was a demonstration — a public exhibit, evidence produced in court. God was not merely saving sinners at Calvary. He was clearing his own name.

And that is what makes verse 26 the summit of the letter: so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Hold the two halves apart for a moment and feel the difficulty, because we have heard it too often to be startled by it. A judge who acquits the guilty is not merciful; he is corrupt, and every legal system on earth knows it. Proverbs says so without qualification: he who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD (Proverbs 17:15). God’s own law forbade the very thing his gospel appears to do. The question of Romans is not how a loving God can forgive. It is how a just God can, and remain just.

The answer is in the word propitiation, and this letter has already prepared for it: wrath is real, personal and being revealed, and at the cross it was absorbed rather than deflected (see on 1:18). Nothing was waived. The sentence was carried out in full — on somebody else, by arrangement, with the Judge providing the substitute out of his own household. That is why God can pronounce a guilty man righteous without a fiction: the penalty is not overlooked, it is paid, and the acquittal rests on an execution that has already taken place.

Note also where Paul locates the mercy seat. The Greek word behind propitiation is the term used in the Greek Old Testament for the lid of the ark — the place in the innermost room where, once a year, blood was sprinkled and God met his people over the covering of a box containing the law they had broken. Only the high priest went in, once, in the dark, with blood that had to be brought again the following year. Paul says God put Christ forward — set him out in the open, in public, in daylight, on a hill outside a city wall, where anybody could see. The holiest thing in Israel had been hidden behind a curtain for a thousand years. At the cross it was carried outside and shown to the crowd.

So here is the test, and it goes to what your assurance is actually made of. Ask yourself why God accepts you, and listen for whether the answer contains any reference to God’s kindness, his willingness to overlook, his understanding of your circumstances. If it does, your assurance is resting on his character as you imagine it, and it will not hold at four in the morning, because a God who overlooks things could presumably also change his mind about overlooking them. The answer this passage gives is harder and infinitely steadier: he accepts you because the debt was paid, and it would be unjust of him to collect it twice. Justice, which is what you feared, has become the ground on which you stand.

Which is why the old preachers loved to say that mercy and truth have met together, and righteousness and peace have kissed each other (Psalm 85:10). At the cross, God did not choose between being loving and being just, and he did not balance them against each other in some compromise where each got less than its due. He satisfied both, completely, at his own expense — and the only person in the transaction who lost anything was himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Boasting — the assertion of merit before God — is “excluded”. Not diminished or complicated or redirected, but categorically shut out. The principle that excludes it is faith, not works: faith is the hand that receives a gift, not the labour that earns a wage. “Justified by faith apart from works of the law” is the Reformation’s anchor text — and rightly so, for it captures the logic that Paul has been building since 1:17. The righteousness of God is his to give, freely, to those who trust him.

The word Paul uses is stronger than “excluded” suggests in modern English. It is the word for shutting a door — barred out, locked outside. Boasting is not discouraged, or moderated, or permitted in small quantities among mature believers. It has been put out of the building and the door has been closed behind it.

And notice what has done the excluding, because it is not what we would expect. Paul does not say boasting is excluded by humility, or by a rule against it, or by a proper sense of proportion. It is excluded by a principle — by the structure of how salvation works. This matters enormously in practice, because a man told to stop boasting will simply learn to boast more quietly, and self-congratulation, once driven underground, becomes considerably harder to detect and no less pleasant to indulge. What Paul describes is not a prohibition but a demolition: there is nothing left to boast about. You cannot be proud of a gift you did not choose, earn, deserve, or contribute to. The impulse is not forbidden. It is unemployed.

Which is the answer to a question every honest Christian eventually asks: why has God arranged salvation this way? Why by faith and not by effort — when effort would at least keep people trying? Part of the answer is here. If any element of your standing rested on you, then somewhere in the last analysis you would have grounds for a comparison, and comparison is the seedbed of everything Paul has been denouncing since chapter 2. God has closed off boasting not because he cannot bear rivals, but because boasting is a poison, and the only cure for it is a salvation in which no one has anything to show.

Then the sentence that changed the history of the West: we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law. The full argument for how this sits with judgment according to works has been given already (see on 2:7–8), and does not need repeating here. But notice the strange verb: we hold — we reckon, we conclude, we count it settled. Paul is not floating a proposal. He has been building a case for two and a half chapters and this is the finding, entered into the record.

It is worth noticing which word Luther added and why the argument has never depended on it. His German translation supplied allein — justified by faith alone — and he was attacked for it for the rest of his life. The word is not in the Greek. It is, however, exactly what the sentence means, because apart from works of the law is what “alone” is for: if works are excluded, faith is the only thing left standing. Luther inserted a word that was already doing its work in the sentence, and every opponent who objected had to explain what else, besides faith, Paul had left in.

And a guard, because this is the point at which people become anxious about their faith instead of their works — which is the same disease with a new address. If you find yourself asking whether your faith is strong enough, sincere enough, or sufficiently free of doubt to count, you have begun to treat faith as a work: something you produce, of a certain quality, which God then rewards. It is not. Faith is not the payment; it is the receiving. A weak hand and a strong hand take hold of the same rope, and the rope does the holding. What saves is not the excellence of your grip but the strength of what you are gripping.

So here is a test, and it is quick. Notice what you find yourself mentioning when you want somebody to think well of you spiritually — how long you have been a Christian, what you have read, what you gave up, how much you serve, the difficulty of your circumstances borne well. Nobody is exempt from this; the currency simply varies with the congregation. In some circles it is zeal, in others it is doctrinal precision, in others suffering, in others how relaxed one is about the things other Christians worry over. Whatever it is, it is a boast, and this verse says the door it is trying to come in by has been locked.

Which turns out to be a kindness rather than a deprivation. A religion of achievement requires you to keep score, and keeping score is exhausting in both directions — it makes you anxious when you are losing and insufferable when you are winning. Paul has removed the scoreboard. There is only one thing left for anybody to say, and he will say it himself later in the same breath: far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Galatians 6:14). Not nothing to boast about. Nothing of ours.

verseByVerse.quote: Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one — and he will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The monotheism of Israel entails the universality of God’s saving purpose. There is one God — not a tribal deity who belongs to one people and ignores the rest. The Shema (“The LORD our God, the LORD is one”) is itself the theological basis of Gentile salvation: if God is one, he is God of all; if he is God of all, he must provide one way of salvation available to all. Justification by faith is the one way — available to circumcised and uncircumcised alike, because it requires nothing that any human group possesses by birth.

Feel the audacity of the argument, because Paul is doing something no one had done with that sentence before. The Shema was the confession every Jewish household said morning and evening; it was the first thing a child learned and the last thing a dying man wanted to hear. And its obvious force, for centuries, was separation: the nations have many gods, we have the one true God, and that is what makes us different from them. Paul takes the same six words and turns them outward. If there is only one God, then he is not our God as opposed to theirs. He is theirs too, whether they know it or not — and a God who belongs to everybody cannot possibly have arranged a way of salvation that only one group is able to use.

Which is why the question in verse 29 is put as a question rather than an assertion. Nobody in that synagogue would have said out loud that God was the God of Jews only; the Scriptures they read every week said the opposite in a hundred places, from the promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed to Isaiah’s house of prayer for all peoples. Paul is not correcting their doctrine. He is showing them that their practice had quietly contradicted a creed they could recite in their sleep — which is a considerably more uncomfortable thing to be shown.

And then a small detail that repays attention, because it looks like ornament and is not. God will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. Two different prepositions. Commentators have argued about whether Paul intends any distinction, and the likeliest answer is the most elegant one: he is refusing to let either group have the standard phrasing. Had he written the same words twice, one form would have become the normal one and the other the variant — the insiders and the people admitted on the insiders’ terms. By varying it, he gives neither party the definite article. Two doors, the same width, and neither of them is the tradesman’s entrance.

All of which sounds settled to us and was not settled at all. This is the argument that nearly tore the early church apart: whether Gentiles had to become Jews first — circumcision, food laws, calendar — before they could be Christians. It filled a council at Jerusalem, it produced the letter to the Galatians, and it put Paul in open conflict with Peter in a public dining room at Antioch. And notice what the fight was actually about. Nobody was denying that Gentiles could be saved. The question was on what terms — and Paul saw, with a clarity that cost him most of his friendships, that a gospel with a cultural entrance fee is not the gospel at all.

The modern form is rarely doctrinal, which is what makes it hard to see. No congregation holds that outsiders must first become like us. It simply turns out, over time, that the people who thrive there are the ones who already share the accent, the education, the politics, the family shape, the taste in music, the level of ease with the particular vocabulary. Nobody ever voted for this. It assembles itself, and the tell is not what a church believes about who may come. It is who is comfortable once they have.

So a test, and it can be run this Sunday. Look around the room and ask who is missing who lives within two miles. Then ask a harder one: think of the last person who came, stayed a few weeks and did not return — and ask whether anyone found out why. If a church requires no circumcision but does require a hundred smaller things that nobody has ever written down, it has reinvented the problem of Romans 3 without ever disputing the doctrine.

And take the comfort in the argument, because it is aimed at individuals as much as at groups. If God justified people on any basis a human being can possess — nationality, upbringing, temperament, intelligence, moral aptitude, religious sensibility — then that basis would be distributed unevenly, and some people would be nearer the door than others through no doing of their own. Faith is the one qualification that levels every field, because it is the one thing that is not an achievement. Which is why the door Paul describes has no step: God is one, and therefore he has exactly one way in, and it is the same width for everybody who ever lived.

verseByVerse.quote: Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul anticipates the charge that the doctrine of justification by faith abolishes the law’s authority. His answer is categorical: “By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.” Faith upholds the law by acknowledging what the law teaches: that God is holy, that sin is real, that judgment is just, and that humanity cannot save itself. The law’s deepest function — to drive sinners to Christ (Galatians 3:24) — is fulfilled, not annulled, when faith receives the righteousness the law could never produce.

This is not a stray thought at the end of a paragraph. It is Paul answering, at last, the slander he reported back at 3:8 — that he was teaching people to do evil so that good might come, a charge he was clearly tired of hearing and which he there refused even to argue with. Now that the doctrine has been fully stated, he turns and faces it. If righteousness comes apart from the law, has the law been thrown away? And he answers with the same violent negative he used at 3:4 and 3:6, the one he reserves for conclusions that are not merely mistaken but intolerable.

Then he claims the exact opposite, and the verb is stronger than “uphold” suggests. It is a word for making something stand — establishing, confirming, setting it firmly on its feet. So the claim is not that the law survives the gospel, nor that a place has been found for it. It is that the law was never standing properly until now.

Which sounds extravagant until you ask what the alternatives actually do to it. A man trying to be justified by the law must, if he is to have any peace at all, lower it. He cannot live with a standard that says you shall not covet and means it, so he quietly translates the commandments into things that can be achieved: no adultery becomes no affair, no murder becomes no violence, honour your father becomes a phone call at Christmas. He has kept the law in the sense that he has redefined it down to his own dimensions. That is not upholding it. It is the most thorough disrespect the law ever suffers, and it is always done by its admirers.

The gospel does the reverse. It lets every commandment stand at full height — the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good, Paul will say four chapters on (7:12) — and then deals with the resulting problem some other way. Nothing is discounted. The demand is met in full by somebody, and the penalty is paid in full by somebody, and the sinner is justified without a single letter of the standard being adjusted in his favour. Only the man who has stopped needing the law to be manageable is free to see how magnificent it is.

And there is a second sense in which faith establishes the law, which is the one he will spend the next chapter proving. Paul has just said something that sounds like a break with the Old Testament, and the obvious objection is that he has invented a new religion. So he does not argue the point abstractly; he goes and gets Abraham. The man the whole nation traced itself to, who was reckoned righteous by believing God — before the law was given, before he was circumcised — is Paul’s proof that justification by faith is not a novelty smuggled in past Moses. It is the oldest thing in the book. Chapter 4 exists to make the four words at the end of chapter 3 stick.

One guard, because this verse is often reached for by people wanting to know what a Christian does with the commandments now, and it does not quite answer that question. Paul is not here discussing the law as a rule of life for the believer, though he holds that too and will get to it in chapters 6, 8 and 12. He is answering a charge about the doctrine. But the instinct is sound, and the answer he gives elsewhere is the same shape: grace does not lower the standard, it produces people who begin, unevenly and gradually, to want it.

So a test, and it is a good one for anybody who has grasped justification by faith and is wondering whether he has grasped it too comfortably. Read the Sermon on the Mount slowly this week and watch your own reaction. If your instinct is to soften it — he cannot mean that literally, this is hyperbole, allowances must be made — then something in you is still trying to pass, because only a candidate needs the exam to be easier. If you can let it stand at full height, agree with every word of it, and find that it does not frighten you, that is what this verse means by upholding the law. The man who is not being examined can afford to admire the standard.

Paul has spent three chapters showing that the law cannot save anybody, and he ends by insisting he has not said a word against it. Both are true, and they are the same truth. The law was never a ladder that broke under the weight; it was always a mirror, and a mirror is not discredited by the fact that it cannot wash a face. It is honoured at last by a man who stops arguing with it and goes to be washed.

4.title: Abraham: The Father of All Who Believe
4.overview:
If justification is by faith and not by works of the law, Paul faces an immediate objection from Jewish readers: what about Abraham? Abraham is the father of the Jewish nation, the recipient of the covenant, the model of obedience. If he was justified by his works, then surely righteousness is earned, not given. Romans 4 is Paul's extended answer — and it is devastating in its exegetical precision and its theological reach.

The answer is simple and irrefutable: Abraham was justified by faith before he was circumcised (Genesis 15:6 precedes Genesis 17), and before the law was given (by four centuries). The very man whom Judaism claimed as the exemplar of covenant faithfulness is in fact the exemplar of justifying faith — and therefore the father not only of circumcised Jewish believers but of all Gentile believers as well. The gospel does not contradict the covenant with Abraham; it fulfils it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Abraham Justified by Faith, Not Works or Circumcision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's argument from Abraham is both simple and lethal to the works-righteousness position. He goes directly to Genesis 15:6: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." The verb "counted" (Greek: logizomai; Hebrew: chashab) is an accounting term — to reckon to someone's account. God reckoned Abraham righteous — not because Abraham had earned it but because Abraham believed. The righteousness was credited; it was not achieved.

Paul then deploys a second argument from David. Psalm 32:1–2 speaks of the blessedness of the man whose sins are not counted against him. David was not speaking of a man who earned God's favour; he was speaking of a man who received forgiveness he did not deserve. Blessed is the man whose iniquity is forgiven — not whose record is clean. The whole Old Testament agrees: righteousness before God is received, not achieved.

The third and clinching argument concerns the timing of Abraham's circumcision. The justification of Genesis 15:6 precedes the circumcision of Genesis 17 by perhaps fourteen to twenty-four years. Abraham was declared righteous while still uncircumcised — which means circumcision was a sign and seal of a righteousness already received by faith, not the means by which that righteousness was obtained. This means Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not: his pattern is faith, not ethnicity.

And at the centre of it stands a phrase so shocking that Paul can only have chosen it deliberately: God “justifies the ungodly” (v. 5). Not the sincere, not the searching, not the imperfect but well-intentioned. The ungodly — the very people the God of the Old Testament had sworn he would not acquit, since his own law had called the justifying of the wicked an abomination. Paul is not softening the difficulty; he is naming it in the strongest available terms, because the cross has already answered it (3:25–26). This is the sentence the whole chapter is arranged around, and every reader who has ever wondered whether he is too far gone should notice which category is being justified here.
verseByVerse.theology:
Imputation: The Reckoning of Righteousness

The word logizomai (count, reckon, credit, impute) appears eleven times in Romans 4. This is deliberate. The doctrine of imputation — that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account — is the hinge of the doctrine of justification. Luther's language of the "wonderful exchange" captures it: Christ takes our sin; we receive His righteousness. Not infused into us (as Rome taught), but credited to us — declared righteous in Christ, clothed in a righteousness that is not ours by achievement but ours by gift. Calvin called this the "alien righteousness" (iustitia aliena) — foreign to us by nature, ours by grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's appeal to Abraham was the ultimate trump card in Jewish theological discussion. If Abraham himself was justified by faith and not by works, the works-righteousness position has lost its founding father. Paul turns the Jewish trump card against itself. Now: Every form of religious merit-earning — "I'm basically a good person," "I attend church," "I pray every day," "I've never done anything really terrible" — collapses before Romans 4. Abraham, the father of the faithful, stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise. So must we.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say was gained by Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul turns to Abraham — the father of the Jewish people and the paradigm of covenant relationship with God — to demonstrate that justification by faith is not a Pauline novelty but the original pattern. If Abraham had been justified by works, he would have grounds for boasting before other men. But the critical phrase is “before God”: no human achievement, no matter how impressive, constitutes grounds for boasting before the Holy One of Israel. The courtroom that matters is not the court of human opinion.

Understand why the whole chapter exists, because it is not a devotional excursion into the life of a patriarch. Paul has just made an enormous claim — that justification by faith establishes the law rather than abolishing it (3:31) — and a claim like that has to be proved from the Scriptures or it is worthless. So he goes and gets the one witness no opponent could dismiss. Not a prophet, not a psalm, but the man the entire nation traced its existence to. If Abraham was justified by faith, the argument is over, because there is nobody further back to appeal to.

And this was a bolder move than it looks, because Abraham was not a neutral exhibit. In the Judaism of Paul’s day he was the great example of obedience. Jewish writers celebrated him as the man who kept the commandments before they were given, who was tested ten times and found faithful. One well-known book of the period quotes the very verse Paul is about to use and attaches it to the binding of Isaac: was not Abraham found faithful when tested, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness? On that reading, Genesis 15:6 is a verdict on Abraham’s proven obedience — which is very nearly the opposite of Paul’s point. He is not merely quoting a text. He is taking it back from an established interpretation, and his instrument will be the calendar: what Genesis 15 says, and when Genesis 15 happened.

Then feel the force of the concession he makes before he takes it away. Paul does not say Abraham had nothing to show. He says that if he was justified by works, he would have something to boast about — and at the human level the man had a genuinely extraordinary record. He left a settled city and a family and an inheritance on the strength of a word from a God he had not previously known. He turned down the spoils of a war he had won so that no king could claim to have made him rich. He argued with God for the life of a wicked city, and would not stop at fifty, or forty, or ten. He was hospitable to strangers who turned out to be more than strangers. And at the end he was willing to give up the one thing he had waited a lifetime for. Any tribunal on earth would have decorated him. He is the only man in Scripture called the friend of God.

And Paul grants the whole of it and then adds four words that empty it: but not before God. That is the hinge of the verse and it is easy to read as a throwaway. It means that the record is real, and that it belongs to a different courtroom. Before other men Abraham towers. Before God he is a man being reckoned righteous on the basis of having believed a promise — which is exactly the position occupied by everybody else who has ever been reckoned righteous.

Which is why boasting keeps coming up in these chapters, and why Paul has already explained what happened to it (see on 3:27). It is not that boasting has been forbidden by a rule. It is that the ground of it has been removed, and here he shows that it was never there even in the strongest case anybody could produce.

So here is a test that fits the verse exactly. Write down the three things you would most want said about you at your funeral — the real ones, the achievements or qualities you quietly hope will be mentioned. Then read them again and ask what weight any of them would carry in a courtroom where the charge is that you have not loved God with all your heart, and have not loved your neighbour as yourself. The point of the exercise is not to make the list look shabby. Most people’s lists are genuinely creditable. The point is that everything on it is testimony in a different case.

Notice, then, what Paul does not do with Abraham. He does not diminish him in order to make room for grace, does not hunt through Genesis for his failures, and does not suggest that his obedience was less than it appears. He leaves the man exactly as tall as he is — and then observes, quietly, that height was never the measurement being taken.

verseByVerse.quote: For what does the Scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Genesis 15:6 is Paul’s proof text, and its logic is decisive: Abraham’s righteousness was “counted” (elogisthē — imputed, reckoned, credited) to him, not earned. The bookkeeping metaphor is precise: wages are not a gift, they are a debt owed to a worker. But Abraham was not working; he was believing. God was not paying a debt; he was giving a gift. The structure of justification is grace from beginning to end: the righteousness credited is not Abraham’s own; it is the verdict of a gracious God upon a trusting man.

This is the verb the chapter is built on, and it is worth noticing how hard Paul leans on it: logizomai appears eleven times in these twenty-five verses. That is not a stylistic habit. He is hammering one nail. The whole argument turns on a single question — how does righteousness get onto a person’s account? — and the answer is that it is put there.

And the accounting picture is exact in a way that repays attention, because a ledger can be altered in only two ways. Either a sum is earned, in which case entering it is not generosity but bookkeeping — the employer who pays on Friday is not being kind, he is settling a debt, and a man who is thanked for his wages is being insulted. Or a sum is credited from outside, in which case the recipient contributed nothing but an account number. Paul says Abraham’s righteousness arrived by the second route. Which means that if you ever find yourself feeling that God owes you something — after a hard season of faithfulness, after the sacrifice nobody noticed — you have quietly moved yourself into the first column, and the first column has no grace in it anywhere. It cannot. Wages and gifts are mutually exclusive by definition, which is precisely why Paul chose the illustration.

Now go back to Genesis and see what the verse is actually describing, because it is not a man in a devotional frame of mind. Abraham is an old man with no children, and God has just taken him outside at night and told him to number the stars if he can, and said: so shall your offspring be. There is no child. There is no evidence. There is a childless man in his eighties standing in the dark, looking up, with nothing in his hands and nothing in his future but a sentence somebody said to him. And the next line is: he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:5–6). Faith in the Bible is not a mood or a temperament. It is taking God at his word when the word is the only thing you have.

And notice what was not counted to him. Not his obedience, which was considerable. Not his character, which was better than most. What was counted was that he believed God — which is why faith can never be reclassified as a small work that earns the rest. There is nothing meritorious in accepting a gift; the hand that takes a parcel has not contributed to its contents. Faith justifies not because it is a fine quality but because of what it lays hold of.

One clarification, because two things are being credited and it is easy to blur them. God does not merely decline to count Abraham’s sins — that comes in verses 6 to 8, and it is only half the transaction. Something positive is put on the account: righteousness, a standing the man did not have. This is what the Reformers meant by imputation, and the distinction they insisted on matters. The righteousness is not infused into you like a medicine that gradually improves your condition; it is credited to you like a sum entered in a book. If it were infused, your standing would rise and fall with your progress, and you would never know where you were on any given evening. Because it is credited, it is complete on the day it is entered — which is why a Christian ten minutes old and a Christian of fifty years stand in exactly the same righteousness, and neither has more of it than the other.

So here is a test, and it exposes which column you are actually keeping your accounts in. Think of the last time you did something genuinely costly for God — the giving that hurt, the forgiveness that was expensive, the years in an unglamorous ministry. Now notice what you expected afterwards. Was there any part of you that looked for a return: that things should go better now, that the prayer should be answered, that God should notice? That expectation is not wickedness and it is nearly universal. But it is the arithmetic of wages, and it is worth catching, because it is the mechanism by which grace quietly turns back into religion.

The great mercy in this verse is what it does to the question of how much you have. Abraham had no child, no land he owned, and no evidence — and he had a righteousness reckoned to him that night which he had done nothing whatever to produce. Everything he was later famous for came afterwards, and none of it was the ground of his standing. God did not enter the sum because the account looked promising. He entered it because he had decided to, and the account was empty.

verseByVerse.quote: And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Justifies the ungodly” — this phrase was scandalous in Paul’s Jewish context, for the law explicitly condemned the justification of the wicked (Proverbs 17:15; Exodus 23:7). Yet this is exactly what God does in the gospel: he declares righteous those who are, in themselves, ungodly. This is the “wonderful exchange” (Calvin): Christ takes our ungodliness; we receive his righteousness. The one who does not work — who has abandoned all trust in personal performance — and simply believes: this person receives the verdict “righteous” as a free gift from the God who alone can give it.

It is difficult to overstate how offensive this sentence was, and we have been anaesthetised to it by familiarity. The texts the entry above cites are not incidental — they are God’s own instructions to his own judges. He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the righteous are both alike an abomination to the LORD (Proverbs 17:15). I will not acquit the guilty (Exodus 23:7). Those are not obscure verses; they are the working standard of Israelite justice. And Paul takes the participle straight out of them and makes it a description of God: he is the one who justifies the ungodly. It is as if a man were to define the Almighty by the one thing his own law calls an abomination.

He is not being careless, and he is not softening the word. Note that he does not say God justifies the weak, or the struggling, or the sincere-but-inconsistent. Asebēs is the word from 1:18 — ungodliness, the thing the wrath of God is revealed against. Paul reaches back to the first charge in the letter and puts the same people in the dock in this verse, and then says they are the ones being acquitted.

The reason he can say it without collapsing into contradiction has already been given, and this verse depends entirely on it: the guilt was not overlooked, it was transferred and dealt with (see on 3:25–26). Justification is not God deciding that the ungodly are not so bad after all. It is God pronouncing a verdict that has already been paid for. Which is why the gospel is not, as it is often heard, the announcement that God is lenient. A lenient God would be a corrupt judge, and there would be no comfort in him at all — because a judge who can be talked round is a judge who can be talked round by your accuser as well.

And now the phrase that decides who this verse is for: to the one who does not work. That is not a commendation of idleness; Paul is describing what a man brings to the transaction. And it means, unavoidably, that the qualification for being justified is having nothing to offer. Which is why this is the hardest verse in the Bible for respectable people. If you have been decent all your life, attended faithfully, given generously and raised your children well, then you must come to God on precisely the same terms as the man who has wrecked everything he ever touched — as one of the ungodly, working nothing, holding nothing out. Most people would rather be forgiven a great deal than be told their record is not currency.

So take the two readers this verse is written for, because they are opposite and it addresses them in the same breath.

If you are the one who has been quietly afraid that you are too far gone — that there is a thing in your past which puts you outside the ordinary offer, and that God might save people like you in general but not you in particular — then read the category again. He justifies the ungodly. Not the improved ungodly, and not those who have been ungodly and have now sorted themselves out sufficiently to be presentable. If God only justified good people, your fear would be entirely rational. He does not, and the whole verse exists to say so.

And if you are the other reader — the one for whom none of this feels urgent, because you have never done anything that would frighten a congregation — then the word ungodly is yours too, and the letter spent three chapters establishing it. Nobody gets a different category. There is one door, and it is marked with a description you would not have chosen for yourself.

Here is the test, and it is short. Complete this sentence honestly: God accepts me even though I… Most Christians can finish it easily. Now complete this one: God accepts me even though there is nothing about me that recommends the arrangement. If the second produces a flicker of resistance — a wish to add something, some small qualification about your sincerity or your effort or your intentions — that flicker is precisely what verse 5 was written to remove, and it will keep coming back for the rest of your life.

Which is why the old writers loved this verse above almost any other. It does not say that God justifies the godly, which would be respectable and useless. It says the opposite, in a word borrowed from a law that forbids it, on the strength of a cross that pays for it. And it means that the only people who are ever justified are people who at that moment had nothing to bring — so that if you are waiting until you are in a fit state to come, you are waiting to be disqualified.

verseByVerse.quote: just as David also speaks of the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s beatitude from Psalm 32 confirms the Abrahamic pattern: the blessed man is not the man who has no lawless deeds but the man whose lawless deeds are forgiven. The blessing is not the absence of sin but the removal of its condemnation. “Covered” is the Old Testament word for atonement (kāpar): the sin is not ignored or minimised but covered — placed under the blood of sacrifice, hidden from the eyes of the righteous Judge. The gospel does not pretend sin away; it deals with it at the cost of the Son.

Notice what Paul is doing with the shape of his argument, because it is a legal habit and a Jewish one: a matter shall be established by the evidence of two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). He has produced Abraham, the founder of the nation, from the age before the law. Now he produces David, the greatest of its kings, from the age under the law. Two men, a thousand years apart, on opposite sides of Sinai — and both of them righteous by reckoning rather than by record. The case is closed by the nation’s own two most authoritative figures, which means no one can answer it by saying that Abraham was a special case from before the rules were made.

And there is a second reason David is the right witness, which the next verse will make explicit and which changes the tone of the whole paragraph. Abraham shows you that a man can be reckoned righteous without having earned it. David shows you that a man can be reckoned righteous after having forfeited it. Abraham answers the question can God credit a man who has done nothing? David answers the harder one: can God credit a man who has done something?

Then look at what the beatitude actually says, because it is not the one any of us would have written. Every instinct in a religious person says the blessed man is the man with a clean record. David says the blessed man is the one whose lawless deeds are forgiven, which means the blessed man is by definition a man with lawless deeds. Read it slowly and it turns out that his blessing does not lie in an area of his life where he did well. It lies precisely at the point of his worst failure — that is where the forgiveness is, and therefore that is where the blessing is. There is no beatitude in this psalm for anything David got right.

The two verbs are worth separating, because they answer two different fears. Forgiven is a word for lifting and carrying away — the load taken off a man’s back and removed. Covered is the sacrificial word, and it does not mean concealed in the sense of a thing hidden that might still be found. It is the language of the mercy seat: the lid over the ark, blood on the covering, the broken law underneath and God meeting his people above it. So one word deals with the weight and the other deals with the exposure. If your trouble is that you cannot carry it, the first word is for you. If your trouble is that you cannot bear to have it seen, the second is.

And it is worth being exact about what covered does not mean, because a false comfort here does real damage. It is not that God has agreed to look the other way, or that the file has been mislaid, or that enough time has passed. That kind of covering would be a fiction and every honest person would know it — which is why the psalm begins where it does, and why David spends its opening verses describing what it was like before the covering: while he kept silent his bones wasted away, day and night God’s hand was heavy on him, his strength dried up as in the heat of summer (Psalm 32:3–4). The relief in this psalm is not the relief of a man who has decided to stop thinking about it. It is the relief of a man who said it out loud and discovered it was dealt with.

So here is the test, and it distinguishes two things that look alike from the outside. Take the thing in your life you would least want read aloud. Now ask which of these two you actually have: is it unmentioned, or is it covered? Unmentioned means nobody knows and you are managing it, and the arrangement holds as long as nothing surfaces. Covered means it has been brought out, named to God without qualification, and dealt with at the cost of blood — and a covered sin is safe precisely because it has already been fully seen. The difference between the two is the difference between the first four verses of Psalm 32 and the first two.

Which is why David, of all people, is the man Paul wanted. The blessing he pronounces is not the sigh of somebody whose life went smoothly. It is the verdict of a man who had wrecked everything that mattered to him, and who found, on the other side of it, that the God against whom he had done it had made his sin disappear from the record — not by pretending, but by covering it, at a price that would not be revealed for another thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: "blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The positive and negative of the same magnificent reality: the Lord “will not count” (ou mē logisētai) the sin of the forgiven person. The same verb used of imputing righteousness (v. 3) is here used of not imputing sin. Double imputation: our sin is counted to Christ; Christ’s righteousness is counted to us. David wrote this after the darkest chapter of his life — adultery, murder, deception — and this is the psalm that resulted. The man who knew his sin most deeply also knew most deeply the grace that does not count it.

The construction Paul quotes is stronger than any English version can carry. It is the double negative that Greek reserves for absolute denial — not merely will not, but will never under any circumstances. It is the same emphatic form our Lord used when he said that those who come to him he will never cast out, and that his sheep will never perish. So this is not a statement about God’s present disposition, which might soften or harden with time. It is a door welded shut. There is no set of future circumstances in which the Lord reopens the ledger and enters the sin after all.

And that raises the question any honest Christian eventually asks, usually at night. What about the sins I have not committed yet? A man converted at thirty has fifty years of failure in front of him, and it is very natural to assume that the past was dealt with at the cross and the future is on some kind of running account. But look at the tense of the promise. It does not say the Lord has not counted his sin. It says he will not count it — the verb faces forward. When Christ died, every sin you would ever commit was still future, and the ones you committed last week were no more visible to you then than they were unknown to him.

Which is why the entry above is right to call this the negative and positive of one reality, and the double transaction is worth stating plainly because half of it is usually missing from how we feel about ourselves. Most Christians are clear that their sins are not counted. Far fewer live as though a positive righteousness has been counted to them. Yet the two halves are inseparable, and the difference between them is enormous. A man whose debts are cancelled has nothing; a man whose debts are cancelled and whose account is then filled from someone else’s fortune is rich. Justification is not being returned to zero. It is being given a positive standing you did not have even before you sinned.

So the test is not whether you believe you are forgiven, since most believers say yes to that. It is what happens next. When you have failed badly and confessed it, do you then keep a distance for a few days — praying less, reading less, not quite able to sing on Sunday — until you feel you have re-established something? That interval is the tell. It is the behaviour of a man who believes his sins are not counted but suspects his standing has to be earned back, and the two halves of this verse are the cure for exactly that. There is nothing to re-establish. The account was never yours in the first place.

One guard, and Paul will spend the whole of chapter 6 on it, so it is enough to name it here. A verdict this absolute is precisely the kind of thing a man can turn into permission — if the Lord will never count my sin, the arithmetic of sinning has changed in my favour. Paul knows the objection is coming and he does not answer it by weakening the promise. He answers it by pointing out what has happened to the person: a man who has been treated like this and concludes that he may now do as he likes has not understood what was done to him. You do not respond to that kind of mercy by testing its limits, any more than a man pardoned at the scaffold spends the afternoon looking for another capital offence.

And notice where David is standing when he says it. This psalm has a superscription and a story: it is written by a man who had done the two things his own law punished with death, who had been caught, who had been confronted by a prophet in his own throne room and had nothing to say. That man wrote blessed. Not relieved, not tolerated, not permitted to remain in office — blessed, the same word the psalter uses of the righteous man who walks in the counsel of God. The Lord will never count his sin, and by the third verse he is telling other sinners where to come.

verseByVerse.quote: Is this blessing then only for the circumcised, or also for the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it counted to him? Was it before or after he had been circumcised? It was not after, but before he had been circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul presses the chronological question with rabbinic precision. Genesis 15 (Abraham’s faith counted as righteousness) precedes Genesis 17 (circumcision) by at least fourteen years. This is not a trivial point — it means Abraham was justified as an uncircumcised man, as a Gentile. His justification is therefore the paradigm for Gentile justification, not a special case reserved for the covenant people. The sign came after the reality; the reality was already present by faith alone.

This is the calendar argument promised earlier (see on 4:1–2), and it is worth appreciating how quietly devastating it is. Paul does not dispute a single word of the text his opponents value. He does not argue that circumcision was unimportant, or that Genesis has been misread, or that the covenant was provisional. He simply asks when. The whole case turns on the order of two chapters, and once the question is put there is no answer available — because Genesis 15 comes before Genesis 17, and no amount of theology can move it.

And the interval is not a technicality. Between the night Abraham was reckoned righteous and the day he was circumcised lie the birth of Ishmael and thirteen further years — the boy is thirteen when the command comes (Genesis 17:25), and he was born after the promise of Genesis 15. So for something like a decade and a half, the man the whole nation traced itself to was walking around justified before God and physically indistinguishable from any pagan in Canaan. Had he died in that period he would have died righteous, with nothing to show for it that anyone could inspect.

Which is exactly Paul’s point, and it does something rather generous to the argument. He is not saying Abraham was a Jew who happened to be justified. He is saying Abraham was justified while he was, in every visible respect, a Gentile — a Mesopotamian from a family of idolaters (Joshua 24:2), with no law, no temple, no priesthood, no sign, and no religious community whatever. The founder of the covenant people entered his righteousness from outside the covenant people, because at that moment there was no covenant people to be inside.

Then notice what Paul is really defending, because the question in verse 9 is not academic. Is this blessing then only for the circumcised? He has just quoted David’s beatitude, and beatitudes are the sort of thing people quietly assume belong to their own kind. The question is whether the forgiveness of Psalm 32 is house property — available to the insiders, on application, through the proper channels. And the answer is settled not by an appeal to God’s generosity but by a date.

All of which has an edge for a reader who has never once thought about circumcision. The instinct Paul is dismantling is not Jewish; it is human, and it survives every change of religion. It is the assumption that the blessing arrives through the arrangement — that the promises in Scripture are addressed, in practice, to people who are properly inside things: baptised, confirmed, on the roll, in the right church, taught by the right people. And the assumption is rarely stated, which is why it is rarely examined. It simply shows up in the quiet confidence of those who have the arrangement, and in the hesitancy of those who do not.

So here is the test, and it is aimed at that hesitancy. Think of a promise of God you find difficult to apply to yourself — that he is near to the brokenhearted, that nothing can separate you from his love, that he will not cast you out. Now ask what you think stands between you and it. If the honest answer involves anything that could be described as a credential — that you came to faith too late, that you were never properly discipled, that your background is wrong, that you are not the sort of person these things are written for — then this passage is about you, and its answer is a date. Abraham had none of it either. He had a promise and he believed it, and the paperwork was completed fourteen years later.

One thing this does not mean, and Paul says the opposite in the very next verse, so it is worth stating: the sign is not thereby made worthless. God commanded it, and Abraham obeyed, and chapter 17 is not an afterthought. The argument is about sequence, not about value. What Paul has established is simply that the sign could not have produced what its owner already had — and that a man who has the sign and nothing else has the receipt without the purchase.

verseByVerse.quote: He received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised. The purpose was to make him the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them as well, and to make him the father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had before he was circumcised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Circumcision was a seal of a righteousness already possessed by faith — a sign that pointed to and confirmed an existing reality. Abraham is therefore the father of two groups: the uncircumcised who believe (the Gentile church) and the circumcised who walk in the footsteps of his faith (believing Israel). Both inherit through faith, not through the sign. The sign matters — it is a God-given seal — but it seals what faith has already received, not what works have earned.

The word seal is worth handling, because it is a legal term and not a decorative one. In the ancient world a seal was pressed into wax on a document to certify it — it did not create the agreement, it authenticated one that had already been made, and it identified whose the thing was. Nobody ever became the owner of a field by acquiring a seal; the seal declared publicly what a transaction had already accomplished privately. That is precisely the relation Paul establishes between the sign and the righteousness, and it settles the order permanently. A seal on an empty page certifies nothing.

Which raises the obvious question for a Christian reader, since we do not circumcise: what is the equivalent, and does this passage devalue it? The answer is no, and the reason is worth seeing. Baptism stands in the same relation to faith as circumcision stood to Abraham’s — commanded by God, genuinely meaningful, and never the thing itself. Paul’s argument in this chapter cuts equally against a man who trusts his circumcision and a man who trusts his baptism, and it protects both from the opposite error too. The sign is not nothing; it is a seal, and a seal is issued by an authority. What it cannot do is manufacture what it certifies.

Then the phrase that turns the whole argument into an inheritance: Abraham is the father of all who believe. Paul has been proving a point about chronology, and he now shows what the chronology was for. Because Abraham was justified before he was circumcised, he is not merely an example that Gentiles may study from a distance; he is their father. The relationship is not analogical. A believing Gentile is not like one of Abraham’s children. He is one.

And that is a considerable thing to say to people with no ancestral claim on the promises at all. If you came to Christ out of a family with no faith in it, or a hostile one, or simply an indifferent one — if you are the first Christian anybody in your line can remember — then this verse hands you a lineage. You are not a recent addition tolerated at the edge of somebody else’s story. Your family history runs back through four thousand years to a man standing under the stars in Mesopotamia, and the connection is not sentiment; Paul argues it as a legal fact from the order of two chapters in Genesis.

Notice too how carefully he describes the second group, because it is the more pointed half. Abraham is father of the circumcised who are not merely circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of his faith. The qualifier does real work: possessing the sign does not by itself put a man in the family. And the metaphor Paul reaches for is walking in footsteps — which is what a child does behind a father in a field, placing his feet where the bigger prints already are. Sonship is demonstrated by direction of travel, not by paperwork.

So the test follows from the metaphor and it is simple to run. Ask which of Abraham’s footprints your own life is currently placing feet into. He left security on the strength of a promise. He waited twenty-five years for something God had said, without any evidence arriving in the meantime. He believed a thing that was, on the face of it, physically impossible. Take one of those and ask where in your life there is anything remotely like it — any point at which you are actually depending on something God has said, in a way that would look foolish if he turned out not to exist. If nothing comes to mind, that is worth knowing. It is possible to hold every one of Abraham’s doctrines and stand in none of his footprints.

And a guard for the reader whose faith feels far too small to be walking in anybody’s footsteps, let alone his: Paul is describing a pattern, not a standard of performance. He will shortly admit that Abraham considered his own body as good as dead. The footsteps are not evidence of a great faith; they are evidence of a faith that is pointed at the same object. A child does not have to fill his father’s footprint. He only has to be going the same way.

Which is how the section ends: with one man, two families, and a single door between them both. The Gentile who believes and the Jew who believes turn out to be brothers, and the thing that makes them brothers is not the sign that once divided them but the faith that pre-dated it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Promise Through Faith: Abraham's Hope Against Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now extends his argument to the promise God made to Abraham — that he would be heir of the world, that his offspring would be numberless, that through him all nations would be blessed. This promise, Paul insists, was given through the righteousness of faith, not through the law. The law cannot be the means of inheriting the promise, because the law can only pronounce wrath (it condemns those who fail to keep it); if the promise depends on law-keeping, the promise is void for everyone.

The portrait of Abraham's faith in vv. 17–21 is one of the most moving passages in the entire New Testament. Abraham — "as good as dead" at a hundred years old, Sarah's womb "dead" — hoped against hope. He did not weaken in faith when he considered the hopeless biological reality. He did not waver in unbelief but grew strong in faith, giving glory to God, fully convinced that what God had promised He was also able to perform. This is faith in its purest form: not faith in the circumstances, not faith in human possibility, but faith in the God who raises the dead and calls into existence things that do not exist (v. 17).

And then the connection to us: this was written not for Abraham's sake alone but for ours — for those who believe in Him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead. Jesus was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification. The resurrection is not merely the proof that Jesus is who He claimed to be; it is the declaration that the justification He accomplished has been accepted. The empty tomb is God's receipt for a debt paid in full.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith and the Resurrection

Romans 4:24–25 ties justification directly to the resurrection of Jesus. Christ was raised "for our justification" — His resurrection is not merely the proof of His deity but the declaration that His atoning work was accepted by the Father. The resurrection is the Father's public vindication of the Son's sacrifice. This means that Christian faith is not merely belief in the ethical teachings of Jesus or even in His death; it is faith in the God who raised Him from the dead. Easter is not the happy ending of a sad story; it is the announcement that the story of sin and death and wrath has been definitively answered.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The promise to Abraham that he would be "heir of the world" (v. 13) goes beyond what Genesis explicitly states but draws on the expansive reading of the Abrahamic covenant in Jewish tradition. Paul is claiming that the full scope of that promise — a redeemed humanity, a renewed creation — is fulfilled in Christ and received by faith. The Jewish hope for the world is the Christian gospel. Now: Abraham's "hope against hope" (v. 18) is the model for Christian faith in every situation where the circumstances shout impossibility. The God who gave life to Abraham's dead body and Sarah's dead womb is the same God who raises the dead today — physically at the last day, spiritually in every conversion. No situation is beyond Him.

verseByVerse.quote: For the promise to Abraham and his offspring that he would be heir of the world did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith. For if it is the adherents of the law who are to be the heirs, faith is emptied and the promise is nullified,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise to Abraham (Genesis 12, 15, 17, 22) was cosmic in scope: “heir of the world”. Paul reads the Abrahamic blessing in its full New Testament dimensions: the inheritance is not merely Canaan but the renewed creation, the world made new. And this promise came through faith, not through law-keeping — because the law did not yet exist. If the inheritance depended on law-observance, faith would be drained of its meaning and the promise made conditional on human performance — which is precisely what the promise was designed to transcend.

It is worth being straightforward about the phrase itself, because a careful reader who goes back to Genesis will not find it there. God promised Abraham a land, an innumerable offspring, and that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed. He did not say heir of the world. Paul is compressing, and he is doing it the way his contemporaries already did: Jewish writers of the period had long since read the promise expansively — an inheritance reaching from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth. The seed of it is in the text (a blessing to all the families of the earth is not a local arrangement), and Paul draws the conclusion: a promise of that scope was never going to be exhausted by a strip of land on the eastern Mediterranean.

Then the two verbs in verse 14, which are stronger than they look. If the inheritance runs through law-keeping, faith is emptied — the word means hollowed out, drained of content, the same verb used of Christ emptying himself — and the promise is nullified, made inoperative, put permanently out of use. Notice that Paul does not say faith would be reduced or the promise weakened. Both are cancelled outright. And it is worth seeing why, because the logic is exact. If the estate goes to those who perform, then performance is the mechanism, and trust has nothing left to do. Faith would survive as a feeling that accompanies the transaction without contributing anything to it — decorative rather than load-bearing. You cannot have two mechanisms operating on the same inheritance. One of them will be doing the work and the other will be sentiment.

Which is why the difference between a promise and a contract is not a nicety. A contract binds two parties and either can void it: each has obligations, each is watching the other, and the whole arrangement is only as secure as the weaker signatory. A promise binds one party and names another as the recipient. The recipient’s conduct is not what keeps it in force, because he never undertook anything in the first place.

And Abraham had been shown that in the most extraordinary way, in the very chapter Paul keeps quoting. When he asked how he could know he would inherit, God told him to bring animals, cut them in half, and lay the pieces opposite each other (Genesis 15:9–10). That was a covenant ceremony, and its meaning was understood by everyone in the ancient world: the parties walked between the severed halves, invoking the same fate on themselves if they broke the agreement. So Abraham prepared the pieces and waited. And then a deep sleep fell upon him, and a dreadful darkness, and when the sun had gone down a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch — God himself — passed between the pieces alone (15:12, 17). Abraham never walked. He was unconscious for the ratification. God swore the oath by himself, took the entire liability, and left the other party asleep on the ground.

Which is a fair description of how every one of us came into this. The word Paul chooses, heir, belongs to the same world: nobody earns an inheritance, and the only thing required of an heir is that he be named. And there is one more feature of an inheritance that Scripture does not leave unstated — it becomes effective by a death (Hebrews 9:16–17). The promise made over the split carcasses in Genesis 15 was finally executed when the one who had walked between them alone kept the terms in his own body.

So here is a test, and it is about the size of your expectations rather than the state of your soul. Try to describe what you are actually going to inherit. Most Christians, pressed, produce something vague and largely elsewhere — a good place, after death, somewhere else. Paul says heir of the world, and he means it: this creation, healed; a body that works; work worth doing; the earth under a good King. If your hope is essentially an evacuation, it is smaller than the promise. The Bible does not end with the saints leaving the world. It ends with the world being handed over to them.

And that is what is at stake in this apparently technical dispute about law and promise. If the inheritance runs on performance, then everything above depends on your keeping it up, and you will spend your life auditing your grip. If it runs on a promise, the security is located somewhere other than in you — in an oath sworn between the pieces by a God who walked that path alone, while the man who would inherit the world lay asleep in the dark, having contributed nothing to the ceremony but the firewood.

verseByVerse.quote: For the law brings wrath, but where there is no law there is no transgression. That is why it depends on faith, in order that the promise may rest on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring — not only to the adherent of the law but also to the one who shares the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Law and promise operate on different principles. Law requires performance; failure triggers judgment. Promise requires trust; reception is by grace. If the inheritance came by law, it would be uncertain — permanently at risk of disqualification by the next failure. Because it comes by promise through faith, it is guaranteed (bebaian — secure, firm, legally certain). Grace makes the promise certain precisely because grace does not depend on the fluctuating performance of the beneficiary.

Take the first half slowly, because it contains a sentence that sounds like an excuse and is not: where there is no law there is no transgression. Paul is not saying that people without the law are innocent — he spent the first chapter proving the opposite, and the second establishing that they have a law written on the heart. He is making a narrower and more technical point. Transgression is a specific word: it means stepping over a line that has been drawn. You can be lost without a map, but you cannot be a trespasser until somebody has put up a fence. So the law does not create human wickedness; it converts it into a chargeable offence.

Which is why the law brings wrath, and why that is a devastating thing to say to people whose whole hope rested on possessing it. They had assumed the law was the mechanism of the inheritance. Paul says it is the mechanism of the indictment — that giving the law to sinners is like installing a speed camera on a road everyone was already speeding down. Nothing has been made worse. Everything has been made explicit, and the fines have started arriving.

Then verse 16 gives the reason the whole arrangement was set up differently, and it is worth reading the logic backwards, because Paul states the purpose before the mechanism. What God wanted was a promise that was guaranteed. That was the requirement. And so, working back from the outcome, it had to depend on faith and rest on grace — because there is no other way to build a promise that cannot fail. Grace is not simply the kinder option. It is the only one that produces certainty, since any arrangement involving human performance is only as reliable as the human, and we have three chapters of evidence about that.

The word for guaranteed belonged to the world of business and law: it described a title that would hold up, a contract that was legally secure, a transaction that could not be overturned later. It is the word for a deed that stands when challenged. So Paul is not offering a warm hope but a valid title — and the difference between the two is the difference between wanting something to be true and being able to produce the paperwork.

Now feel what this does to the ordinary Christian week, because it is the pastoral point of the verse. If your standing depends on your performance, then it necessarily moves, and you will know exactly where you are by how the last few days have gone. There will be Sundays when you can sing and Sundays when you cannot quite. There will be a low-grade audit running in the back of your mind at all times, and it will be at its loudest precisely when you most need to pray. That is not a defect in your temperament. It is the inevitable operating condition of anyone whose inheritance runs on law, and the only cure is to change the instrument.

So here is a test that catches it. Think about how you feel when you approach God after a week in which you have done well — you prayed, you resisted something, you were generous. Now compare it with how you feel approaching him after a week in which you did none of it. If those two feel materially different, notice what has happened: something has been fluctuating, and it is not the promise. This does not make you a hypocrite; almost every believer lives with some version of it. But it locates the work still to be done, and the work is not more effort. It is learning to believe that the title is secure on both weeks.

One guard, because a guarantee can be misheard as an invitation to relax into nothing at all. Paul is not saying that the beneficiary’s life is irrelevant; he is saying it is not the ground. The promise is guaranteed to all his offspring, and the previous verses have just described what Abraham’s offspring look like — people who walk in the footsteps of his faith. Security and indifference are not the same thing, and a man who has understood that his inheritance cannot be lost does not become careless about the Father who gave it. He becomes free to obey without negotiating.

And the last four words of the verse are the quiet triumph of the whole argument: Abraham is the father of us all. Not the father of one nation with an annexe for outsiders. Paul has been arguing about law and promise and wrath and guarantee, and it lands on a family — which is what a promise, unlike a contract, is finally able to produce.

verseByVerse.quote: as it is written, "I have made you the father of many nations" — in the presence of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist. In hope he believed against hope, that he should become the father of many nations, as he had been told, "So shall your offspring be."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s faith is defined by its object: the God who raises the dead and calls things into existence from nothing. This is creation-faith and resurrection-faith — trusting the God for whom impossibility is simply the normal starting point of his greatest works. “In hope he believed against hope” — there was no natural basis for hope; every human indicator pointed to hopelessness. But Abraham’s hope was not natural; it was theological: he knew who God was. Keller: “Faith is not optimism about circumstances; it is confidence in the character of God.”

Notice which two things Paul selects to describe God, because he has the whole Old Testament to choose from and picks these. God gives life to the dead, and God calls into existence the things that do not exist. Resurrection and creation. Between them they cover the only two situations in which a human being has nothing whatever to contribute: when there is nothing there yet, and when what was there has died. Every other predicament admits of some human input — effort, ingenuity, time. These two do not. A corpse cannot cooperate with its own raising, and nothing cannot assist in its own creation.

And that is the exact reason Paul brings them in here, because both apply to Abraham literally. The offspring did not yet exist — nothing, waiting to be called. And the bodies through which they would come were finished — dead, waiting to be quickened. Abraham was standing in the only two circumstances where God works without a collaborator, and he is about to become the father of many nations from inside both of them.

Then look at the tense of the quotation, which is easily read past and is the whole thing. God does not say I will make you the father of many nations. He says I have made you — past tense, spoken to a childless old man with no evidence of any kind. God speaks of the not-yet as though it were already done, because for him it is; and that is what it means to call into existence the things that do not exist. He does not describe reality. He establishes it. Which is why Abraham’s name was changed before anything happened: he spent those years being addressed, by everyone he met, as father of a multitude while possessing no children at all. Every conversation was a small act of faith or a small humiliation, depending on whether the man who named him could be relied upon.

And there is a phrase in the middle of the sentence that decides the whole character of this faith: Abraham believed in the presence of the God in whom he believed. This is not a man reasoning his way to a conclusion about a distant deity. He is standing before someone. Faith in the Bible is never a calculation about probabilities; it is a posture in front of a Person — which is why it can survive evidence that a calculation could not.

Then the phrase everybody remembers, and it is worth translating out of its familiarity. In hope he believed against hope — that is, with nothing in the situation to hope for, he hoped. Note carefully what this does not mean. It is not positive thinking, and it is not the refusal to admit facts; the next verse says outright that he faced them. Hope in Scripture is not a mood about the future but a settled expectation resting on something said. So the question is never how much hope you can generate. It is whether the one who spoke can do it.

Which is the pastoral point of the passage and the reason it is here at all. Paul is writing to people who will have to believe something at least as unlikely: that a man they never met, executed in a province they have never visited, is alive, and that his death has settled their account with God. Every visible indicator argues against it. So he gives them a father who was in precisely that position, and points out what his faith actually rested on — not a reason to expect a child, but a God who does this sort of thing.

So here is a test, and it is not about the strength of your faith. Take the thing you are currently praying for and cannot see any way through — the marriage, the son, the diagnosis, the part of your own character that has not moved in twenty years. Now ask which of the two descriptions in verse 17 your situation actually falls under. Is it a case of something that does not exist and would have to be created? Or of something that was alive and is now dead? Because those are the two categories named in this verse, and they are named as the specialities of the God you are praying to. There is no third category listed here — no department for cases that are merely difficult — which suggests that difficulty was never the relevant measurement.

One guard, because this verse has been used to promise people outcomes God never promised them. Abraham had a specific word from God about a specific thing, and his faith was in that word — not in his own conviction that it ought to happen. Believing hard that a particular result will come is not the faith described here, and when it does not come the collapse is severe. Faith fastens on what God has said. Where he has spoken plainly — that he will forgive, that he will keep you, that he will raise the dead, that he is working all things toward good — you may believe against every appearance and you will not be embarrassed. Where he has not spoken about your particular case, the right posture is to ask, and to leave the answer with him, and to keep believing about the things he has said while you wait.

Which finally explains why Paul chose the two descriptions he did. If God were merely very powerful, then hopeless cases would still be hopeless, and the question of any prayer would be whether your situation had gone too far. But God is not described here as the God who improves things. He is the God who works with nothing and with the dead — which means that having nothing to work with is not a disadvantage in his hands. It is the usual raw material.

verseByVerse.quote: He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb. No unbelief made him waver concerning the promise of God, but he grew strong in his faith as he gave glory to God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham “considered” his circumstances — he was not naive about them. He looked at his body, recognised its deadness, looked at Sarah’s womb, recognised its barrenness — and still did not waver. This is mature faith: not the refusal to face facts, but the refusal to allow facts to have the final word. The final word belongs to the one who spoke the promise.
