He says it abounds — the word means to overflow, to exceed the container. Which means the gospel is not the restoration of Eden. Adam lost a garden; we are promised a city. Adam had innocence, which is a fragile thing and was lost in an afternoon; the believer has a righteousness that is not his own and therefore cannot be forfeited by him. Adam could fall. The man in Christ cannot, because he is not standing on his own record. We do not end where Adam began. We end considerably further on, and the difference is not sentiment but the specific gain of having been redeemed rather than merely restored.

So here is a test, and it is about which of the two men you instinctively think you belong to. Take the last serious failure you had — the one you would not want repeated — and notice how you described it to yourself afterwards. Did you find yourself calculating: how much ground have I lost, how long before things are normal again, how many good weeks does this cost me? That calculation is Adam’s arithmetic, and it is entirely reasonable inside his system, where everything runs on your record. The whole point of these two verses is that you are not in that system. There is no ground to make up, because the ground was never yours; and there is no quantity at which the gift becomes insufficient, because it was never being weighed against you.

Which is why Paul’s refusal to tidy the parallel is itself the good news. If Adam and Christ balanced, the Christian life would be an anxious accounting — losses on one side, gains on the other, and the outcome genuinely in doubt. They do not balance. One man’s trespass brought a verdict; one man’s obedience brought a gift that exceeded it, and the scales were broken deliberately by the God who put his own Son on one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, because of one man's trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reversal is total: where death once reigned as king over humanity, those who receive the abundance of grace will themselves reign in life. The direction of sovereignty is inverted. Union with Adam meant being ruled by death; union with Christ means ruling with life. The “abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness” received by faith transforms subjects of death into co-regents of life. This is the eschatological destiny of the justified: not merely survival but glorified reign, sharing in the victory of the Last Adam.

Watch what Paul does not write, because the sentence he was building would have finished itself. Death reigned through one man’s trespass — so the matching clause should be that life will reign through Jesus Christ. That is the tidy version, and it is not what he says. He says that those who receive will themselves reign in life. The parallel breaks again, and it breaks upward: the second half is not about a power replacing a power, but about people replacing a power. Under Adam we were the territory being ruled. Under Christ we are not merely liberated subjects; we are given a throne.

Which is a far larger claim than most Christians have noticed, and it is worth letting it be as strange as it is. Whatever else salvation means in this letter, it does not mean being restored to a safe neutrality. It means being handed authority — the destiny Genesis described before anything went wrong, when the creature made in God’s image was told to have dominion, and which has been in ruins ever since. Adam was made to rule and ended as a subject of death. The man in Christ was a subject of death and ends by ruling.

And the tense is worth marking, because it does two things at once. Will reign — future. The full thing is not yet, and anybody who looks at his own life and cannot find much evidence of sovereignty is reading his situation correctly. We are not there. But the participle beside it is present: those who are receiving the abundance of grace. So the receiving is now and the reigning is later, which is exactly the shape of the Christian life — a king in exile, whose title is already granted, whose coronation is on a date he does not know.

Notice too the single condition, stated in one word: receive. It is the only verb in the sentence that we perform, and it is the one verb that contributes nothing. Everything else is done by somebody else — the grace is given, the righteousness is a gift, the reign is conferred. And Paul chooses his nouns to make refusal look absurd: not grace but the abundance of grace, not righteousness but the free gift of righteousness. A man in a burning building does not earn his rescue by climbing the ladder. He does have to climb it.

So here is a test, and it is aimed at how you actually picture your future. Ask what you expect to be doing a thousand years from now. Most Christians, honestly, imagine something essentially passive — rest, peace, worship understood as an endless service, a kind of pleasant weightlessness. Paul says reign, and elsewhere the New Testament fills it in with real content: authority over cities (Luke 19:17), judging angels (1 Corinthians 6:3), work with consequence. If your hope has no future in it that involves doing anything, it is smaller than the one this verse describes — and a hope that is only relief will not carry you through a hard decade, because relief is not something you can look forward to with any energy.

One guard, because the language of reigning has been badly misused. This is not a promise that the Christian exercises dominion over his circumstances now — that faith gives you command over illness, finances or other people, and that a defeated-looking life indicates a failure to claim your authority. The verb is future, the men who wrote these letters were beaten and imprisoned and executed, and Paul himself is about to describe the whole creation groaning and Christians groaning with it (8:22–23). Reigning in life is not a technique for the present. It is a destination.

And it is the reversal that makes the chapter’s arithmetic land. In Adam, death was the king and you were its subject; and death is a thorough ruler, taking everything eventually and giving nothing back. In Christ, you receive — and the thing you receive, in the end, is the throne that death was sitting on.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as one trespass led to condemnation for all men, so one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. For as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous. — Romans 5:18–19
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parallel is now stated with maximum clarity: one trespass → condemnation for all / one act of righteousness → justification for all. The “one act of righteousness” refers most naturally to the obedience of Christ’s entire life culminating in the cross — the perfect, comprehensive obedience that the law required and that Adam failed to render. Where Adam disobeyed, Christ obeyed — at every point, at every pressure, to the ultimate degree of giving his life.

“Made sinners” and “made righteous” are legal or covenantal terms — not descriptions of personal moral character but of standing before God. Those in Adam are constituted sinners by their representative’s act; those in Christ are constituted righteous by their representative’s act. This is the doctrine of imputation operating symmetrically: the same mechanism that makes us guilty in Adam makes us righteous in Christ. To reject one side of the parallel is to undermine the other.

Notice, first, that the sentence begun at verse 12 is finally finished here. Paul wrote just as six verses ago and then broke off to clear obstacles; now, at last, the so also arrives. Everything between has been parenthesis. This is the thought he set out to think, and it took him half a chapter to get permission from himself to say it.

Then the phrase that has to be handled, because it is the plainest-sounding universalism in the New Testament: one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men. Read alone, that appears to say everybody is saved. And it should be said at once that the people who have believed this have usually not been frivolous — the sentence really does look like that, and pretending otherwise helps nobody.

But three things settle it. The first is the immediate context: the previous verse said the gift belongs to those who receive it (v. 17), which is a limiting phrase Paul had no reason to insert if everyone receives it regardless. The second is Paul’s own summary in the very next sentence, where all men becomes the many in both halves — he is plainly using the phrases interchangeably, and he is contrasting two humanities, not counting heads. And the third is the rest of the letter and the rest of the man: the same apostle wrote chapter 2 on the day of wrath, and chapter 9 on vessels of wrath, and told the Thessalonians about those who will suffer the punishment of eternal destruction. A sentence must be read with its author.

So what is Paul saying? That the two acts have the same kind of universality within their own spheres. Adam’s trespass reaches every single person who is in Adam — with no exceptions, no one too remote, no one who escaped by being born far away or late. And Christ’s obedience reaches, with exactly the same completeness, every single person who is in Christ. The all is not a headcount of the human race. It is a statement that neither representative leaves anybody out of his own constituency, which is precisely what you would want to know if you were wondering whether you might be an exception at the edges of the second group.

Then verse 19, which supplies the other half of what the cross accomplished, and it is the half most Christians have never been taught. Where Adam disobeyed, Christ obeyed — and Paul does not say Christ died for our sins here, though he believes it with every fibre. He says obedience. Which means the thirty-three years count. Not merely the six hours: the whole life of perfect love for God and neighbour, the temptations refused in a wilderness with nobody watching, the ordinary decades in a workshop, every commandment kept in the only human life that ever kept them.

And that is why justification is more than pardon. A pardon cancels a record and leaves the man with none — forgiven, and possessing nothing. What the New Testament describes is an exchange: your record was reckoned to him and his record was reckoned to you, so that you stand before God not merely as one against whom nothing is charged but as one who has kept the law entirely. The old writers called these the passive and active obedience of Christ — what he suffered, and what he did — and both are needed, because a man with a clean slate and no righteousness is not yet fit for the presence of God.

So here is a test, and it distinguishes two things most of us have quietly merged. Ask which sentence you actually believe about yourself: God has forgiven me, or God is as pleased with me as he is with Jesus Christ. Nearly every Christian can affirm the first. The second sounds close to blasphemy the first time you hear it, and it is the plain implication of verse 19 — because if his obedience is what constitutes your standing, then the Father regards you in it. Notice which of the two you can say without flinching. The gap between them is the amount of this verse you have not yet believed.

Which is finally why Paul insisted on breaking his own parallel while still using it. The two men are alike in structure and unlike in everything else. One act of disobedience put you in a position you never chose; one act of obedience can put you in a position you could never earn. And you contributed to neither — which is the offence of this passage, and the whole of its comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the law came in to increase the trespass, but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, so that, as sin reigned in death, grace also might reign through righteousness leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord. — Romans 5:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” — this sentence has fuelled both hope and misunderstanding across two millennia. The misunderstanding: it licenses more sinning to get more grace (which Paul will demolish immediately in 6:1). The hope: no depth of human sin is beyond the reach of divine grace. The greatest sinner is not beyond the scope of the gospel. The most spectacular prodigal is not past the point at which grace can abound.

The reign of grace through righteousness is the great theme of Romans 6–8: the justified person does not merely receive a changed verdict; she enters a new dominion. She is no longer under the reign of sin and death — no longer defined by Adam’s inheritance or her own accumulated failures. She is under the reign of grace, moving toward eternal life, claimed and kept by the God who abounds.

Take the first clause on its own, because it is one of the strangest statements in Scripture: the law came in to increase the trespass. That is not a description of an unfortunate side effect. It is a statement of purpose. God gave the law, at Sinai, with fire and trumpet and a mountain that shook, in order that sin might get worse. Any reader who is not slightly shocked has read it too quickly.

And the word Paul uses for the law’s arrival is telling: it came in alongside, a verb suggesting something entering a situation already underway. The law is not the main plot. It arrived after Adam and before Christ, into a story that was already running, and it had a defined job to do in the middle of it. Which is a considerable thing to say to people who had organised their entire national identity around it.

So how does law increase trespass? Not by making people worse in themselves — chapter 4 has already set the mechanism out: where there is no law there is no transgression, so drawing the line converts wrongdoing into chargeable offence. But there is a second and more uncomfortable way, which Paul will describe from his own experience in chapter 7: a prohibition provokes. Tell a man not to and something in him wakes up that was asleep a moment earlier. Every parent knows this and every one of us has felt it — the cupboard you had no interest in until you were told not to open it. The law does not create the appetite. It exposes it, and in exposing it inflames it, which is precisely how a diagnosis works when the disease is rebellion.

Why would God do that? Because a sin that is vague cannot be forgiven — not because God cannot forgive it, but because nobody asks. A man with a general sense that he is not all he should be does not go anywhere in particular with it. The law’s work is to take that fog and turn it into an itemised bill, so that the man is finally holding something specific enough to bring to a Saviour. Sin had to be made visible before grace could be seen to be sufficient.

Which is where the second clause lands, and the Greek is more extravagant than the English. Sin increased; grace did not merely increase but super-abounded — Paul has stacked a preposition on the front of an already strong verb, and the word is close to being coined for the occasion. It is language for a thing that overflows the vessel and keeps coming. Wherever sin has gone, grace has gone further, and it did not arrive with a measure in its hand.

So take the comfort exactly where it is aimed, because it is aimed at people who think they are the exception. The one who came to Christ late, having done real damage that cannot now be repaired. The believer with the same failure on his record for the fifteenth year. The man reading this who has one thing in his past he has never said out loud to another human being and assumes it sits outside the ordinary terms. This verse is not a general encouragement; it is specifically about the places where sin went deepest, and it says grace got there first and went further. Not that grace is adequate to it — that grace super-abounds over it.

And then, in the same breath, the guard, because Paul knows exactly what a certain kind of mind will do with the sentence he has just written. If more sin means more grace, why not oblige? He does not soften the statement to prevent the abuse; he lets it stand at full strength and then turns on the objection in the first line of the next chapter. But notice the answer is already embedded here. Grace reigns through righteousness. It does not reign by suspending righteousness or negotiating with it. So a man who concludes from this verse that he may now sin freely has misunderstood the kind of king he is dealing with — grace is not permission, it is a dominion, and dominions have a character.

Which is what makes the last line of the chapter so satisfying. Two reigns have been set against each other: sin reigned in death, and grace reigns through righteousness — and note that a reign is not a mood or an influence, it is a government you live under. You do not negotiate with a reign; you are transferred out of one and into another. Paul has spent twenty verses on two men and their two kingdoms, and it ends where the whole letter ends, on a name: through Jesus Christ our Lord. The law came in alongside. He came in to reign.

6.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
6.overview:
Romans 6 opens with the most dangerous question the gospel generates: "What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?" If grace covers all sin, and more sin produces more grace, why not sin freely? Paul's answer — "By no means!" — is the most vehement denial in the letter. The question misunderstands both the nature of grace and the nature of the union with Christ that is the foundation of the justified life.

The answer Paul gives is not primarily ethical (you should not sin) but theological (you cannot sin in the way that question imagines, because of who you now are in Christ). Union with Christ in His death and resurrection has changed the believer's fundamental status with respect to sin. She has died to it. It no longer has jurisdiction over her. The command that follows — "So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus" — is not a technique for sin management but a theological reality to be reckoned with and lived from.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — United with Christ in Death and Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's answer to the antinomian question is grounded in baptism — not as a magical ritual but as the enacted sign of the believer's union with Christ in His death and resurrection. "Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?" Baptism is the visible declaration of an invisible reality: the believer has been co-crucified with Christ, co-buried with Him, and co-raised with Him into newness of life. These are not future aspirations; they are present realities that define who the Christian is.

The key concept is "our old self was crucified with him" (v. 6) — the person we were in Adam, defined by sin's dominion, is dead. Not sick, not weakened, not being rehabilitated — dead. Sin still exists in the believer (7:14–25 will be painfully honest about this), but sin no longer reigns. The one who is in Christ has been transferred out of sin's kingdom and into grace's kingdom. She is not a sinner desperately trying to become a saint; she is a saint who still struggles with sin. The identity has changed, even while the struggle continues.

The imperatives of vv. 11–14 flow from the indicatives of vv. 1–10. "Consider yourselves dead to sin" (v. 11) — reckon it, take it into account, live from this reality. "Do not let sin reign" (v. 12) — the fact that sin no longer must reign does not mean the battle is over; it means the battle is now winnable. "Present yourselves to God" (v. 13) — the person whose old self has been crucified with Christ is now free to offer herself as a living sacrifice to the God she could not truly serve before.

Two things at the edges of the section carry the argument and should not be lost. The first is that Paul grounds our security in Christ’s experience before he applies anything to ours: the death he died he died to sin once for all, and being raised from the dead he will never die again — death no longer has dominion over him (vv. 9–10). That is the anchor. Our dying and rising are real because they are participation in his, and his cannot be undone or repeated. The second is the promise the section ends on: sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace (v. 14). It is stated as a fact about the future rather than a target to aim at — and the reason given is the opposite of what any moralist would expect. Sin loses its grip not because the rules have been tightened but because the government has changed.
verseByVerse.theology:
Union with Christ: The Foundation of Sanctification

Romans 6 grounds sanctification in union with Christ, not in moral effort or spiritual discipline alone. The Reformed tradition has always insisted that justification and sanctification, though distinct, are inseparable — both are fruits of union with Christ. John Murray's landmark study Redemption Accomplished and Applied showed that union with Christ is not an add-on to the Christian life but its very foundation: every blessing of salvation flows from being in Christ. We are justified in Christ, sanctified in Christ, glorified in Christ. The call to holiness in Romans 6 is not the demand to earn what we have not yet received; it is the call to live consistently with what is already true of us in Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The antinomian objection Paul addresses — "let us sin that grace may abound" — was apparently a real misreading of his gospel in his own day (v. 1 and 3:8). Some had heard his message of free grace and concluded that moral behaviour was irrelevant. Paul's reply is not to retreat into moralism but to deepen the gospel: the same grace that justifies also transforms. Grace is not a license; it is a power that liberates from the dominion of sin. Now: The same objection recurs whenever grace is preached with full biblical clarity. The person who is never accused of antinomianism by those who prefer a works-based gospel has probably not yet preached grace clearly enough. But Paul's answer stands: grace does not produce moral indifference; it produces the only genuine moral transformation available — the transformation of a person who has died and risen with Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“By no means!” (mē genoito) — the strongest negation available in Greek. The question itself reveals how explosive the doctrine of grace is: if justification is entirely free, apart from works, does it not remove the incentive for holiness? Paul’s answer is not a legal constraint (“you must not sin”) but an ontological impossibility (“how can we?”). Those who have died to sin cannot continue living in it, not because they are compelled from outside but because their very relationship to sin has been fundamentally altered by union with Christ.

Before the answer, notice that the question exists at all — and that Paul has heard it before. He reported it as an actual slander back at 3:8, where people were saying that he taught let us do evil that good may come. So this is not a hypothetical objection invented for the sake of argument. It is what his preaching provoked in real congregations, and it is worth asking why. Nobody ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging sin. You only get this objection if you have said something that sounds dangerously like God accepts the ungodly and their record contributes nothing — which is precisely what Paul has been saying for five chapters. A gospel that has never once been misheard this way may not yet have been stated clearly.

And having provoked it, he does not retreat an inch. He could have protected himself in the previous chapter by softening where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, and he let it stand at full strength (see on 5:20–21). Now he answers — and the shape of the answer is the whole point, as the entry above says. He does not say you must not. He asks how can we? Those are different kinds of sentence. One is a fence; the other is an incongruity. You do not tell a man released from a life sentence that he is forbidden to sleep in his old cell. You ask him why on earth he would want to.

The verb in the question is worth having, too, because it is more specific than English suggests. Continue in sin is not the word for committing a sin; it means to remain, to persist, to go on dwelling somewhere. Paul is not asking whether a Christian ever sins — chapter 7 will be painfully clear about that. He is asking whether a Christian takes up residence in it. Which gives a far better diagnostic than a tally of failures: the question is not whether you have trespassed but whether you have built a house on the property.

Then the phrase everything turns on: we died to sin. And because this has been made to mean things it does not mean, and has left sincere Christians concluding that whatever happened to Paul has not happened to them, it is worth being exact. It does not mean that sin no longer attracts you. It does not mean the pull has gone, or that temptation has become theoretical, or that you are now incapable of doing what you did last year. The man who wrote this sentence is the man who wrote chapter 7, and he did not change his mind in between.

What death does — and this is the whole force of the metaphor — is end a jurisdiction. A dead man is beyond the reach of the court that had a warrant out for him; the warrant is not cancelled, it is simply no longer enforceable against him, because the person it named is not available. So think of sin as a former employer rather than a departed feeling. He still has your number and he still rings, often, and he knows exactly what to say. What he has lost is not his voice but his authority. He can make suggestions. He cannot any longer give you an instruction you are obliged to carry out — and the reason is not that you have grown stronger but that you no longer work there.

Notice also the tense. Died, not are dying — a completed act, done to you rather than achieved by you, and dated at a cross you were not present at and applied to you when you were united to him. This is not a state you enter by sufficient effort or maintain by vigilance. It is the fact from which the whole of the Christian life proceeds, which is why every command in this chapter comes after it and not before.

So here is the test, and it follows the verb rather than the general subject. Do not ask whether you sinned this week; you did. Ask instead whether there is anything in your life you have stopped fighting — not lost to repeatedly, but quietly stopped contesting. Something you have arranged your week around, made room for, and no longer bring to God because you have privately settled that this is simply how things are. That is not a lapse. That is an address. And Paul’s question is not how could you have done that? — he knows perfectly well how — but how can you still be living there?

Which is why the objection collapses on inspection. The man who hears about free grace and concludes that he may now sin as he likes has revealed something: he still regards sin as the good thing he is being asked to give up, and grace as the permission slip. Paul is telling him he has the transaction backwards. You were not let off a punishment and left in the same house. You were taken out of the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Baptism into Christ is baptism into his death — union with Christ in his representative dying. “Buried with him” — the burial is significant: it marks the definitiveness of the death, the irreversibility of the transition. But the burial is not the end: the purpose clause is resurrection: “in order that… we too might walk in newness of life”. The new life is not an aspiration but a present reality — the resurrection of Christ has created a new existence into which believers have been incorporated. Walking in it is the daily actualisation of what has already occurred definitionally.

Notice how Paul opens: do you not know? He is not teaching them something new. He is reminding them of something they were told at the beginning and have evidently not been using — which is worth pausing on, because it is the commonest condition in the Christian life. Most of us are not short of information. We are short of the habit of standing on what we already have.

And a word about the subject before we go further, since this is one of the passages where Christians divide. Paul is not here settling how much water, or at what age, or whether the candidate must first profess. Those are real questions and this is not the paragraph that answers them, and if you come to these verses looking for ammunition you will miss what they are about entirely. Paul’s subject is union with Christ, and baptism appears because it is the moment at which that union was publicly declared over you. Whatever your convictions about the water, the thing signified is the same, and it is the thing signified that this chapter is arguing from.

Then the little word that does the heaviest lifting, and it appears twice: baptised into Christ Jesus, baptised into his death. Not baptised because of his death, or in memory of it. Into. Paul is not describing a benefit transferred to you at a distance, like a payment made into your account by a stranger. He is describing your being placed inside an event. What happened to Christ is reckoned to have happened to you, because you are in him — which is why this letter can say you died, and were buried, and were raised, of things that occurred in Judea before you existed.

And that is why the burial gets a mention, which otherwise looks like a decorative detail. Why mention being buried at all, when the death is the thing that matters? Because burial is what a society does to confirm that a death is real and final. A man in a coma may recover; a man in the ground has been formally and publicly given up on. The burial is the certificate. Paul includes it because he wants no possibility left open that the old life is merely convalescing somewhere.

Then the purpose clause, and it is worth noticing what it is not. Paul does not say we were raised in order to feel new, or to have new experiences, or even to be new — he says in order that we might walk in newness of life. Walking is the least dramatic verb available. It is ordinary, repetitive, unglamorous, and it gets you somewhere over time. Whatever the new life is, its natural expression is not an event but a gait.

And note the strange phrase attached to the resurrection: Christ was raised by the glory of the Father. Not by the power of the Father, which is what we would have written. Glory is the weight and blazing reality of who God is — so the raising of Jesus was not merely an exercise of strength but an expression of the Father’s whole character, his verdict on his Son made visible. And the same glory stands behind your newness of life. The energy available for an ordinary Christian’s Tuesday is the energy that emptied the tomb.

So here is a test, and it uses Paul’s opening question rather than a new one. Take the sin you fight most often, and ask what you actually say to yourself in the moment of temptation. Most of us say some version of I must not — which is a fence, and fences are climbed. Paul’s argument in these verses supplies a different sentence: I am not that man any longer; that man is buried. It is not a stronger effort; it is a truer description. And notice which one comes to you unbidden. If it is always the first, then you know the doctrine of this chapter and have not yet started using it, which is exactly the condition Paul’s question is designed to expose.

Which is why he begins with do you not know rather than you ought to try. The Christian life in this chapter does not run on resolutions. It runs on remembering what was done to you when you were put into Christ — and the water you went under was the public notice that a funeral had taken place.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that our old self was crucified with him in order that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Union with Christ in death guarantees union with Christ in resurrection — the logic is inexorable. The “old self” (palaios anthrōpos) — the entire pre-conversion person defined by Adam’s solidarity — was crucified with Christ. This is not a process to be achieved but an event that occurred when Christ died: the representative death that abolished the old humanity’s defining relationship to sin. The purpose: that “the body of sin might be brought to nothing” — not destroyed physically but rendered powerless, deprived of dominion.

The word Paul chooses for our union with Christ in verse 5 is worth seeing, because it is not a legal term at all. It is a horticultural one — the word used of a graft, where a shoot is cut into the stock of another tree and the two grow together until they share one life and cannot be separated without killing both. So this is not a partnership or an arrangement. What happens to the tree happens to the branch, because the branch is now living on sap it did not produce. His death is your death for the same reason that his life is your life.

And notice the certainty Paul draws from it: if we have been united with him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. The second follows from the first without any further condition. You cannot be grafted into a living tree and share only its dying; nobody has ever been joined to Christ for the funeral and excluded from the resurrection.

But now the question that this passage raises for every honest reader, and it must be faced squarely: if my old self was crucified, why does it keep getting up? Paul says the old man is dead. My experience says he was in the kitchen this morning, in a bad temper, saying something unkind. Either the doctrine is false or something has been misunderstood.

Two distinctions clear it, and both matter. The first is between the old self and remaining sin. The old self is not a part of you, like a compartment or a shadow self that survives alongside the new one — Paul’s phrase means the entire person you were, defined by Adam, standing under that head. That person is dead: the position is gone, the jurisdiction has ended, the man who belonged to Adam has been executed. What remains is not the old self but the habits, appetites and reflexes that he trained into a body over many years, and those are a different thing entirely. A country can change its government overnight; the officials who served the old regime are still in their offices on Monday morning, still know the procedures, and will carry on running things exactly as before unless somebody stops them. Their authority is gone. Their filing cabinets are not.

The second distinction is in Paul’s own words: the body of sin is not destroyed but brought to nothing — rendered inoperative, put out of a job. He is careful. He does not say sin is gone, or that its pull has ceased, or that you will not lose to it this week. He says it has been deposed. And a deposed power that still has adherents in the country is exactly what you experience every day: real fighting, genuine losses, and a war whose outcome is not actually in question.

Which changes what the struggle means, and this is where the comfort lies for a reader who has been discouraged by his own life. The presence of a fight is not evidence that the doctrine has failed; it is evidence that there are two parties. A man wholly under sin’s dominion does not fight it. He is not conflicted about it; he simply lives, and the accusations that trouble you would not trouble him. So the very thing that makes you doubt this passage — that you find yourself resisting, grieving, getting up again — is the thing the passage predicts. You are not failing to be dead. You are experiencing the resistance of a regime that has already lost.

So here is a test, and it does not measure your success. Think about the last time you sinned in the way you most habitually sin. Now ask what happened afterwards. Not whether you fell — you did — but what the falling produced: relief and no further thought, or a heaviness that would not settle until it had been dealt with? The second is not a sign of a weak Christian but of a live one. Corpses do not ache. The discomfort you feel about your own sin is one of the few pieces of evidence in the Christian life that cannot be manufactured, and it is the direct consequence of the crucifixion this verse describes.

And note, finally, the purpose stated at the end: so that we would no longer be enslaved to sin. Freedom is the aim, not merely forgiveness. The verse is not describing a man who has been pardoned and left in the same condition. It is describing a man who has been taken out of service — and if you have ever wondered why the Christian life feels like a fight rather than a holiday, it is because you have been freed from an owner who has not yet accepted the verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: For one who has died has been set free from sin. Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“One who has died has been set free from sin” — this is a principle: death terminates legal obligation. A dead man owes no more taxes, stands before no more courts. The believer who has died with Christ is therefore legally freed from sin’s claim. And this death with Christ carries its own guarantee: if we have died with him, we will also live with him. The resurrection life is not a separate benefit to be hoped for; it is the inseparable other side of the death that has already occurred.

The principle in verse 7 was a commonplace, and that is exactly why Paul uses it. Every legal system in the ancient world knew that death dissolves obligation — the rabbis said it, Roman law assumed it, and anyone in the room could have supplied an example. A creditor may pursue a debtor across three provinces and has no case against a corpse. The claim was perfectly valid yesterday. It is not that it has been forgiven; it is that the party it was filed against is no longer within the jurisdiction of the court.

Which is worth setting beside the way most Christians actually think about their sin. We tend to imagine forgiveness as a debt written off by a generous creditor — which is true, and this letter has said so. But Paul is making a different point here, and it is stronger. The debtor has died. Sin is not standing at the counter having its claim graciously waived; it is standing at the counter discovering that the man it came for is not available, and never will be.

Then verse 8 makes a move that ought to be noticed, because it changes the register. Everything up to this point has been argument: we know, do you not know, the reasoning from baptism and burial and grafting. Now Paul says we believe. He is not weakening the claim; he is being honest about how the second half of it is held. The death is behind us and can be argued from. The life with him is ahead of us and has to be trusted, because nobody has seen it yet — and Paul, who had a great deal of confidence, does not pretend otherwise.

And that matters for the ordinary Christian, because it names where the faith is actually required. It is not usually difficult to believe that Christ died; the difficulty is believing that this arrangement ends well for you — that there is a life on the far side of your own grave, with him, in a body, and that the whole thing is not a sustaining story. Paul does not offer proof of that. He offers a link: if the first is true of you, the second follows, and the two cannot be separated because they are one union with one Person.

Note also the tense he chooses. Not we will live with him as a distant prospect only — the sentence is future, but it hangs on a past event that has already happened to you, which is why the New Testament can speak of the Christian’s future in the same breath as his history. Your death is dated. Your life with him is not yet dated, and is no less certain.

So here is a test, and it goes to which half of the verse you are actually resting on. Ask yourself what you think about, in a quiet moment, when you consider your own death. Not what you would say at a funeral — what arrives when it is your own. If the honest answer is a blank, or a vague hope, or a subject you steer away from, that is not necessarily unbelief. But notice that Paul, sitting in the same mortality as you, wrote we believe that we will also live with him, and treated it as the settled second half of something already begun. The Christian’s confidence about the far side is not bravery. It is arithmetic done on a union that is already in force.

And that is the shape of the whole chapter in two verses. Behind you, a death that has ended a jurisdiction; ahead of you, a life you have not seen. Both belong to the same Man, and you are in him — which means the only question about your future is one that was settled about his past.

verseByVerse.quote: We know that Christ, being raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer has dominion over him. For the death he died he died to sin, once for all, but the life he lives he lives to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The resurrection of Christ is permanent — “death no longer has dominion over him”. He died to sin “once for all” (ephapax) — his engagement with sin in death was total, definitive, unrepeatable. There is no second death for Christ, no renewed exposure to sin’s domain. He now lives entirely and permanently to God. This is the shape of the believer’s new existence: having died to sin once (in solidarity with Christ’s death), living now to God — entirely, permanently, in the new sphere where God is the only horizon.

Observe where Paul has gone. He has been making claims about us — you died, you were buried, you will live — and a reader might reasonably ask how firm any of that is. So he stops talking about us altogether and spends two verses on Christ. Everything the chapter asserts about your security rests on facts about somebody else’s history, and that is deliberate. If you want to know how permanent your position is, do not examine your position. Examine his.

And what he says about him is a fact with a date and no possibility of revision: Christ, being raised, will never die again. That had never been true of anyone before. Lazarus came out of a tomb and was buried again later; the widow’s son at Nain grew old; every previous raising in Scripture was a reprieve, a postponement of an appointment that was eventually kept. The resurrection of Jesus is the only one in history that did not end in a second funeral. Death has been in charge of every human story ever told, and it lost one — permanently.

Then once for all, which is one of the great words of the New Testament and the hinge of the letter to the Hebrews. It means once in a way that settles the matter and forbids repetition — not once so far, but once and therefore never again. And the argument it carries is this: a thing that must be repeated has not worked. The old sacrificial system ran on repetition precisely because nothing was ever finished; the same priest offered the same blood in the same room the following year, and the queue outside was made of the same people. This death ended the queue.

Now be careful with the phrase he died to sin, because it cannot mean for him what it means for us. We die to sin as men leaving a dominion that owned us. He had never sinned and was never owned. What ended at the cross was his relationship to sin as the one who had taken responsibility for it — he entered its territory voluntarily, bore its full penalty, and when it was paid, that transaction was complete and is now permanently behind him. Sin has no further business with him at all: nothing outstanding, no residual claim, no reason ever to speak to him again.

Which is exactly why this matters for you rather than being a piece of Christological housekeeping. If you are in him, then sin’s claim on you was settled in the same transaction, and it cannot be reopened for the same reason it cannot be reopened against him. Your security is not that you have moved beyond sin’s reach by your own progress. It is that the account was closed on a Friday in Jerusalem and the receipt was issued on the Sunday, and neither can be recalled.

So here is a test, and it will show you where your assurance actually sits. When you are anxious about your standing with God, notice what you instinctively go looking at. Almost all of us look inward — at the state of our faith, the quality of last week, whether we feel anything, whether the repentance was sincere enough. That is looking at a thing which genuinely does fluctuate, and the anxiety is therefore permanent. Paul in these two verses looks somewhere else entirely: at what happened to Christ, once, and cannot happen differently. Try it deliberately the next time the accusation comes. The question is not how am I doing? but is he still risen? — and there is only one possible answer, and it does not depend on your week.

And the last clause gives the pattern for everything that follows in this chapter: the life he lives he lives to God. Not to sin, not against sin, not in reaction to it — to God. The negative is finished and does not need revisiting; what remains is a life with a single direction. Which is what Paul is about to ask of you, and it is why he has spent ten verses on the indicative before issuing a single command.

verseByVerse.quote: So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Consider yourselves” (logizesthe) — the same verb used of imputation. Paul calls believers to reckon as true what is already true: “You are dead to sin. Believe it about yourself.” This is the indicative that grounds the imperative. Because you are dead to sin and alive to God in Christ, do not let sin reign. The command presupposes freedom — sin cannot compel; it can only attempt to reign where it has been dethroned. The mortal body is not itself sinful (Paul will insist on bodily resurrection), but it is the arena in which the daily battle over sin’s attempted restoration is fought.

Stop at the verb, because it has a history in this letter and the history is the whole point. Logizomai is the accountant’s word — to reckon, to enter in the books. It made its first appearance back at 2:26, where God credited an outsider with a standing he did not physically possess. It then dominated chapter 4, where Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, eleven times in twenty-five verses. And now, at the first command in the chapter, Paul takes the same verb and turns it round: God has been doing the reckoning all this time, and here he tells you to do some.

Which settles what the command is not. It is not visualisation, and it is not talking yourself into a mood. An accountant who enters a sum that is not in the account is committing fraud; the entry is only honest if the money is there. So Paul is not asking you to pretend you are dead to sin. He is telling you to write down what is already the case — the same operation God performed when he credited righteousness that was genuinely Christ’s to people who genuinely had none. Reckoning never creates the fact. It aligns the books with it.

And notice that this is the first imperative in the chapter. Ten verses of what is true of you, and only then something to do — and the something to do is not an action but an act of mind. Paul does not begin the practical section by telling you to fight harder or avoid more. He begins by telling you to believe something about yourself, on the grounds that a man who does not know who he is will fight the wrong war his whole life.

Then the two halves, which must be held together. Dead to sin and alive to God. Most attempts at holiness are entirely negative — a list of things not done, a campaign of subtraction — and they fail predictably, because a life cannot be organised around an absence. You cannot make a room warm by removing the cold. Paul’s reckoning has a positive half: you are alive to God, which means available to him, responsive to him, in the room with him. The man who fights sin without cultivating that will find sin winning on ground he has left empty.

Then verse 12, which is the sober half and stops the chapter becoming a fantasy. Let not sin reign. That command would be pointless if sin were not making the attempt, so read the grammar honestly: Paul assumes an active, ongoing, daily campaign to restore a deposed regime. And note precisely what is forbidden — not the presence of sin but its reign. He does not say let sin have no existence in you; he will spend chapter 7 on why that is not yet on offer. He says do not let it govern.

Which is a hugely important distinction for anyone measuring his own progress. The question is not whether sin is present — it is, and will be until you are buried — but whether it is giving orders that are being obeyed. A defeated army in the hills is a serious nuisance and a genuine danger. It is not the government.

And observe how it operates, because Paul names the mechanism: sin reigns by making you obey its passions. It does not rule by force. It has no power to compel a Christian; what it has is persuasion, and its whole method is to present a desire as though it were an instruction. That is why temptation so rarely feels like a summons from an enemy and so often feels like simply wanting something. The lie is not usually about the thing desired. It is about your position: the suggestion that you have no real choice, that this is just how you are, that resistance is theoretical.

So here is the test, and it is the practical form of the command. Next time you are tempted, do not begin by measuring how strong the pull is; that is a number that will always discourage you. Instead say two sentences to yourself, deliberately, in words: I am dead to this. I am alive to God. Then notice what happens to the temptation when it has been named as an ex-employer making a request rather than a master issuing an order. It may not evaporate — usually it does not. But it will have been correctly classified, and a great deal of the Christian fight is simply refusing to accept a false description of who you are.

Which is why Paul’s first order is an accounting instruction rather than a moral one. The books have been correct in heaven since the cross. He is telling you to bring your own copy into line.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Instruments for righteousness” — the same body that sin once conscripted for unrighteousness is now to be offered to God as the tool of his purposes. Paul’s double command has a directional force: stop yielding to sin as you have been doing, and make a deliberate, whole-hearted surrender to God — body, hands, tongue, mind — as those who have been brought from death to life. “Sin will have no dominion over you” — this is not a command but a promise, grounded in the believer’s standing: not under law (where sin exploits condemnation) but under grace (where sin has been dethroned).

The two commands have different tenses in Greek and the difference is the practical heart of the verse. The first is a standing prohibition — do not go on presenting your members to sin, describing a habit already in progress that must be broken. The second is a decisive act: present yourselves to God, once, definitely, as a thing done rather than a policy maintained. So Paul is asking for two different operations. One is the daily refusal of a groove already worn. The other is a single act of handing over, of the sort a man can name and date.

And the word he chooses for what you present is worth having. Members is not a vague term for the self; it means the parts of the body, and Paul means them literally — hands, tongue, eyes, feet, the physical equipment you actually sin and serve with. This is what saves the chapter from becoming interior and abstract. Holiness in Romans 6 is not primarily a state of mind. It is what your hands did this afternoon.

The other word is military and industrial: instruments can mean tools, but in Paul it more often means weapons — the equipment issued to a soldier. Which fits everything the chapter has been saying about two regimes and a deposed power. Your body is not neutral territory in that conflict; it is materiel. It will be used by one side or the other today, and there is no third option in which it is used by nobody.

Which is why the reason he gives for presenting yourself to God is not because you should but as those who have been brought from death to life. That is a phrase about corpses. A man does not present a dead body to God for useful service; the thing has to be raised first, and it has been. So the surrender Paul asks for is not the desperate effort of somebody trying to be good enough. It is the natural act of somebody who has been given a life he did not have and is now deciding what to do with it.

Then verse 14, and it should be read slowly, because it is a promise and not an instruction. Sin will have no dominion over you. Paul has spent the chapter issuing commands, and here he stops commanding and simply states an outcome. He does not say sin ought not to have dominion, or that it will not if you are diligent. He says it will not. That is a sentence to take to bed on the evening of a bad failure.

And the reason attached to it is the opposite of what any serious person would expect: since you are not under law but under grace. Every instinct says the reverse — that if you want a man to stop sinning, what he needs is more law: firmer rules, clearer boundaries, sharper accountability. Paul says law is precisely what keeps sin in power. It tells you what is right and supplies no ability to do it; it provokes what it forbids (as 5:20 has already said); and it leaves you under a condemnation that makes real repentance almost impossible, because a man who believes he is one failure away from being finished cannot afford to look honestly at himself. Sin thrives on that arrangement. Grace dismantles it.

So a guard, because this is where the chapter is most often misused in both directions. Being under grace does not mean the commandments have no claim on you — Paul has just given you three commands in two verses, and he will give thirty more before the letter ends. And being under grace certainly does not mean you will not sin, which is why v. 13 is written at all. What it means is that your standing does not depend on your performance, and therefore your failures cannot destroy you, and therefore you are finally free to fight them without terror — which is the only condition in which anybody has ever fought them successfully.

So here is a test, and it comes straight out of the promise. When you fail badly, what do you reach for as the remedy? Most of us reach instinctively for law: a tightened rule, a new system, a resolution with more teeth, a private undertaking to be stricter. Notice how many times you have done that and how long each one lasted. Paul’s remedy is the other direction entirely: go back to what is true of you — brought from death to life, not under law — and present the same members again today. The reason this feels too easy is that it costs you nothing in self-punishment, and self-punishment is the one payment sin is always happy to accept, since it keeps you looking at yourself.

Which is the whole logic of the section. Sin lost its dominion not when you started keeping the rules better but when you changed kingdoms — and Paul’s command is simply to hand over to the new government the equipment the old one used to requisition.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Slaves of Righteousness: Freedom and Its Direction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The question of v. 15 replays the question of v. 1 in a new key: "Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace?" This is the libertarian version of the antinomian objection — if the law is not our master, then surely we are free to do anything. Paul's answer is again a flat denial, followed by a theological argument: freedom from sin does not mean freedom from all master; it means a change of master. Every human being serves either sin or righteousness — there is no neutral ground, no autonomous freedom that is subject to nothing.

The language of slavery runs throughout the passage and is deliberately shocking. Sin is a slave-master. Righteousness is a slave-master. The difference is in the direction: slavery to sin leads to death; slavery to righteousness leads to life and holiness. The Christian is not more free than the unbeliever in the sense of being subject to nothing; she is more free in the sense that she now serves the master whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light — the master whose service is perfect freedom.

The concluding verse is one of the most famous in the letter: "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord." The contrast between wages and gift is the contrast between law and gospel. Death is what sin earns — a wage paid in proportion to the work done. Eternal life is what God gives — a gift, free, unearned, proportionate not to the recipient's merit but to the giver's generosity. The entire letter is in this sentence.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace and the New Obedience

Romans 6:15–23 establishes that grace does not produce lawlessness but a new and deeper obedience — obedience that flows from a changed heart rather than a legal compulsion. The Reformers distinguished between the "old obedience" (driven by fear of punishment and desire for reward) and the "new obedience" (driven by love for God and gratitude for grace). Calvin was particularly insistent that the justified Christian is not released from obedience but liberated for it — the law now functions as a guide for the regenerate, not as a court that condemns. The third use of the law: the Christian, freed from condemnation, embraces the law as the expression of the will of the God she loves.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's slavery metaphor was immediately intelligible to a first-century audience in which slavery was the defining social institution. Every person knew what it meant to be owned by a master, to have their labour and their body subject to another's will. Paul's redeployment of this metaphor is arresting: you were a slave before, and you are a slave now — the only question is whose slave you are. The liberated Christian is not autonomous; she is re-owned, by a Master who purchased her with His own blood. Now: The modern West prizes autonomy above almost everything — the right to define oneself, to determine one's own values, to answer to no authority beyond the self. Romans 6 is a direct challenge to this: the autonomous self is a myth. Every person serves something — appetite, ambition, approval, comfort, identity. The gospel does not offer escape from all masters; it offers the only master worth serving.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we to sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The antinomian question returns in a slightly different form (cf. 6:1), and receives the same categorical answer. Paul’s counter-argument is the logic of slavery: whatever you obey, that is your master. Freedom from law does not mean freedom from all authority — it means transfer to a new master. The only question is which master you serve: sin, whose wages are death, or obedience, whose end is righteousness. Grace does not create a moral vacuum; it creates the freedom to serve the right master.

Notice that the objection has changed since verse 1, and the difference is worth marking. There the question was shall we continue in sin — shall we stay where we are? Here it is shall we sin — a single act, an occasional liberty, the reasonable proposition that if the law is no longer my master then the odd indulgence costs nothing. It is the more plausible objection of the two, and most of us have made it without noticing, usually in the form this once will not matter.

Paul’s reply does not argue about the size of the act at all. He says: look at what obedience does. Present yourself to someone as an obedient slave and you are that person’s slave — not because a court has ruled it, but because that is what obedience is. Each act of yielding is a small act of enlistment. Which is why the question can I get away with this once? is the wrong question entirely: the issue was never whether you would be caught but what you were becoming while you did it.

And that principle is observable in ordinary life, which is why Paul assumes his readers will grant it immediately. Nobody decides to become an alcoholic; a man decides, several thousand times, to have a drink. Nobody chooses to become the sort of person who cannot be trusted with a confidence; he chooses to repeat one interesting thing. Habits are not formed by decisions about habits. They are formed by decisions about single occasions, which is precisely the ground the objection in verse 15 is standing on.

Then the assumption underneath the whole passage, which is the part a modern reader must be told outright because his culture has trained him against it: there is no third option. Paul offers two masters and no independent territory. The idea that a person could serve nothing — self-directed, autonomous, answerable to no authority beyond his own preferences — is not presented as a dangerous choice. It is not presented at all, because Paul does not regard it as a possibility.

And on inspection he is right, which anyone can verify without leaving his own life. The man who has thrown off every external authority is not thereby unruled; he is ruled by his appetites, and appetites are the least merciful masters available, because they never say thank you and never say enough. Consider what actually governs a free modern person’s decisions: what he wants, what others will think, how he wishes to be seen, what he is afraid of losing. Those are not the absence of a master. They are four of them, and none was chosen deliberately, and none can be resigned from.

Which is why the word freedom means something different in this chapter from what it means in ordinary speech. We use it to mean the absence of constraint. Paul uses it to mean being under the right authority — being owned by the one for whom you were made, which is the only condition in which any creature functions properly. A fish in a net is constrained; a fish on a riverbank is free of the water and dying of it.

So here is a test, and it is more revealing than asking what you believe. Over the last month, what actually decided your choices at the points where it cost you something? Not what you would have said governs you — what did. Trace three or four real decisions back to their reasons: the evening you spent as you did, the thing you did not say, the money, the way you handled the awkward conversation. Whatever turns up repeatedly at the end of those chains is a master, whether or not you would ever have used the word. Almost nobody finds only one, and almost nobody finds the one he would have named.

And the comfort in Paul’s framing is easily missed. If freedom meant self-rule, then the Christian life would be a matter of achieving independence, and every failure would be evidence that you are not yet free enough. It does not. Your standing was never that you had become your own man. You were bought, and the deed of sale names a Master who has already died for the slave — which is the one arrangement in the history of ownership where the property is safer than the owner.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, that you who were once slaves of sin have become obedient from the heart to the standard of teaching to which you were committed, and, having been set free from sin, have become slaves of righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Thanks be to God” — a spontaneous doxology in the middle of an argument. The transfer of masters is an act of divine grace, not human decision: God is the one who freed them and transferred them. “Obedient from the heart” — the new obedience is not external compliance but internal transformation. The heart has been reoriented; the submission is genuine. “The standard of teaching to which you were committed” — the apostolic gospel is the mould into which grace has pressed them. Slavery to righteousness is the paradoxical freedom of those who have found the master who made them for himself.

Look at what Paul does not say, because it is the most instructive thing in the verse. These Christians have turned from a genuinely wicked past and now obey from the heart. Any pastor would want to encourage that. Paul does not congratulate them. He thanks God — and the grammatical result is that the only party commended in a sentence about their obedience is somebody else.

That is not false modesty on their behalf. It follows from everything the chapter has argued: a slave does not transfer himself, and a dead man does not decide to be raised. If they are obeying from the heart, it is because they were given a different heart, and the appropriate response to somebody else’s work is gratitude rather than applause. Which is worth noticing the next time you catch yourself quietly pleased with your own spiritual progress. The progress may be entirely real. It is simply not yours to be pleased about.

And the phrase obedient from the heart deserves its own moment, because it names the thing that distinguishes Christian obedience from every counterfeit. Slaves in the ancient world obeyed with their hands. Nobody expected a slave to agree; compliance was the whole transaction, and what he thought about it in the evening was his own affair. Paul says these slaves obey from the heart, which is a category error in the original metaphor and is exactly his point. The new master has done something no owner has ever managed: he has changed what the servant wants.

Then the odd phrase in the middle, which most translations render woodenly and which is more vivid in Greek. They were handed over to a pattern of teaching — and the word for pattern is typos, the mould or die into which molten metal is poured, or the stamp that leaves its shape on a coin. Note the direction, which is the reverse of what we would write. We would say the teaching was delivered to them. Paul says they were delivered to the teaching. The gospel is not a substance you take possession of and store; it is a shape you are poured into, and what comes out bears the impression of the mould.

Which explains something about doctrine that is easily missed by people who find it dry. If teaching is a mould, then what you steadily attend to will steadily form you, and this happens whether or not you are trying. Nobody sits under years of preaching and remains unshaped; the question is only what shape. And it is also why a Christian cannot be indifferent to what is taught in the place he attends. You are not merely evaluating a message. You are standing in a mould.

So here is a test, and it goes to the phrase from the heart. Take an area of obedience where you are currently doing the right thing, and ask what would happen if the external pressure came off — if nobody would ever know, if the person you would disappoint were not watching, if there were no consequence at all. Would you still do it? Obedience that survives the removal of the audience is obedience from the heart. Obedience that does not is compliance, and compliance is what the old master got, and it is worth knowing which one you are giving.

One guard, because that test can be turned into a whip. Almost nobody obeys from the heart perfectly or consistently; motives in this life come mixed, and a man who waits until his are pure before he acts will never act at all. The right response to discovering mixed motives is not to stop obeying but to bring them, mixed, to the God who is changing them — and to notice, as evidence, that you mind about the mixture at all. A slave who merely complies does not lie awake examining his sincerity.

Which is why Paul’s thanksgiving is the right note and not a pious flourish. Something happened to these people that they did not do: they were slaves, and now they obey from the heart, and the change ran deeper than behaviour. If that has happened to you, the appropriate response is the one he models — not satisfaction at how far you have come, but gratitude to the One who moved you.

verseByVerse.quote: I am speaking in human terms, because of your natural limitations. For just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to more lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. For when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul apologises for the slavery metaphor (“I am speaking in human terms”) — no metaphor fully captures the reality of the Christian’s relationship to God. But the metaphor illuminates by contrast: in the old life, members were freely offered to impurity, and impurity led not to satisfaction but to more lawlessness in an escalating spiral. The new life reverses the spiral: righteousness, presented as a slave’s service, leads to sanctification — the progressive reorientation of the whole person toward God. The former “freedom from righteousness” was the most enslaving condition possible.

The apology is worth pausing over, because it tells you something about how Paul handles language. He has just built an entire argument on slavery, and now he half-withdraws it: I am speaking in human terms. Not because the metaphor is wrong, but because it is inadequate in one direction — no image drawn from a brutal human institution can carry what it is like to belong to God. Slavery communicates ownership, obligation and total claim, all of which are true. It cannot communicate that the Master is a Father, that the service is freedom, or that the slave is loved. So Paul uses it, and then tells you not to press it too far. That is the mark of a careful writer, and a useful rule for reading every biblical image: find what it was chosen to convey, and do not make it say what it was never built to say.

Then the phrase behind the apology, because of your natural limitations — literally, the weakness of your flesh. He is not insulting them. He means that we are creatures who think in pictures, who grasp ownership and obligation more readily than we grasp union, and who therefore need concrete images to get hold of spiritual realities. That is a description of everyone, and it is worth noting that God has arranged his book accordingly: it is full of vineyards, sheep, courtrooms, marriages and slaves rather than definitions.

Now the sentence that carries the real weight, and it is a diagnosis of how sin actually works over time. You presented your members to impurity and to lawlessness — and the result was not satisfaction but more lawlessness. Sin does not deliver and then rest. It escalates. What served last year does not serve this year; the dose that once produced an effect produces nothing, and the appetite that was fed has grown by being fed.

Anyone who has watched an addiction, in himself or somebody he loves, recognises the mechanism immediately, and Paul’s point is that it is not confined to the obvious vices. The man who begins by shading the truth in small ways finds it takes progressively larger departures to serve the same purpose. The habit of criticism does not fill up and stop; it needs fresh material. Pornography is the plainest modern example precisely because the escalation is so measurable, and it is the same law operating that operates in a man’s ambition or his temper. Sin cannot be kept at a fixed level by an act of will, because increase is not an abuse of it. It is what it does.

And then Paul does something quietly hopeful: he says the other direction has a slope too. Present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification. The same escalating grammar, running upward. Obedience also compounds. The thing you resisted with difficulty at thirty is not the same size at fifty, not because you have become impressive but because ten thousand small refusals have worn a channel. Neither slope is fast. Both are real.

So here is a test, and it is about direction rather than position, which is the only fair way to measure a slope. Take something you struggle with and compare it not with last week but with five years ago. Is it costing you more to sin than it used to, or less? Does it take more to satisfy it, or less? And on the other side: is there anything that used to be a battle and is now largely settled — not because you gave up, but because it stopped being a live question? Those two answers, taken together, will tell you which slope you are actually standing on far more accurately than an audit of the last seven days.

Then verse 20, which is one of the great ironies in the letter: when you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness. He says it flatly, without comment, and the sarcasm is all the sharper for being unstated. That was the freedom on offer. Free from any obligation to be good, free from the whole business of holiness, entirely at liberty in that department — and the previous verse has just described where that liberty was heading. It is worth remembering the next time freedom is presented as an escape from God’s claims. That freedom is genuinely available. Paul has just told you what it produces.

verseByVerse.quote: But what fruit were you getting at that time from the things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul invites a backward look: what did sin actually produce? Shame — the fruit that leaves you unable to look at what you have done. And the ultimate end: death. The contrast with the present is stark: freedom from sin, slavery to God, fruit that leads to sanctification, and at the end, eternal life. The same framework (master → service → fruit → end) produces radically different results depending on the master. Eternal life is not earned by the service — it is the gracious end to which God brings those who belong to him.

Notice the form of the question, because Paul is not lecturing here — he is asking, and the answer is meant to come from the reader rather than from him. What fruit were you getting at that time? It is the question sin never invites you to ask, because sin lives entirely in the future tense. Its whole method is anticipation: what this will feel like, what it will settle, how much better the evening will be. It has nothing whatever to say about the morning after, and it never volunteers a retrospective.

So Paul makes them look backwards, and the answer he expects is not a list of pleasures regretted but something more devastating: nothing. The construction almost certainly means that the honest answer to what fruit did you get? is that there was none. Not bad fruit — no fruit. Sin is not an alternative crop; it is a season of work with an empty barn at the end of it, and the only thing left in the hand is the shame.

Which is worth being concrete about, because everyone reading this has the material. Think of something you did that you would not want said aloud. Now ask what it actually yielded. Not what it promised — what you have, now, as a result. Almost always the honest inventory reads the same way: an hour that no longer exists, a relationship altered by a degree nobody else noticed, a memory that arrives uninvited while you are doing something else years later. That is the harvest. It is why Paul does not need to argue the point; he only has to ask the question and wait.

And the word ashamed is chosen carefully, because shame has a particular characteristic that guilt does not. Guilt says I did something bad; shame says I cannot look at it. It is the impulse to turn the face away — which is exactly what Adam did in the garden, and exactly why sin requires concealment to survive. A man does not hide what has done him good.

Then a guard that this passage needs, because a backward look can be turned into a weapon against the wrong person. Paul says of which you are NOW ashamed — present tense, and note who is speaking: he is describing Christians looking back at a life they have left, and he does it in one sentence and moves on to the fruit they are bearing now. He does not have them dwell there. If you are a believer who cannot stop rehearsing an old sin, replaying it at night, unable to let it be finished, understand that this verse is not asking that of you. The shame here has a purpose and it is diagnostic, not punitive: it is meant to make the old master look like what he is, and then you are meant to look at the new one. Chapter 8 will say there is now no condemnation, and it will not add except for that.

Then the great structural point of the two verses, which is easy to read past. The same four stages run in both directions: a master, a service, a fruit, and an end. Sin as master produced a service, whose fruit was shame, whose end is death. God as master produces a service, whose fruit is sanctification, whose end is eternal life. Nothing in the framework changes. Only the first term does — and everything downstream follows from it. Which is why this chapter has spent twenty verses on the question of ownership rather than on techniques for behaving better. Change the master and the rest of the chain reorganises itself.

And one more thing about the word fruit, since Paul has chosen an agricultural image rather than a mechanical one. Fruit is slow, it is seasonal, and it is not produced by the branch straining.
