Nobody ever grew an apple by effort. It appears because the tree is alive and attached and has been standing in the right place for long enough — which is the honest answer to any Christian who is discouraged by how gradual his own sanctification looks. You are not assembling something. You are growing, and growth is not visible on the timescale at which we tend to inspect ourselves.

So look both ways, as Paul asks. Behind you, a service that paid nothing and left you unable to look at the receipts. Ahead of you, an end you have not earned and cannot forfeit. And between them, the only thing that changed: not your capacity, not your resolve, but who owns you.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. — Romans 6:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
The economy of sin and the economy of grace are placed side by side in one unforgettable sentence. Wages are earned; gifts are given. Death is what sin produces — the inevitable outcome of a life lived under sin’s dominion, the just consequence of rebellion against the source of all life. Eternal life is what God gives — not what we produce, not what we earn, not what we deserve. It is a gift, and it comes through a Person: Jesus Christ our Lord.

The specificity of “in Christ Jesus our Lord” is crucial. Eternal life is not a free-floating spiritual benefit that God distributes to deserving people. It is located in a Person — the Person who is himself the resurrection and the life (John 11:25). To receive eternal life is to receive Christ; to have Christ is to have eternal life. This is why John can say that whoever has the Son has life (1 John 5:12). Life is not a commodity God can give; it is a relationship with the God who is life.

The word Paul chooses for wages is not the general term for payment. It is the soldier’s word — the ration money paid out to troops, issued at intervals, the small regular allowance a man drew for his service. Which sharpens the picture considerably, and in an unexpected direction. Sin does not pay its people in a single catastrophic settlement at the end. It pays them in instalments, on time, throughout the campaign.

And that is worth sitting with, because it corrects the way we usually hear this verse. We imagine death as the bill arriving at the end of a long life — the reckoning we shall have to face eventually. The soldier’s ration is drawn weekly. Sin has been paying you all along, in the currency of the thing it deals in: the friendship that thinned and was never repaired, the capacity for wonder that dulled, the prayer that got harder to say, the person you can no longer be honest with. Those are not warnings of a future wage. They are the wage, being paid, in small coin, on schedule. The final payment is not a different currency. It is the same one, in full.

Then notice the grammar of the second half, because Paul deliberately breaks the parallel he has just built — as he did throughout chapter 5. The tidy version would be the wages of sin is death, but the wages of righteousness is eternal life. Nobody has ever earned the second wage, so he changes the noun. Not wages. Free gift. The two halves of the sentence do not balance, and the whole gospel is in the imbalance.

Which produces a curious asymmetry worth stating plainly: hell is earned and heaven is not. Nobody will be in hell who did not work for it, and nobody will be in heaven who did. That sentence offends most people the first time they meet it — but it is the only arrangement in which God is both just and merciful, and it is precisely what this letter has been arguing since 3:26.

And notice how the verse ends, because it does not end with a benefit. It ends with a preposition and a name: in Christ Jesus our Lord. The entry above is right that this is crucial, and it is worth putting bluntly. Eternal life is not a substance God has, which he transfers to you at conversion and which you then possess independently, the way a man might be given a sum of money and go home with it. It is in a Person. Which means it is not stored anywhere you could lose it, and it is not held in an account you could overdraw. To have it, you must have him; and if you have him, you cannot have less of it than he has.

Which is where the chapter ends, and the last word of it is Lord. That is not a flourish. Twenty-three verses about two masters, two slaveries, two harvests and two ends, and Paul finishes by naming the owner. He does not sign off with our Saviour, though he is that. The chapter has been about who you belong to, and it closes by saying so.

So here is a test, and it is the plainest in the chapter. Ask which half of the verse you expect to receive, and then ask why. If your reason contains anything about yourself — that you have tried, that you believe the right things, that you are not as bad as some — you have answered from the first half of the sentence, where things are earned. The only answer the verse permits is a name that is not yours.

And the last thing to say is about how ordinary this makes it. There is no third category in the verse: no wages of moderate sin, no partial gift, no arrangement for people who fall between the two. Everyone in the world is drawing one of two things — a wage they have earned or a gift they have not. The wage is being paid now, in instalments, and the gift is held in a Person who is alive and cannot be lost. That is the whole of the offer, and it fits in twenty words.

7.title: The Law, the Flesh, and the Struggle Within
7.overview:
Romans 7 is one of the most debated chapters in the New Testament. The first six verses use the analogy of marriage to explain the Christian's release from the law — just as death dissolves a marriage, so the death of the old self has dissolved the law's claim on the believer. Verses 7–25 then address the relationship between the law and sin in a passage of such raw psychological honesty that it has divided interpreters for centuries: is Paul describing his experience before or after his conversion?

The Reformed tradition, following Luther, Calvin, and Lloyd-Jones, has generally argued that vv. 7–25 describe the experience of the regenerate person — not as the normal steady state of the mature Christian, but as the honest account of the ongoing struggle that even the believer has with indwelling sin. The person who says "I delight in the law of God in my inner being" (v. 22) is not an unregenerate person; the unregenerate person has no such delight. The chapter is not a counsel of despair but a radical honesty about the nature of the Christian struggle — which ends, in v. 25, with the triumphant answer: thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Released from the Law to Bear Fruit for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul uses the analogy of marriage to make a point about the law's jurisdiction. A woman is bound to her husband by law as long as he lives; if he dies, she is free to marry another. In the same way, the Christian has "died" to the law through her union with Christ's death — she is no longer bound to the law as a system of earning and condemnation. She is now married to another — to Christ who was raised from the dead — so that she might bear fruit for God.

The point is not that the law is bad (v. 7 will explicitly deny this) but that the law was never the instrument of life. Under the law's jurisdiction, the sinful passions "aroused by the law were at work in our members to bear fruit for death" (v. 5). This does not mean the law created those sinful passions; it means that the sinful nature, encountering prohibition, is provoked — not helped — by the law. The law reveals and aggravates what is already there; it cannot remove it.

But now — freed from the law, joined to Christ — the Christian serves "in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code" (v. 6). This is not antinomianism; it is the fulfilment of Jeremiah 31 and Ezekiel 36 — the new covenant in which the law is written on the heart by the Spirit, not merely imposed from without by the letter. The motive for obedience has changed: from fear of penalty to love of the God who has shown such grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Death to Law: Liberation for Obedience

The believer's death to the law (vv. 4, 6) has been the source of great misunderstanding. Paul is not teaching that the Christian is released from the moral content of the law — he will demonstrate in chapters 12–15 that the redeemed life is the life of love, which is the fulfilment of the law (13:8–10). He is teaching that the believer's relationship to the law has changed: no longer subject to it as a court that condemns, the Christian is now free to embrace its moral demands as the expression of the will of the God she loves. Calvin's third use of the law: a guide for the regenerate, not a goad for the condemned.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The marriage analogy was immediately accessible to Paul's Jewish readers, for whom marriage law was well understood. The death that dissolves the marriage — the death of the old self in union with Christ's death — was the theologically startling element. Paul is saying: you belong to a new husband now. The old master (law as condemning power) is dead to you; the new master (Christ) is alive to you. Serve him accordingly. Now: Many Christians live as though they are still married to the law — haunted by condemnation, driven by religious duty, exhausted by the performance of obligation. Romans 7:1–6 is the declaration of liberty: you have died to that system. You are joined to Christ. Serve him from love, not from fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you not know, brothers — for I am speaking to those who know the law — that the law is binding on a person only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives, but if her husband dies she is released from the law of marriage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul introduces a legal principle: law’s authority terminates at death. He illustrates from marriage law, which his readers who “know the law” would recognise immediately. The binding force of the marriage covenant is real and serious — but it is dissolved by death. This is not an attempt to allegorise marriage but to establish the principle of death as the termination of legal obligation, a principle he will apply to the believer’s relationship to the Mosaic law.

Note who he says he is addressing: those who know the law. Paul is arguing from something his readers already grant, which is the strongest kind of argument and the most respectful. And that respect runs through the whole chapter — this is the passage in which he will insist that the law is holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good (v. 12). Whatever he is about to say about being released from it, he is not disparaging it. He is doing something more delicate: explaining how a good thing can be the wrong thing to be married to.

And the choice of illustration is not incidental. Paul has debt and slavery available and has used both already in this letter. He picks marriage — and for a reader who knows the Old Testament that is not a random legal example but the covenant image. Israel is the wife; her idolatry is adultery; Hosea was told to marry a woman who would betray him so the nation could see what it had done. So the illustration carries what a lesson about debt could not: exclusive belonging, a covenant rather than a contract, and — as v. 4 will say — fruitfulness. Marriages are meant to produce something.

Now the difficulty a careful reader will have noticed, and it should be said out loud rather than smoothed over. In the illustration, the husband dies and the wife goes free. In the application, it is not the law that dies — Paul says you have died to the law (v. 4). The correspondence appears to swap round halfway through. Commentators have tied themselves in knots trying to make every element line up, and the honest answer is that Paul is not building an allegory in which each part maps onto another. He is establishing a single principle — death dissolves legal obligation — and then applying it. Whoever does the dying, the bond is over. Pressing an illustration further than its author intended is one of the commonest ways to misread the Bible, and it is a mistake this passage catches people out with.

A second guard, briefly: this is not a passage about divorce and remarriage. Paul is citing a commonplace everyone accepted in order to make a point about the law; he is not legislating for the woman whose marriage has ended, and anybody looking for teaching on that must go where it is actually given (Matthew 19; 1 Corinthians 7).

Then what the illustration is really for, which is where it stops being technical. A great many Christians are, in practice, still married to the law — and it is worth describing what that marriage is like, because people living in it rarely name it. It is life with a spouse who is never satisfied. He is not cruel and he is not wrong; his standards are perfectly reasonable and every criticism he makes is accurate. He simply notices everything you fail at and never once says well done. He offers no help — he tells you what is required and leaves you to it. And you cannot leave, because he is entirely in the right and you have nothing to plead.

That is religion under law, and it produces exactly what you would expect: a conscientious person, permanently tired, who cannot enjoy God and cannot admit it. The remedy this passage offers is not that the spouse lowers his standards. He does not; the law is holy and stays holy. It is that the marriage has ended, by a death, and you are now joined to someone else — and Paul’s way of describing that new husband, in the next verses, is that he was raised from the dead. This one does not die, and this one is not waiting to be satisfied.

So here is the test, and it will find the residue in most of us. A woman long married to a severe man often goes on behaving as though he were watching, years after the funeral — checking herself, bracing, anticipating the criticism. So take an ordinary act of obedience: your praying, your giving, your Sunday. Ask honestly which husband it is being done for. Is it done to avoid a bad conscience, to keep something at bay, to stay in credit? Or is it done because you belong to somebody and want to be with him? The act is identical in both marriages. The person doing it is not.

And that is the whole of what Paul is establishing here. The law has not been abolished, weakened, or found at fault. It is alive and perfectly holy and still says exactly what it always said. What has happened is that the person it had a claim on has died — and the one now standing in her place is married to someone who has already met every demand the first husband ever made.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, she will be called an adulteress if she lives with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, she is free from that law, and if she marries another man she is not an adulteress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The illustration completes its point: the law that bound her is no longer operative once her husband has died — and the act that would have been adultery (belonging to another) is now perfectly lawful. Death has changed everything. Paul will apply this to the believer’s death to the law through union with Christ: what would have been lawlessness (living outside the law’s jurisdiction) is now freedom, because the death that terminates the old relationship has occurred in Christ.

Feel the force of the word Paul is willing to use. Adulteress — not an impropriety, not a technical irregularity, but the strongest word available for covenant betrayal. He is making the point that the bond is not a formality that lapses quietly. While the first husband lives, going to another is not merely disallowed; it is treachery, and everyone would call it that. The law’s claim is that serious.

Which is why the second half of the verse is so startling. The same act — belonging to another man — is treachery in one circumstance and entirely blameless in the other, and the only thing that has changed is a death. Nothing about the woman has altered. Her character is the same, her history is the same, and the man she goes to may be the very same man. What has changed is her standing, and standing is not a matter of degree. There is no partial adultery and no half-widow. She is either bound or she is free, and a funeral is what moves her from one category to the other.

That is the whole reason Paul chose an illustration with such uncomfortable vocabulary. He needs a case where the transition is absolute rather than gradual, because that is precisely what he is claiming about the believer. Christians are not people whom the law is gradually letting off, whose obligations are slowly being reduced as they improve. The change is a change of category, effected by a death, complete on the day it happened.

And note who is free to do what. The woman is free from that law — not from all law, not from marriage as such, and certainly not free in the sense of belonging to nobody. She is free to be married again. Freedom in this passage is never freedom from attachment; it is freedom to be attached to someone new, which is exactly what verse 4 is about to say and exactly what chapter 6 spent twenty-three verses establishing.

So here is the pastoral weight of it, and it is aimed at a particular reader. Some Christians carry a permanent, low-level sense that their happiness in Christ is somehow illegitimate — that they have got away with something, that a stricter accounting would find them out, that their peace is a little too easy for what they know about themselves. If that describes you, notice what this verse says about the woman in her second marriage. She is not living in a technically permitted irregularity. She is not being tolerated. She is not an adulteress — Paul says it flatly, and the word he chose is the one that would have accused her. Your standing with Christ is not a generous arrangement that would collapse under scrutiny. It is lawful. It would survive any court in the universe, because the death that made it lawful has already taken place.

Which is worth a moment, because it is the difference between two ways of holding the gospel. One says: God has kindly overlooked the problem. The other says: the problem has been legally resolved and there is nothing left to overlook. Only the second can be rested on at three in the morning, since a thing that has been overlooked can always be looked at again.

And it is worth saying what did not happen. The woman was not divorced from the first husband; nobody negotiated a release, and she did not walk out on an obligation she found burdensome. She was widowed. Which means she has no case to answer, nothing to justify, and no reason to avoid the neighbours. That is the position Paul is claiming for every Christian in relation to the law — not that you escaped it, but that the bond was ended in the only way it ever could be, and by somebody else’s death.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, my brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who has been raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For while we were living in the flesh, our sinful passions, aroused by the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The application reverses the illustration’s terms: it is not the husband (the law) who has died but the believer — “you have died to the law through the body of Christ”. Death with Christ terminated the believer’s legal obligation to the law as a covenant of works. The purpose is not lawlessness but a new marriage: belonging to the risen Christ, bearing fruit for God. The former state under law is described starkly: sinful passions, aroused by the law (which will be unpacked in vv. 7–13), bearing fruit for death. The law could diagnose and inflame but never cure.

Notice the instrument: you died to the law through the body of Christ. Not through a decision, a ceremony, or a change of conviction — through a body, which is to say through an execution that took place at a particular hour on a particular hill. Paul keeps the Christian life anchored to something physical and dated. Your release from the law is not a spiritual principle you have grasped; it is a consequence of what happened to somebody’s body, and you were in him when it happened.

Then the purpose clause, and it is worth noticing that Paul gives two, one inside the other. The first is so that you may belong to another. That is the point of the death — not liberty, but a change of possession. He does not say you died to the law so that you might be free, full stop; a widow left alone is not what he is describing. The whole object of the exercise was a second marriage.

And the man she is married to is identified by one characteristic, which is not the one we would choose: him who has been raised from the dead. Paul could have said the one who loved us, or died for us, or is the Son of God, and all are true. He names the resurrection because of what the illustration required. The first marriage ended by a death; the second cannot end the same way. This husband has been through death already and come out the other side, which means the wife is not going to be widowed twice.

Then the second purpose, further out: in order that we may bear fruit for God. This is what marriages are for in the ancient world and it is what Paul has been driving at since verse 1. And it changes what holiness is. A childless marriage is a grief; a fruitless one, in this metaphor, is a contradiction. But note where fruit comes from. It is not manufactured by the wife through effort. It is the natural consequence of a union — which is why the New Testament so rarely tells Christians to try harder and so often tells them to abide, remain, stay joined.

Which brings the diagnosis in verse 5, and it is a strange and important sentence: our sinful passions were aroused by the law. Not restrained by it. Aroused. The chapter will unpack this at vv. 7–13 and the mechanism has already been named at 5:20 — but here the point is the outcome. The law, applied to a sinful nature, does not produce holiness. It produces provocation, and then failure, and then fruit — for death. Both marriages are fertile. That is the horror of the first one: it was not barren, it was productive, and you have the children to prove it.

So here is a test, and it distinguishes the two marriages by what they yield rather than by how they feel. Take an area where you have made real moral effort — a habit fought, a temper managed, a discipline attempted. Now ask what it actually produced over five years. Under the first husband the pattern is recognisable: a rule, a period of success, a collapse, a worse collapse, and then either despair or a quiet lowering of the standard so the failure stops showing. Under the second, the pattern is different and slower: something you did not particularly work at has quietly changed, and you noticed afterwards. The first produces effort and shame. The second produces fruit, which is a thing that grows while you are asleep.

And one guard, because this passage can be read as though obedience no longer matters. Paul has not said the new marriage is easier or that nothing is asked. He has said the wife now belongs to somebody who is alive and can help her, rather than to a husband who could only ever tell her what was required. The demands have not gone. The relationship in which they are met has entirely changed — which is what the last verse of this section is about to say.

verseByVerse.quote: But now we are released from the law, having died to that which held us captive, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Released” — the same word used of the widow freed from the marriage law. The believer has been discharged from the law as a binding covenant of death. The contrast is between two modes of service: the old way of the written code (external rule producing only condemnation and failure) and the new way of the Spirit (internal transformation producing genuine obedience from the heart). The law written on stone is replaced by the law written by the Spirit on the heart — the fulfilment of Jeremiah’s new covenant promise (31:31–34).

Do not miss the two words that open the verse, because they are the same two that opened the gospel at 3:21. But now. Paul uses them at exactly the moments where the argument turns from what was to what is, and both times they follow a description of something inescapable. There the courtroom had fallen silent with every mouth stopped; here the first marriage has been described in all its fertility for death. And then: but now.

The phrase he uses for the old bond is worth having, too — we have died to that which held us captive. It is the language of being gripped, held down, kept in custody. Which is a striking thing to say about a good law, and it is why Paul spends the rest of the chapter clearing the law of blame. The law was not the jailer by design. It became a prison because of what we brought to it, in the way that a mirror becomes unbearable to a man who cannot change his face.

Then the contrast the verse turns on, and it needs care because it is the most misread sentence in this section. The old way of the written code against the new way of the Spirit is not a contrast between the Old Testament and the New, and it is certainly not a contrast between law as bad and Spirit as good. The written code is God’s own word. What Paul is contrasting is two ways of serving — and note that both halves of the sentence have the same verb in them. He does not say we no longer serve. He says we serve differently. The question was never whether a Christian obeys, but out of what.

And the difference between the two is the difference between a rule outside you and a life inside you. A written code can tell you what is required and can do nothing whatever to make you want it; that is not a defect in the code but a limit built into the medium. Instructions pinned to a wall have never yet moved anybody. What the new covenant promised, and what this verse says has arrived, is not clearer instructions but a different interior: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33), and I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (Ezekiel 36:27). Note what the statutes do in that sentence. They do not change. The walking does.

Which is where this becomes practical, because most Christians default to the old way without ever deciding to. It is the natural language of the religious mind — I must, I should, I ought, I will try — and it produces a life that is genuinely disciplined and quietly joyless. The new way does not abolish the shoulds. It relocates the engine. The difference is not between a man who obeys and a man who does not, but between a man driving a car and a man pushing one, and from the outside on a flat road the two can look remarkably similar for quite a long way.

So here is the test, and it is about fuel rather than performance. Take the last thing you did that you did not want to do — the visit, the apology, the money, the honest word. Now trace why you did it. Was it because not doing it would have made you feel bad about yourself, or because someone would have noticed, or because you have a standard and standards must be kept? Or was it because you belong to Christ and it seemed like the thing that would please him? The action is identical either way; you cannot tell from outside; and the two are different marriages. Most of us will find a mixture, which is normal and not a crisis. What is worth noticing is which one is doing the heavier lifting when you are tired.

And that is the whole of this section in one sentence. The law is not your husband and never was a good one for people in our condition — but you have not been released into having no master, no service and no obligation. You have been released into a house where the same things are asked and somebody lives in you who wants them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–25 — The Law and the Ongoing Conflict
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means!" Paul's defence of the law is passionate and complete: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (v. 12). The problem is not the law; the problem is sin — which used the good commandment as a foothold for its own agenda. When the commandment "you shall not covet" entered Paul's consciousness, it awakened the very covetousness it forbade. Not because the commandment was defective, but because sin is so pervasive that even the confrontation with prohibition provokes the prohibited desire.

The famous passage beginning in v. 14 — "For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate" — is the most honest description of the experience of indwelling sin in all of Scripture. Whether Paul is describing pre-conversion or post-conversion experience has been debated exhaustively. The weight of the evidence — the delight in God's law (v. 22), the willing of the good (v. 18), the self-awareness of the conflict — points to the regenerate person, not the unregenerate.

The climax of the chapter is both a cry and a triumph: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!" (vv. 24–25). The cry of anguish is honest; the gratitude that follows is immediate. Paul does not wallow in the wretchedness. He knows the answer. He has the answer. The very struggle he describes is the evidence that the Spirit is at work — because the person without the Spirit does not experience this conflict; she simply does what sin desires. The one who hates what she does and loves the law of God in her inner being is alive in Christ, even while she wars against the flesh.

Two things in the middle of the chapter carry the argument and should not be lost. The first is Paul’s conclusion at v. 13, which is the point of the whole autobiographical section: the law did not kill him, sin did — working death in him through what is good, so that sin might be shown to be sin and might become sinful beyond measure. That is the purpose of the exercise. The law was given partly to provoke sin into the open, where its true character could be seen; a disease that is invisible cannot be treated, and sin’s worst feature is exactly its capacity to use a holy commandment as its instrument. The second is the image at v. 23, which supplies the vocabulary for everything Christians have said since about the inner conflict: another law waging war against the law of the mind, and taking the man captive. Paul does not describe an imbalance or a tension. He describes a campaign, with two sides, prisoners, and territory — which is why the chapter can end in a cry rather than a conclusion.
verseByVerse.theology:
Indwelling Sin and the Doctrine of Sanctification

Romans 7:14–25 is the biblical foundation for the Reformed doctrine that sanctification is a lifelong struggle, not a crisis experience of eradication. John Wesley and the Holiness tradition argued for the possibility of entire sanctification — the complete eradication of the sinful nature — in this life. The Reformed tradition, following Augustine, Luther, and Calvin, has insisted that indwelling sin remains until glorification. This is not defeatism but realism: the Christian who understands this will not be surprised or destroyed by the ongoing struggle. She will be equipped to fight it with the means God has provided — the Word, prayer, the sacraments, the community of believers — rather than pretending it does not exist or despairing when it does.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The experience Paul describes in vv. 14–25 had a parallel in Stoic philosophy — Ovid's famous line: "I see the better and approve it; I follow the worse." But the Stoic solution (more reason, more discipline, more willpower) is precisely what Paul finds inadequate. The problem is not ignorance; it is the power of indwelling sin that reason alone cannot overcome. The solution is not philosophy; it is the liberating power of "Jesus Christ our Lord" (v. 25). Now: The Christian who has experienced Romans 7 — who has tried harder, prayed more, committed afresh, and still found the same sins returning — is not a failure. She is a normal Christian, living in the honest tension between the new self and the old, between the delight in God's law and the drag of indwelling sin. The answer is not more effort; it is more Christ. Chapter 8 is the answer to chapter 7.

verseByVerse.quote: What then shall we say? That the law is sin? By no means! Yet if it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. For I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet." But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The law is sin? By no means!” — the law is holy (v. 12), but it has an unexpected and alarming effect: it arouses what it forbids. Sin, Paul says, “seizes an opportunity” (aphormē — a military bridgehead) through the commandment. Prohibition awakens desire; the forbidden becomes attractive precisely because it is forbidden. This is not the law’s fault — it is sin’s cunning. The law reveals the command; sin uses the knowledge of the command as the occasion for transgression. Apart from the law, sin “lies dead” — not absent, but dormant, unexposed.

Notice that Paul is answering a question his own argument has created, and he knows it. He has just said the law arouses sinful passions (v. 5) and that we have been released from it (v. 6). Any fair reader will draw the obvious inference — then the law is the problem — and Paul reaches for his strongest denial and then spends nineteen verses defending the law he has just described as a captor. Very few writers are willing to state their opponent’s case that clearly before answering it.

And the commandment he picks to illustrate with is not accidental. Of the ten he could have chosen, he takes the tenth — you shall not covet — and it is the only one of them that nobody can be observed breaking. You can be seen stealing, or committing adultery, or dishonouring a parent; there are witnesses and there is evidence. Coveting happens entirely inside a man, and this is the commandment that had exposed Paul. Elsewhere he says that as to righteousness under the law he was blameless (Philippians 3:6) — and he means it. He had the other nine. It was the tenth that got in past his defences, because it is the one that asks what you want.

Then the military word, which the entry above rightly flags and which repays a moment. Aphormē was the term for a base of operations — the bridgehead from which a campaign is launched. So sin does not merely react to the commandment; it establishes a position on it and operates from there. Which is a description of something everyone has experienced and few have named: the prohibition itself becomes the staging ground. A thing you had not thought about for months becomes interesting within an hour of being told it is off limits.

The mechanism is so ordinary that it hardly needs arguing. A wet-paint sign creates an impulse to touch that did not exist a moment before. Tell a child not to put beans up his nose and you have introduced a possibility he had not previously entertained. Every parent knows the law of the forbidden shelf. And it would be comfortable to conclude from this that prohibitions are unwise — until you notice what it actually reveals. The wet paint is not the problem. The child is not corrupted by the sign. What the sign does is bring into daylight something that was in him all along and had simply never been provoked into showing itself.

Which is exactly Paul’s point in the last clause: apart from the law, sin lies dead. Not absent — dormant. And that is the most unsettling sentence in the paragraph, because it means that a quiet conscience is not necessarily evidence of a clean heart. It may only be evidence that nothing has yet come along to wake what is sleeping. Most of us have a high opinion of our own patience until we live with the right person, and of our own honesty until real money is involved.

So here is a test, and it uses the tenth commandment the way Paul used it. Do not audit your behaviour; you will pass. Audit your wanting. Over the last week, what did you find yourself wishing you had — not merely admiring, but wanting in a way that made your own life look thinner when you thought about it? Somebody’s marriage, their ease, their platform, their health, their children, the fact that things seem to work out for them. Nobody sees that and nobody can charge you with it. Which is precisely why it is the commandment Paul reached for when he wanted to explain how a blameless man discovered he was lost.

And note where this leaves the law: entirely exonerated, and more dangerous than ever. It is holy, and it did not create the appetite; it walked into the house and turned the lights on. What Paul is describing is not a defect in God’s commandment but a diagnosis of what we are — creatures in whom even a perfect word from God can be turned into a bridgehead by an enemy who was already inside.

verseByVerse.quote: I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin came alive and I died. The very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whether Paul describes his own pre-conversion experience, Israel’s experience at Sinai, or Adam’s experience in the garden (or all three simultaneously), the pattern is clear: arrival of the commandment meant death for the one who transgressed it. The commandment “promised life” — this was its design (Leviticus 18:5, “keep my statutes and live”). But sin intercepted the promise and turned the instrument of life into the occasion of death. This is the tragedy of the law’s relationship to fallen humanity: the perfect tool in the hands of a broken workman.

The entry above is right to leave the identification open, and it is worth seeing why all three readings keep suggesting themselves — because the sentence has the shape of a story that has been told more than once. I was once alive apart from the law; the commandment came; I died. That is precisely the shape of Eden: a man in a garden with no prohibition in sight, then a single commandment, then death arriving exactly as promised. It is also the shape of Israel: a people brought out of Egypt on sheer mercy, then Sinai, then a golden calf before Moses was down the mountain. And it is the shape of a devout boy’s own life, secure in a religious home until the tenth commandment reached the place where he actually lived. Paul is not being vague. He is telling one story that has happened at every scale at which it could happen.

And the phrase I was once alive should not be read as a claim that he was genuinely safe. He is describing how it felt, not how it was — which is exactly the condition of every unawakened person. Nobody who has not met the commandment in earnest believes himself to be in danger. That is not because he has examined the matter and reached a conclusion; it is because the question has never been put to him with any force. There is a kind of peace which is simply the absence of information.

Then the sentence turns on four words that ought to stop us: sin came alive and I died. Two things swapped places. Sin had been lying dormant (v. 8) and now it is the living party; the man who thought himself alive turns out to be the corpse. The arrival of the commandment did not change the amount of sin in him. It changed which of the two was standing up.

And then the tragedy in verse 10, which Paul states almost flatly: the very commandment that promised life proved to be death to me. Note the last two words. He does not say the commandment is death; he says it proved to be death to him, and the qualification is the whole defence of the law that this chapter is conducting. The same word that was life to a man who kept it is death to a man who cannot — not because it changed, but because he was what he was.

Which is worth a picture, because the principle is not confined to religion. The same sunlight that ripens fruit blisters skin that cannot take it; the same water that a swimmer moves through kills a man who cannot swim. Nothing is wrong with the light or the water. Something is wrong with what meets it. And this is why every attempt to fix the human problem by improving the instruction has failed: the trouble was never the quality of the instruction.

So here is a test, and it is really the question this passage exists to ask. When did the commandment come to you? Not when did you first hear the Ten Commandments — most readers could recite several by nine years old. When did one of them find you: when did a sentence of God’s stop being a general statement about right and wrong and become an accusation with your name on it? Some people can date it. Others found it happening slowly over a year. But a Christian who cannot recall anything of the kind — who has always regarded himself as broadly all right and has never been genuinely alarmed by anything God has said — should consider whether he is standing in the first half of verse 9 rather than the second. That position feels considerably better and is the more dangerous of the two.

And take the strange comfort in the sequence, because it runs the opposite way to what we would design. In this verse, dying is progress. The man who is alive at the start is lost, and the man who is dead at the end is the one who will be writing about grace for the next nine chapters. God’s ordinary way of saving people is to let a commandment kill them first — which is what the law was for, and why the man who has never been wounded by it has not yet been helped by it.

verseByVerse.quote: For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The echo of Genesis 3 is unmistakable: “sin… deceived me”. The serpent used God’s prohibition to entice; sin uses God’s commandment to destroy. But the culprit is sin, not the law. The law is “holy and righteous and good” — Paul is emphatic and threefold. The problem is not in the physician’s prescription; the problem is in the patient’s condition. To blame the law for producing death is to blame the mirror for the ugliness it reflects.

Follow the Genesis echo further, because it is more exact than a general resemblance. Eve’s own account of what happened was the serpent deceived me, and I ate (Genesis 3:13), and Paul uses the same verb. So watch the method, since it has not changed in the intervening millennia. The serpent did not begin by denying the commandment; he began by misquoting it — did God really say you shall not eat of any tree? — inflating the prohibition until God looked mean. Then he impugned the motive: God knows that when you eat you will be like him, which is to say, he is holding out on you. And only then the flat denial: you will not surely die.

Every one of those three moves is available today and all three are still in service. The commandment is exaggerated until it sounds like deprivation for its own sake. The Giver’s motive is questioned — he is restrictive, he does not want you happy, other people manage this perfectly well. And the consequence is quietly denied: not that judgment is disproved, only that it recedes into the theoretical and stops being the sort of thing that will actually happen to you.

Which locates the real damage precisely, and it is not where we usually look. Sin’s primary work is not to overpower you; it is to misinform you. Nobody sins while clear-sighted about what he is doing and what it will cost. The moment of temptation always contains a lie, and the lie is not usually about the thing itself but about the arithmetic — that this will satisfy, that it will not cost much, that you will be able to stop, that God is being unreasonable. Which is why the counter to temptation is so often simply telling yourself the truth, out loud if necessary, since what is being attacked is your information.

And then verse 12, which is a remarkable thing for Paul to write at this point. He has just spent five verses describing how the commandment was used to kill him. The obvious conclusion lies ready to hand — and he refuses it, in the strongest terms he has: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good. Three adjectives where one would have done. He is not conceding the point grudgingly; he is defending the law with more warmth than he has used about almost anything else in the letter.

That is worth pausing on, because it is a rare quality of mind. Paul has been genuinely damaged by his encounter with the commandment; he calls himself dead as a result. And he will not allow his own experience to be evidence against God. Most of us do the reverse instinctively — we take the thing that hurt us and conclude something about God from it, and the conclusion always flatters us. Here is a man who was wounded, who says so plainly, and who then says the instrument that wounded him was holy and righteous and good.

Which gives a test, and it is a searching one. Think of a commandment of God that has cost you something — the one that has stood in the way of what you wanted, or that you have failed at so often you have stopped hoping. Now ask what you actually think of that commandment when you are honest. Is it holy, righteous and good? Or is there a quiet, unexamined sense that it is excessive, that God was asking too much, that a reasonable God would have made an exception for your case? That resentment is not usually stated even to oneself. But it is the serpent’s second move, still working, and it lives in a great many believers who would sign every doctrinal statement they were handed.

So the verdict of the passage is not that the law is dangerous but that we are. The commandment came into the world of a fallen man, and something in him took it, twisted it, and used it as a weapon against him. And the extraordinary thing about Paul is that he can describe that whole process, name himself as the casualty, and finish the sentence by calling the weapon good.

verseByVerse.quote: Did that which is good, then, bring death to me? By no means! It was sin, producing death in me through what is good, in order that sin might be shown to be sin, and through the commandment might become sinful beyond measure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law did not cause death; sin hijacked the law to produce death — and in doing so, exposed itself as sin. The law’s function in this process is diagnostic and revelatory: it makes sin “sinful beyond measure”, forces it into the open, strips away the excuse of ignorance. The commandment is the instrument by which sin is unmasked in its true character: not mere human weakness, but active, cunning rebellion against the holy God. The law that cannot save has an indispensable role: it shows us exactly what we need saving from.

This verse is the conclusion the whole autobiographical section has been building toward, and it answers a question that ought to trouble a thoughtful reader. If God knew the law would provoke sin rather than restrain it, why give it? Paul does not say it was a miscalculation. He says it was the purpose: in order that sin might be shown to be sin.

So the law was given, among other things, to make the disease declare itself. And the reason is straightforward once stated: a sickness that produces no symptoms is not thereby harmless — it is merely untreatable, because nobody goes to a physician for a condition he cannot feel. The cruellest illnesses are the silent ones. What the commandment did was force a hidden thing to produce symptoms, and the symptoms were violent, and that is why the patient finally went for help.

Then the phrase Paul finishes with, which is stronger than English easily carries: sin becomes, through the commandment, sinful beyond measure. The word is the one behind our hyperbole — excessive, past all proportion. And notice how sin earns that description. Not by producing something spectacular; the passage has been about a man wanting things he should not want. Sin becomes sinful beyond measure by what it is willing to use. It took the holiest thing God had given — a good commandment, from a good God, designed for life — and turned it into an instrument of death. That is the measure of the thing we are dealing with.

Which is worth stating plainly, because it corrects the picture most people carry. We tend to imagine sin as weakness: appetite, lapse, the failure of a good intention. Paul is describing something with strategy. It waits, it seizes opportunities, it deceives, and it is prepared to take the best material available and repurpose it. Anything can be conscripted. Religion can be. Doctrine can be — a man may use accurate theology to avoid God, and does. Even repentance can be, when it becomes a performance that manages guilt without ever reaching the thing that caused it.

So here is a test, and it goes at the thing this verse exposes. Ask what good thing in your life is currently being used against you. Not a bad thing — a genuinely good one. Your work, which is a gift, and which has become the place you go to avoid a difficulty at home. Your theological knowledge, which is real, and which has become a way of being superior to other Christians. Your service, which helps people, and which has become how you avoid asking whether anybody knows you. Sin does not need bad material. It prefers good material, because good material is not inspected.

And that is why this apparently technical verse is one of the most useful in the letter. It explains why serious Christians are so often blindsided — why the man who has successfully fought an obvious sin for twenty years is taken from an angle he never watched. He was guarding the disreputable ground. The enemy was working through the commandment.

Then take the comfort at the end of it, because the verse is not finally about how bad things are. God’s purpose in all this was revelation, not destruction. He let sin have the commandment and use it, precisely so that a man could see what was in him and stop negotiating with it. Nobody has ever been saved from a problem he did not believe he had. The chapter is about to end in a cry for rescue — and that cry is the whole point of the exercise, because it is the first thing this man has said that could be answered.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am of the flesh, sold under sin. For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Romans 7:14–25 is one of the most debated passages in Scripture — and one of the most comforting. Every reader wonders: is Paul describing his experience before or after conversion? Some have read it as his pre-Christian struggle under the law, since Romans 6 has declared the believer “dead to sin” and “freed from sin”. But this reading cannot account for what the person in vv. 14–25 actually does: he delights in God’s law with his inner self (v. 22), which is the language of the renewed heart; an unconverted person does not delight in God’s law but is hostile to it (8:7). And the cry of v. 24 — “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” — is not the cry of someone who is comfortable in sin; it is the anguish of someone with a new nature who hates what the old nature keeps doing. Only the regenerate person grieves over indwelling sin this way. The unregenerate person simply lives in it without distress.

Calvin, Luther, Owen, Lloyd-Jones, and Sproul all read this as Paul’s ongoing Christian experience — not his worst moments or his spiritual low tide, but the structural reality of a believer who still lives in unredeemed flesh even while possessing a renewed heart. This is the experience that gives the passage its staggering pastoral power: “I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.” Anyone who has genuinely tried to live for God knows exactly what Paul is describing. “Sold under sin” — a slave owned by a master he despises — captures the captivity that remains even after justification. The good news is that the chapter does not end in v. 25a with defeat; it ends in 8:1 with “no condemnation”. The struggle is real; the verdict is grace.

Since the entry above commits to a reading, honesty requires stating the strongest case against it, because a reader who consults other commentaries will meet it and should not be ambushed. There are two real difficulties. The first is the phrase sold under sin (v. 14) — which is very hard language for a man Paul has just described as freed from sin (6:18, 22), and it is the single strongest argument on the other side. The second is the tense in this very chapter: while we were living in the flesh (v. 5), past tense, describing a condition left behind — and then vv. 14–25 in the present tense describing what looks like exactly that condition.

Those are not trivial, and the answers are not knockdown. On the first: Paul is describing the flesh — the unredeemed part of him, which really is sold under sin and will be until it is buried — rather than his standing before God, and he says as much in the next breath by distinguishing what he wills from what his flesh does. On the second: the present tenses run unbroken for twelve verses in a letter by a writer who has just used the past tense deliberately, which is difficult to explain if he has moved back to his pre-Christian life; and the delight of v. 22 remains the immovable obstacle for the other reading, since 8:7 says flatly that the unconverted mind does not and cannot submit to God’s law.

But here is the thing that matters most pastorally, and it should be said plainly so that nobody is left hanging on a disputed point: the comfort of this passage survives either reading. If Paul is describing the Christian, then your experience of failure is normal and you are not disqualified. If he is describing life under law before Christ, then the passage is telling you what you have been rescued from and where to look instead of at yourself — and the answer in both cases is the same, arrives in the same sentence, and is a Person rather than a technique. Nobody who takes either view is left without help.

Now the sentence itself, because it is the most exact description of a common experience in all literature: I do not understand my own actions. Not I regret them; not I cannot justify them. He cannot make sense of them. And that is the honest report of anybody who has fought a besetting sin: the strangest feature is not that it is powerful but that it is unintelligible. You did the thing you had genuinely resolved not to do, for reasons that seemed adequate at the time and evaporate on inspection, and afterwards you cannot reconstruct why. The man in this verse is not making excuses. He is baffled.

And notice the strange grammar of the desire. He does not do what he wants — which means he wants the right thing. That single word rules out a great deal. This is not a man making a show of reluctance while enjoying his sin; the wanting is real, and it is the source of the anguish. A man who wanted only the wrong thing would have no conflict and nothing to report.

So here is the test, and it turns the passage into a diagnosis rather than a mirror for despair. Ask what your sin does to you afterwards. If it produces the bafflement of this verse — why did I do that, I did not even want it — then you are experiencing what Paul is describing, and the experience is evidence of two parties rather than one. There is someone in you who wanted otherwise. That someone did not exist before God put him there, and his presence is the reason the whole thing hurts.

One guard, because this passage has been misused in both directions. It is not a licence: a man who quotes Romans 7 to excuse a sin he has stopped fighting has taken a description of anguish and used it as a permission slip, and the anguish is precisely what he no longer has. And it is not a ceiling: Paul does not say the Christian life never improves — chapter 6 has just insisted that it does, chapter 8 is about to describe the Spirit putting sin to death, and obedience compounds over years (see on 6:19–20). This chapter describes the floor of Christian experience, the ground you may find yourself on at any point and are not thereby lost. It does not describe the ceiling.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is an argument in the self-division: if I do what I do not want, my very unwillingness is a testimony to the goodness of the law I am violating. The conscience that feels guilt is itself a witness to the moral order it is breaking. And the distinction between “I” and “sin that dwells within me” is not an evasion of responsibility but a diagnosis: there is an alien power operating within the self, a power that is not the true self but that the true self cannot expel. This is the experience of indwelling sin — not the whole person, but a power the person has not yet been able to defeat.

The argument in verse 16 is quietly brilliant and easy to walk past. Paul is still defending the law, and here is his final piece of evidence: my own failure proves the law is good. Because if I do what I do not want, then my wanting is on the law’s side. My conscience has cast its vote for the commandment even while my hands were voting against it. So even the sinner’s misery is testimony — the law is not condemned by the man who breaks it, it is endorsed by his shame.

Which is why guilt, uncomfortable as it is, is a form of evidence rather than merely a form of suffering. It is the sound of a moral order being acknowledged by somebody who has just contravened it. A man with no sense of the law’s goodness feels nothing after breaking it and has nothing to report.

Then verse 17, which is the sentence people find alarming: it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. Read carelessly that is the oldest excuse in the world, and the entry above is right to say it is not one. But the guard needs stating in the strongest possible terms, because this verse has genuinely been used as a dodge. Paul is not saying it was not me. He has just spent an entire chapter accepting responsibility — I do, I practise, I keep on doing — and he never once asks to be excused. If you have ever caught yourself saying, in effect, that was not the real me about something you did last Tuesday, you have not found this verse; you have found its counterfeit. The tell is simple: Paul’s sentence produces anguish and a cry for deliverance. The excuse produces relief and no cry at all.

So what is he doing? He is making a distinction between what he is and what is in him — and the word he chooses for the latter is worth having: sin dwells in me. It is the word for taking up residence, having an address, being a settled inhabitant rather than a visitor. Which is exactly right, and exactly uncomfortable. Sin in a Christian is not an occasional intruder who breaks a window and leaves. It has a room. It has been there for years, knows the layout, and is not paying rent.

And that image is more helpful than the tidy alternative, because it explains something otherwise baffling: why sin in a believer so often looks like a habit rather than a decision. A lodger does not need to be invited each time. He simply moves about the house, and long after you have stopped wanting him there you will find that the arrangement carries on out of sheer familiarity. Which is why Paul does not say expel it, in this chapter, and does not promise that you can. He says something about it is not the real occupier of the house, and then he cries out for somebody stronger to come and deal with it.

Now the pastoral use of the distinction, and this is what it is actually for. It gives a Christian a way to hold two things that otherwise tear him apart: I did that and that is not who I am. Most believers can only manage one at a time. Hold the first alone and you get despair — I did it, therefore that is what I am, therefore nothing has changed. Hold the second alone and you get evasion — that is not who I am, therefore it does not really count. Paul holds both in a single sentence: full responsibility, and an identity that is not defined by the failure. The first keeps you honest; the second keeps you standing.

So here is a test, and it distinguishes the true use of this verse from the counterfeit cleanly. After your last serious failure, which sentence did you arrive at? That was not really me, so there is no need to make anything of it — that is the dodge, and it always ends the conversation. Or that was me, and it is also not what I am, and I want it out of my house — which does not end the conversation but starts one, and the next thing it produces is a cry. Paul’s version of this doctrine has a prayer at the end of it. The counterfeit has a shrug.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” — Paul carefully qualifies: not in me as a whole, but in my flesh — the unredeemed, sin-corrupted nature that persists even in the believer. The desire is present; the ability is absent. This is the frustration of the regenerate conscience trapped in unredeemed flesh: seeing clearly what ought to be done, willing it genuinely, and yet finding the performance elusive. Lloyd-Jones noted that this description is impossible for an unregenerate person — only the regenerate person has the spiritual understanding to see the gap between what is and what ought to be.

Notice the correction Paul makes to himself mid-sentence, because it is the most careful thing in the chapter. He begins nothing good dwells in me — and then stops, and adds four words: that is, in my flesh. He will not let the first half stand alone. If he had stopped there he would have said something untrue about a Christian, because something good does dwell in a believer; the Spirit does, and the delight of v. 22 does. So he narrows it. The statement is about the flesh, and the flesh is not the whole of him.

That correction is worth copying, because a great many Christians make the sentence Paul refused to make. There is nothing good in me at all. It sounds humble and it is not accurate, and the difference matters pastorally. A man who believes there is nothing good in him anywhere has no basis for hope, no evidence to reason from, and no explanation for the fact that he minds about his sin. Paul is precise: the flesh is unimproved and unimprovable; the man is not the flesh.

And a word on flesh, because English misleads. It does not mean the body, and it does not mean that physical appetites are the problem while the mind is clean. The vice lists in this letter are full of pride, envy, gossip and malice — sins with no bodily component at all. Flesh means human nature organised without God: the whole self as it operated before grace arrived, which is why a thoroughly ascetic man can be entirely fleshly and a man enjoying his dinner need not be.

Then the sentence that names the condition exactly: I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. Two things are true at once, and both need saying. The desire is real — this is not a man pretending to want holiness. And the ability is absent, which is the discovery that undoes every self-improvement scheme ever devised. Most moral advice assumes the missing ingredient is wanting, and therefore supplies motivation: consider the consequences, remember who you are, try harder. Paul has the motivation. He is drowning anyway.

Which is why the honest Christian recognises this verse instantly and the merely religious person does not. You have to have made the attempt in earnest to know that earnestness is not enough. Nobody discovers his own inability by reading about it; he discovers it on the fifth occasion of resolving the same thing with complete sincerity and failing by Thursday.

And verse 19 adds the detail that makes it grim: the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing. Not what I did once. The tense is continuous — this is a pattern, a returning, a thing with a history. Paul is not describing a bad week. He is describing the shape of a lifetime, which is why this passage is either the most depressing in the New Testament or the most liberating, depending entirely on what comes next.

So here is the test, and it is diagnostic rather than accusing. Take the sin you return to. Now ask which of these two is actually true of you: I do not really want to stop, or I want to stop and cannot. Be honest, because the two require different medicine. If it is the first, the problem is not ability but affection, and the answer is not more effort but repentance — you are enjoying it and have not yet decided otherwise. If it is the second, you are exactly where verse 18 is, and the news is better than you think: your wanting is not nothing. It is the strongest evidence in this chapter that God has already been at work in you, because that desire was not there before and you did not manufacture it.

And note what Paul does not do here, because it is the most important omission in the chapter. He does not offer a technique. There is no method, no seven steps, no promise that the ability will arrive if the desire is sufficiently sincere. He states the problem in its full hopelessness and lets it stand — for five more verses — because the answer to this condition is not a better strategy but a person, and he wants you to have exhausted every alternative before he names him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me. So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The observation crystallises into a general “law” (principle, pattern): evil is always close at hand when the good is desired. The presence of the desire for good does not displace the presence of evil — they coexist in painful proximity within the same person. This is the experience that moves the passage toward its climax of desperation: not occasional failure but a structural condition, a law as reliable as gravity. The only exit from this condition is not self-improvement but divine deliverance — which is exactly where the argument arrives in v. 25 and chapter 8.

The word Paul reaches for is the important thing here, and the entry above is right to flag it. He calls it a law — not a tendency, not a weakness, not a bad patch. In this letter that word has meant the Mosaic law throughout, and he now uses it in the sense we use when we speak of the law of gravity: a regularity you can count on, which operates whether or not you are attending to it, and which does not make exceptions for people who are trying hard.

And what he says is regular is this: when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand. Note the timing, because it is the whole observation. Not evil is always around, which is obvious and would hardly need saying. The evil arrives when the good is wanted. The intention and the opposition appear together, and the second is summoned by the first.

Which is worth stating plainly, because almost every Christian has experienced it and very few have been told to expect it. You resolve to pray more; the following week is the busiest in a year and you are more distracted at prayer than you have been in months. You determine to be patient with a particular person; that person becomes markedly more irritating within about thirty-six hours. You decide to take your marriage in hand, and the next fortnight supplies more friction than the previous six. Nobody warned you that the decision itself would be the trigger, so you conclude that the resolve was insincere, or that God is not helping, or that you imagined the whole thing.

Paul says it is a law. It is what happens. The moment a man moves toward the good, something moves to meet him — and the fact that it happened is not evidence that the movement was false. It is evidence that it was real. Nothing opposes a resolution nobody intends to keep.

So take the encouragement, because it is genuinely available here and it is the opposite of what the verse first sounds like. If your Christian life were merely a matter of drifting, you would meet very little resistance; drifting is downhill and nothing contests it. The friction you feel is the friction of moving against something. A man walking with the current is not aware of the river.

And the guard on the other side, so this is not made into a superstition: not every difficulty that follows a good decision is a spiritual assault, and reading life that way makes people strange and frightened. Sometimes the week really was busy. Sometimes the person really is having a hard time and it has nothing to do with you. Paul is describing a pattern, not issuing a decoder for events, and a Christian who begins interpreting every inconvenience as warfare will exhaust himself and misjudge his neighbours.

So here is the test, and it is about expectation rather than performance. Think of the last time you made a genuine resolve about something spiritual and it collapsed within a week or two. Now ask what conclusion you drew. Most of us conclude something about ourselves — that we are not serious, that we never change, that there is no point starting again. Verse 21 offers a different reading of the same evidence: the collapse followed the resolve because that is what this law does, and the right response is not to stop resolving but to stop being surprised. A man who expects the counter-attack is not defeated by it. He is merely inconvenienced by something he was told about in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delight in the law of God, in my inner being, but I see in my members another law waging war against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that dwells in my members.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The inner conflict is now described as warfare: two laws (principles) in combat within the same person. The inner person delights in God’s law — this is the deepest self, the self created and renewed by God. But the members (the body as the site of physical desire and habit) house another law that wages war and takes captive. “Makes me captive” — the language of a prisoner of war: defeated, bound, carried off. The delight of the inner person is real; so is the captivity. This is not hypocrisy but the genuine anguish of a divided person.

Verse 22 is the hinge of the entire debate about this chapter, and it is worth seeing why. I delight in the law of God, in my inner being. Not I approve of it, not I concede that it is right — I delight in it. That is the language of Psalm 1 and Psalm 119, the vocabulary of a man who loves what God has said. And it is precisely what the next chapter says the unconverted cannot do: the mind set on the flesh is hostile to God, for it does not submit to God’s law, indeed it cannot (8:7). Whatever else is disputed here, the man of verse 22 is not that man.

Then verse 23 supplies the military vocabulary that Christians have used ever since, and the two verbs are worth separating. The other law is waging war — a campaign, sustained, with strategy and objectives, not a series of accidents. And it is making me captive, which is the word for what happens to a soldier after a battle is lost: taken alive, bound, marched off in the direction the victor chooses. Paul does not say he is tempted. He says he is taken prisoner, which is a considerably more humiliating admission and a far more accurate one.

And notice that the fighting is located in his members — hands, eyes, tongue, the body with its trained reflexes. The delight is in the inner being; the defeat happens where the habits live. Which is exactly the shape of most Christian failure. Nobody sins because his theology collapsed that morning. The convictions were intact throughout, and were simply not where the battle was being fought.

Which yields something practical, because if the war is fought in the members then that is where the defences belong. It is why the New Testament so often tells people to do physical, unspiritual-sounding things: flee (1 Corinthians 6:18), cut it off (Matthew 5:30), make no provision for the flesh (Romans 13:14). Those are not commands about the inner life. They are commands about your hands, your feet, and your evening. A man who prays earnestly about a temptation and takes no practical steps to make it harder has fortified the wrong position entirely.

Now the pastoral weight of these two verses together, which is where they are usually needed. A Christian who reads this passage and recognises himself in the captivity often concludes that the delight of v. 22 must therefore be false — that a man genuinely delighting in God’s law would not keep losing like this. Paul puts both in the same sentence and does not treat them as contradictory. The delight is real. The captivity is real. And the one does not cancel the other, because they are happening in different places: one in the inner being, one in the members.

So here is the test, and it is aimed at the reader who suspects his own delight. Do not ask whether you always obey; verse 23 has already answered that. Ask what you feel about the commandment you keep breaking. When you consider the standard you have failed — not the failure, the standard — is there anything in you that says that is good, and I wish I were like that? An unconverted man does not think that. He thinks the standard is unreasonable, or irrelevant, or somebody else’s business. If you find yourself agreeing with the very law that is currently defeating you, that agreement is not nothing. It is the deepest thing in you, and it was put there.

Which is why the chapter can end as it does. A prisoner of war has not changed sides. He is in enemy hands, and he is still loyal, and everything now depends on whether anybody is coming for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Wretched man that I am!” — the cry of genuine desperation, the bankruptcy of every human program for self-improvement. The question is not “what will deliver me?” but “who?” — deliverance requires a person, a deliverer, not a technique or a discipline. And the answer erupts before the argument demands it: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” The deliverer has come. Chapter 8 will unfold what this looks like; but the doxology breaks out here because the gospel cannot be contained. The summary of v. 25b acknowledges that the conflict described is real and ongoing — but the outcome is certain, because the deliverer is named.

The word translated wretched is worth having, because it is not self-pity. It describes a person worn out by hardship — battered, exhausted by a struggle that has gone on too long. The risen Christ uses it of the church at Laodicea, who did not know it applied to them (Revelation 3:17). Paul knows. And that is the difference between the man in this verse and almost everybody else: he has stopped explaining himself.

Then the phrase this body of death, which is more vivid than it looks. There is an old story, repeated by commentators for centuries, that certain ancient tyrants punished a murderer by binding the corpse of his victim to him — face to face, hand to hand — and leaving him to carry it until the decay killed him. Whether or not Paul had that in mind, the picture is exactly right for what he has described: something dead, strapped to a living man, which he cannot reach round to untie and cannot outrun. He does not ask to be improved. He asks to be delivered, which is what you ask when the problem is attached to you.

And the entry above is right that the interrogative is the whole thing. Who will deliver me. Not what — not which discipline, which method, which conference, which resolution. By this point in the chapter every technique has been tried and reported on: he knows the law, he approves the law, he delights in the law, he wills the good, and he is still being carried off. There is nothing left to attempt. The only remaining category of answer is a rescuer.

Then the thing that ought to arrest every reader: the answer comes in the very next breath. There is no interval. Paul does not describe a period of waiting, a dark night, a process of qualifying. Cry and answer are separated by a question mark. Which tells you what the chapter is finally about — not the length of the misery but the nearness of the deliverer.

And notice the form of the answer, because it is not what the question asked for. He asked who will deliver me, future tense, and the reply is thanks be to God — gratitude, in the present, for something already true. He does not say Jesus will rescue me one day. He gives thanks, which is what a man does when the rescue has happened and he is looking back at it.

Which brings the last clause, and it is the sentence that keeps this passage honest. After the doxology, Paul does not announce that the war is over. He restates it: with the mind I serve the law of God, with the flesh the law of sin. That order matters. A lesser writer, having reached a triumphant note, would have stopped there and left the impression that the struggle was finished. Paul deliberately puts the tension after the thanksgiving, which is his way of saying that the deliverance is certain and not yet complete. You may be rescued and still be carrying the body. Chapter 8 opens on that same man, and its first word to him is that there is now no condemnation.

So here is the test, and it is the one this whole chapter has been constructing. Ask what you have been asking for. If your prayers about your besetting sin are essentially requests for assistance — help me to try harder, give me strength to keep the resolution, make me more disciplined — then you are still asking what. The prayer of this verse is different in kind. It is not a request for improved equipment; it is the cry of a man who has given up on himself entirely and wants a person to come and get him. Most Christians do not pray that prayer until they have exhausted the other kind, which is exactly why God so often lets them be exhausted.

And that is the design of the chapter. It was never written to describe a problem.
